subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Simon Commission of 1927–1930.
parts.answer: A commission of seven British MPs led by Sir John Simon, appointed in 1927 to review the 1919 reforms; it had no Indian member; it was met by 'Simon Go Back' protests and black flags when it arrived in 1928; its report (1930) proposed responsible government in the provinces and ending dyarchy there, and kept separate electorates.
parts.working: 1 mark per accurate point, up to 4: appointed 1927 / to review the working of the 1919 Act; led by Sir John Simon; seven members, all British MPs; no Indian member; arrived 1928; boycotted by Congress and part of the Muslim League; 'Simon Go Back' protests / black flags; report 1930 recommended ending dyarchy in provinces / provincial responsible government; separate electorates retained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Simon Commission was opposed by many Indian politicians.
parts.answer: It had no Indian members, which was seen as an insult because Indians were not allowed to decide their own constitution; Congress wanted dominion status at once and the commission only promised a review; it split the Muslim League (Jinnah's group boycotted, Shafi's group co-operated) because some Muslims feared their interests would be ignored; its report offered no clear move towards self-government at the centre.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: all-white membership seen as an insult; Indians denied a say in their own future; Congress demand for dominion status ignored; recommendations too limited (no responsible government at the centre); fear that minority interests would not be protected.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Delhi Muslim Proposals of 1927.
parts.answer: Muslim leaders meeting in Delhi (March 1927) offered to give up separate electorates in return for: one-third of the seats in the central legislature; Sindh to be separated from Bombay as a new province; reforms in the NWFP and Balochistan to bring them level with other provinces; representation according to population in Punjab and Bengal.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 4: 1927, Muslim leaders in Delhi; willing to accept joint electorates; on conditions: one-third of central seats; Sindh a separate province; reforms in NWFP and Balochistan; seats by population in Punjab and Bengal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Nehru Report (1928) was rejected by most Muslim leaders.
parts.answer: It proposed joint electorates, ending the separate electorates Muslims had held since 1909; it gave Muslims about a quarter of central seats instead of the one-third Jinnah asked for; it proposed a strong centre with residual powers, which would leave Muslim-majority provinces under a Hindu-majority centre; no seats were reserved for Muslims in Punjab and Bengal; Congress refused Jinnah's amendments at the Calcutta convention, which Jinnah called the 'parting of the ways'.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: joint electorates; less than one-third representation at the centre; strong unitary centre / residual powers to centre; no reserved seats in Muslim-majority provinces; Congress refusal of amendments.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four of Jinnah's Fourteen Points of 1929.
parts.answer: Any four, e.g.: a federal constitution with residual powers for the provinces; uniform autonomy for all provinces; one-third Muslim representation in the central legislature; separate electorates to continue; Sindh to be separated from Bombay; reforms in the NWFP and Balochistan; religious freedom for all communities; a fair share of government jobs for Muslims; protection of Muslim culture, education and language; one-third Muslim ministers in central and provincial cabinets.
parts.working: 1 mark for each accurately stated point, up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Jinnah produced the Fourteen Points.
parts.answer: As a reply to the Nehru Report, which had ignored Muslim demands; to set out the minimum safeguards Muslims needed in any future constitution; to unite the divided Muslim League behind one clear programme; to show the British that Muslims had their own demands that had to be considered at future talks.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: response to the Nehru Report; Congress rejected his amendments in 1928; protect Muslim rights as a minority; reunite the League (Shafi and Jinnah groups); state Muslim position before the Round Table Conferences.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the outcome of the First Round Table Conference (1930–1931).
parts.answer: It met in London from November 1930; Congress boycotted it because of the Civil Disobedience Movement; the princes, Muslim leaders and other groups agreed that India should become a federation; little else was decided without Congress, so the British released Gandhi and made the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931) to bring Congress to the next conference.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: London, Nov 1930–Jan 1931; Congress absent; princes agreed to join a federation; agreement on federal idea / responsible provincial government; no final settlement; led to Gandhi–Irwin Pact.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The Round Table Conferences (1930–1932) achieved nothing.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: the second conference broke down over the minorities question when Gandhi claimed to speak for all Indians; Congress boycotted the first and third conferences; no agreement was reached between communities, so the British had to impose the Communal Award. Disagree: the idea of an all-India federation was accepted; Muslim leaders (including Iqbal at the second conference) put their case directly; the discussions led to the White Paper of 1933 and the Government of India Act 1935, which gave provincial autonomy. Judgement: they failed to produce agreement between Indians, but they shaped the 1935 Act.
parts.working: Level marking (14 marks). L1 (1–2): general statements with no relevant detail. L2 (3–6): identifies or describes relevant factors without explaining them. L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). L4 (9–13): explains factors on both sides (more developed points and accurate detail move the answer up the band). L5 (14): as L4, plus a supported judgement that answers 'how far' (or 'was it the most important'). Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point; each needs explaining, not just stating) — Achieved nothing: Second RTC deadlocked over minorities; Gandhi's claim to speak for all Indians; Congress boycotted first and third conferences; no communal agreement, so the Communal Award was imposed. Achieved something: princes and Muslims accepted an all-India federation; provincial responsible government agreed in principle; Muslim case (Jinnah, Aga Khan, Iqbal at the third) heard directly; led to the 1933 White Paper and the Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy). A judgement must weigh the stated factor against the others, not just repeat the question.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Allama Iqbal's Allahabad Address of 1930.
parts.answer: Given in December 1930 as President of the Muslim League's annual session at Allahabad; Iqbal said Muslims were a separate nation with their own religion and culture; he proposed that Punjab, the NWFP, Sindh and Balochistan be joined into a single Muslim state; it could be self-governing within or outside the British Empire.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: date/place; Muslim League session; Muslims a separate nation; north-western provinces named; single state; self-government within or without the Empire; first major call for a Muslim homeland from the League platform.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Chaudhry Rahmat Ali's ideas were important to the Pakistan Movement.
parts.answer: In his 1933 pamphlet 'Now or Never' he coined the name 'Pakistan', formed from the names of the Muslim-majority regions, which gave the demand a name people could rally around; he argued Muslims were a separate nation who should not accept an Indian federation; although the League did not adopt his scheme at the time, his name and idea spread among students and later became the accepted name of the new state.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: coined the name Pakistan; popularised the separate-homeland idea among students (pamphlet published in England, 1933); rejected federation; built on Iqbal's address; later adopted for the state.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Communal Award of 1932.
parts.answer: Announced by the British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald in August 1932 because Indians could not agree on minority representation at the Round Table Conferences; it kept separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Europeans and others; it also gave the depressed classes (untouchables) separate electorates; Gandhi fasted against this, and the Poona Pact (1932) replaced it with reserved seats for the depressed classes within joint electorates.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many Muslims were not satisfied with the Communal Award.
parts.answer: Separate electorates were kept, but Muslims in Punjab and Bengal were not given a clear majority of seats in line with their share of the population, so they could not be sure of controlling their own provinces; the Award was a British decision rather than an agreement with Congress, so it did not solve communal mistrust; Muslim demands such as one-third of central seats were not settled by it.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Credit: no statutory majority in Punjab/Bengal; imposed not agreed; did not settle central representation; showed the failure of the RTCs.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the Government of India Act 1935.
parts.answer: Any four: a proposed all-India federation of British provinces and princely states (never put into effect because the princes did not join); dyarchy ended in the provinces, which got provincial autonomy with elected ministers; dyarchy introduced at the centre; Sindh separated from Bombay and Orissa from Bihar; Burma separated from India; a Federal Court set up; the franchise widened to millions more voters; separate electorates kept; the Governor-General and governors kept emergency powers.
parts.working: 1 mark per accurate feature, up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both Congress and the Muslim League criticised the 1935 Act.
parts.answer: Congress: it fell far short of dominion status; the Governor-General and governors kept wide emergency powers; the princes' nominees would be unelected in the federal legislature. Muslim League: the federal centre would be dominated by Hindus, threatening Muslim interests; the governors' powers meant provincial autonomy was limited; Jinnah called the federal scheme 'thoroughly rotten, fundamentally bad and totally unacceptable'. Both nevertheless fought the 1937 provincial elections under it.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Credit explained reasons from both parties; one party only max 5.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Lahore Resolution of March 1940.
parts.answer: Passed at the Muslim League session in Lahore (22–24 March 1940), moved by A. K. Fazlul Huq; it said that areas where Muslims were in a majority, in the north-west and east of India, should be grouped to form 'independent states'; the units would be autonomous and sovereign; minorities in these areas would have safeguards; it rejected any federal plan for India; it became known as the Pakistan Resolution.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Muslim League demanded a separate homeland in 1940.
parts.answer: Experience of Congress rule 1937–39 convinced many Muslims that they would be treated unfairly in a Hindu-majority India; Jinnah argued Muslims and Hindus were two separate nations with different religion, culture and history; the League needed a clear goal to rally Muslims after its poor 1937 election result; with war in Europe the British needed Muslim support, which gave the League a chance to press its claim.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: Congress ministries; Two-Nation Theory; need for a clear aim; wartime bargaining position; failure of federal schemes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the proposals of the Cripps Mission of 1942.
parts.answer: Sir Stafford Cripps came to India in March 1942; he offered dominion status after the Second World War; an elected body would draw up a new constitution after the war; any province could refuse to join the new union and stay out (this hinted at Pakistan); Indians would be given more places in the Viceroy's Council during the war, but Britain would keep control of defence.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Cripps Mission failed.
parts.answer: Congress wanted immediate self-government and control of defence, not promises for after the war; Gandhi called it a 'post-dated cheque' because Britain seemed to be losing the war in Asia; the Muslim League rejected it because Pakistan was not clearly accepted; Congress then launched the Quit India Movement (August 1942) instead of co-operating.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: Congress demands (immediate power, defence); fear of Japanese victory; League objection that Pakistan not conceded; opt-out clause disliked by Congress.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Simla Conference of 1945.
parts.answer: Called by Viceroy Lord Wavell in June 1945; he proposed a new Executive Council in which caste Hindus and Muslims would have equal numbers and all members except the Viceroy and the commander-in-chief would be Indian; the conference broke down because Jinnah insisted that the League alone should nominate all Muslim members, while Congress wanted to nominate a Muslim (Maulana Azad, its president); Wavell then called new elections.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the 1945–46 elections were important for the Muslim League.
parts.answer: The League won all the Muslim seats in the central legislature and a large majority of Muslim seats in the provinces, which proved it was the sole representative of India's Muslims; this destroyed Congress's claim to speak for all Indians; it strengthened Jinnah's position in talks with the British; it showed mass Muslim support for Pakistan, which the British could no longer ignore.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.
parts.answer: Three British cabinet ministers (Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps and A. V. Alexander) arrived in March 1946; their plan of May 1946 rejected a fully separate Pakistan; it proposed a union government in charge of foreign affairs, defence and communications; provinces would be placed in three groups: Hindu-majority provinces; Punjab, NWFP, Sindh and Balochistan; and Bengal and Assam; an interim government would be formed.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Nehru's statements in July 1946 were the main reason why the Cabinet Mission Plan failed.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: the League had accepted the plan in June 1946, but Nehru said Congress would not be bound by the grouping arrangements once in the Constituent Assembly; the League then withdrew its acceptance and called Direct Action Day (16 August 1946). Other factors: deep distrust between Congress and the League; disagreement over who should nominate Muslims to the interim government; the British invited Congress to form the interim government alone; the plan itself was complex and both sides read it differently; communal violence after August 1946 made co-operation impossible. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking (14 marks). L1 (1–2): general statements with no relevant detail. L2 (3–6): identifies or describes relevant factors without explaining them. L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). L4 (9–13): explains factors on both sides (more developed points and accurate detail move the answer up the band). L5 (14): as L4, plus a supported judgement that answers 'how far' (or 'was it the most important'). Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point; each needs explaining, not just stating) — Nehru: League accepted plan June 1946; Nehru's July statement that Congress was not bound by grouping; League withdrew acceptance; Direct Action Day 16 Aug 1946. Other factors: Congress–League distrust; dispute over nominating Muslims to the interim government; Congress invited to form interim government alone; complex plan read differently by each side; communal violence after Aug 1946. A judgement must weigh the stated factor against the others, not just repeat the question.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the 3 June Plan of 1947.
parts.answer: Announced by Lord Mountbatten; British India would be divided into two dominions, India and Pakistan; the Punjab and Bengal assemblies would vote on whether to divide their provinces; boundary commissions would draw the borders of divided provinces; referendums would be held in the NWFP and in Sylhet; Sindh's assembly and Balochistan would decide which country to join; the date of independence was brought forward to August 1947.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Radcliffe Award caused problems for Pakistan.
parts.answer: Sir Cyril Radcliffe drew the boundaries in a few weeks with little local knowledge; Muslim-majority areas such as most of Gurdaspur district were given to India, which gave India a land route to Kashmir; headworks controlling canals that watered Pakistani land (e.g. at Ferozepur and Madhopur) were left in India, which later caused the canal water dispute; the award was announced only after independence, causing confusion and mass migration with terrible violence; Pakistan received a share of refugees it struggled to settle.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the aims of the Khilafat Movement.
parts.answer: To preserve the position of the Ottoman Sultan as Caliph (Khalifa) of the Muslim world; to protect the holy places of Islam (Makkah and Madinah) from non-Muslim control; to stop the Ottoman Empire being broken up by the Allies after the First World War; to put pressure on Britain to keep its wartime promises to Indian Muslims.
parts.working: 1 mark per aim up to 4; credit leaders (Ali brothers, Maulana Azad) only if linked to aims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Indian Muslims supported the Khilafat Movement.
parts.answer: Religious loyalty: the Caliph was seen as the spiritual head of Muslims worldwide; anger that Britain, after Muslim soldiers fought for it in the war, was helping to divide the Ottoman lands (Treaty of Sèvres, 1920); the holy places were at risk; strong leaders such as Muhammad Ali Jauhar and Shaukat Ali mobilised support; Gandhi's backing and the alliance with Congress made it a mass movement.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Hijrat Movement of 1920.
parts.answer: Some religious leaders declared India 'Dar-ul-Harb' (a land where Muslims could not freely practise their faith); thousands of Muslims, mainly from Sindh and the NWFP, sold their land and possessions and migrated to Afghanistan; the Afghan government, unable to cope, closed the border; many migrants died on the journey or returned to find they had lost everything.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Hijrat Movement failed.
parts.answer: Afghanistan could not feed, house or employ so many migrants and closed its border; the migrants had sold their property cheaply and had nothing to return to; the journey through mountains was harsh and many died; it was poorly planned and had no real leadership or organisation; it weakened rather than strengthened the Khilafat cause.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–1922.
parts.answer: Launched by Gandhi with Khilafat support in 1920; Indians were asked to return British titles and honours; boycott British schools, law courts and elections; boycott foreign cloth and use home-spun cloth (khaddar); it was called off by Gandhi in February 1922 after the violence at Chauri Chaura, where a police station was burned and policemen were killed.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Gandhi's decision to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement angered many Muslims.
parts.answer: He took the decision without consulting the Khilafat leaders, many of whom were in prison; Muslims had made great sacrifices (jobs, titles, Hijrat) and felt let down; the joint campaign was the main pressure on Britain over the Khilafat, so its end weakened their cause; it increased mistrust of Congress and contributed to the breakdown of Hindu–Muslim unity and to communal riots in the 1920s.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of the Moplah uprising of 1921.
parts.answer: The Moplahs were Muslim tenant farmers of Malabar in south-west India; in 1921, stirred up by the Khilafat campaign and grievances against Hindu landlords, they rebelled against British rule; there was violence against Hindu landlords and officials; the British used troops to crush the revolt, and many Moplahs were killed or imprisoned.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The abolition of the Caliphate by Turkey in 1924 was the main reason why the Khilafat Movement failed.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: when Mustafa Kemal's government abolished the Caliphate in March 1924, the movement lost the very thing it existed to defend; Turkish nationalists had already abolished the Sultanate in 1922. Other reasons: Gandhi's ending of Non-Cooperation in 1922 broke the Hindu–Muslim alliance; the Hijrat disaster and the Moplah uprising damaged the movement; arrest of leaders such as the Ali brothers; the British refused to change their policy. Judgement: the abolition ended the movement, but it was already weakened.
parts.working: Level marking (14 marks). L1 (1–2): general statements with no relevant detail. L2 (3–6): identifies or describes relevant factors without explaining them. L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). L4 (9–13): explains factors on both sides (more developed points and accurate detail move the answer up the band). L5 (14): as L4, plus a supported judgement that answers 'how far' (or 'was it the most important'). Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point; each needs explaining, not just stating) — Abolition: Caliphate abolished March 1924 by Mustafa Kemal; Sultanate already abolished 1922; movement lost its purpose. Other reasons: Gandhi called off Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura 1922, ending Hindu–Muslim unity; Hijrat to Afghanistan 1920 a disaster; Moplah uprising damaged unity; Ali brothers and other leaders arrested; British refused to change Turkish policy. A judgement must weigh the stated factor against the others, not just repeat the question.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Read this extract, written for this exercise: 'On Khilafat Day the shops of the bazaar stayed shut from morning until evening. Men gathered in the mosque to pray for the Khalifa, and in the afternoon a crowd of Hindus and Muslims marched together to the town square to hear speeches against the peace terms.' According to the extract, identify three ways in which people took part in Khilafat Day.
parts.answer: Shops stayed closed (strike) all day; men prayed in the mosque for the Khalifa; Hindus and Muslims marched together to hear speeches against the peace terms.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point taken from the extract (no own knowledge).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Hindus and Muslims co-operated during the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements.
parts.answer: Both were angry with Britain after the First World War: Muslims over the treatment of Turkey, Hindus and Muslims together over the Rowlatt Act and the Amritsar massacre of 1919; Gandhi saw supporting the Khilafat as a way to win Muslim support for a united national campaign; a combined movement put far more pressure on Britain; the Lucknow Pact (1916) had already brought Congress and the League closer.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Partition of Bengal of 1905.
parts.answer: Ordered by the Viceroy Lord Curzon and put into effect in October 1905; Bengal was divided into two provinces; East Bengal and Assam, with its capital at Dacca, had a Muslim majority; West Bengal, with Bihar and Orissa and its capital at Calcutta, had a Hindu majority; the official reason was that Bengal was too large to govern efficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the British partitioned Bengal in 1905.
parts.answer: Bengal was too large and populous to be governed well from Calcutta, so administration, tax collection and law and order suffered; the eastern districts were neglected and poor, and a new province would bring roads, schools and development; the British may also have wanted to weaken the growing nationalist movement among Bengali Hindus in Calcutta (divide and rule).
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Hindus reacted to the Partition of Bengal.
parts.answer: Mass protests and meetings, led by Congress; the Swadeshi movement: a boycott of British goods, especially cloth, which was burned in public; acts of violence and terrorism against British officials; newspapers and lawyers in Calcutta campaigned against it; 16 October 1905 was treated as a day of mourning.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the partition was reversed in 1911.
parts.answer: The Hindu protests, boycotts and violence were damaging British trade and order; the British feared growing support for extreme nationalists; they wanted to win back the loyalty of Congress moderates; the new King-Emperor George V announced the reversal at the Delhi Durbar in December 1911, together with moving the capital from Calcutta to Delhi to soften the blow to Muslims.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Simla Deputation of 1906.
parts.answer: On 1 October 1906 about 35 Muslim leaders, led by the Aga Khan, met the Viceroy Lord Minto at Simla; they asked for separate electorates for Muslims; they asked for representation greater than their share of the population (weightage), because of their political importance; they asked for a fair share of government jobs and seats on councils; Minto received them sympathetically.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Muslim leaders felt it necessary to send the Simla Deputation.
parts.answer: The British had announced that reforms with more elected seats were coming, and Muslims feared that in joint elections the Hindu majority would win almost all seats; they wanted to protect Muslim interests in councils and jobs; Congress was seen as a Hindu body that did not speak for Muslims; Hindu agitation against the Partition of Bengal showed Muslims needed to put their own case to the British.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the founding of the All-India Muslim League in 1906.
parts.answer: Founded at Dacca on 30 December 1906, during a meeting of the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference; Nawab Salimullah Khan of Dacca proposed the resolution; Nawab Viqar-ul-Mulk chaired the meeting and the Aga Khan became its first president; its aims were to promote loyalty to the British government, to protect and advance the political rights of Muslims, and to do this without hostility to other communities.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The Partition of Bengal was the main reason for the founding of the Muslim League in 1906.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: Hindu agitation against a partition that benefited Muslims showed Muslims needed their own organisation to defend their gains. Other reasons: the success of the Simla Deputation showed the value of organised Muslim political action; fear that elected councils would be dominated by Hindus; Congress was seen as representing Hindu interests (e.g. Hindi–Urdu controversy); the legacy of Sir Syed's educated Muslim leadership. Judgement required.

L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). L4 (9–13): explains factors on both sides (more developed points and accurate detail move the answer up the band). L5 (14): as L4, plus a supported judgement that answers 'how far' (or 'was it the most important'). Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point; each needs explaining, not just stating) — Partition of Bengal: Hindu agitation against a partition that benefited Muslims; Muslims needed an organisation to defend gains. Other reasons: success of the Simla Deputation (Oct 1906) showed value of organised action; fear of Hindu domination in elected councils (Minto–Morley reforms coming); Congress seen as a Hindu body; Hindi–Urdu controversy; legacy of Sir Syed and the educated Aligarh leadership; Muhammadan Educational Conference at Dhaka, Dec 1906. A judgement must weigh the stated factor against the others, not just repeat the question.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Muslims reacted to the reversal of the Partition of Bengal in 1911.
parts.answer: Muslims of East Bengal felt betrayed by the British; they believed the British had given in to Hindu violence; they lost the benefits of a Muslim-majority province (jobs, education, development in Dacca); Muslim leaders began to doubt British promises, and the Muslim League moved towards seeking self-government (adopted as an aim in 1913).
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reversal of the partition changed the attitude of the Muslim League towards the British.
parts.answer: It showed that British support could not be relied on, because they reversed a decision that helped Muslims as soon as Hindus protested; Muslims concluded that agitation, not loyalty, got results; British refusal to support Turkey in the Balkan Wars and the Kanpur mosque incident (1913) added to the anger; so the League began to co-operate with Congress, leading to the Lucknow Pact of 1916.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Morley–Minto Reforms of 1909.
parts.answer: Also called the Indian Councils Act 1909; Muslims were given separate electorates; the central and provincial legislative councils were enlarged and more members were elected; members could discuss the budget and ask questions; an Indian was appointed to the Viceroy's Executive Council for the first time.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Morley–Minto Reforms were welcomed by Muslims but criticised by Congress.
parts.answer: Muslims: separate electorates meant Muslim representatives would be chosen by Muslim voters, protecting their interests and recognising them as a separate community; it was a success for the Simla Deputation and the new League. Congress: separate electorates were seen as dividing Indians; the councils had no real power because officials kept control; the reforms fell far short of self-government.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Both sides needed for top level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Lucknow Pact of 1916.
parts.answer: An agreement between Congress and the Muslim League at their joint sessions in Lucknow, largely arranged by Jinnah; Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims; Muslims would have one-third of the seats in the central legislature; no bill affecting a community could pass if three-quarters of that community's members opposed it; both parties would jointly demand self-government from the British.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Lucknow Pact was important.
parts.answer: It was the first time Congress formally accepted that Muslims were a separate community with the right to separate electorates; it showed Hindus and Muslims could work together against British rule, which strengthened the demand for self-government; it established Jinnah as a leader trusted by both parties ('ambassador of Hindu–Muslim unity'); its ideas influenced the 1919 reforms.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms of 1919.
parts.answer: Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces: subjects such as education, health and agriculture were transferred to elected Indian ministers, while law and order and finance were reserved for officials; the central legislature became two houses; the number of voters was increased; separate electorates were kept and extended to Sikhs; a commission would review the reforms after ten years.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many Indians were disappointed by the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms.
parts.answer: They had expected self-government after supporting Britain in the First World War; the Viceroy and governors kept the important powers (finance, police) so ministers had little real control; only a small fraction of the population could vote; the reforms came at the same time as the Rowlatt Act and the Amritsar massacre, which destroyed trust in British intentions.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919.
parts.answer: On 13 April 1919 a large unarmed crowd gathered in the Jallianwala Bagh, an enclosed ground in Amritsar, in defiance of a ban on meetings; General Dyer blocked the exit with troops and ordered them to fire without warning; firing continued until ammunition ran low; hundreds were killed (officially 379) and over a thousand wounded; martial law followed in the Punjab.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The Rowlatt Act was the main cause of unrest in India in 1919.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: the Rowlatt Act (March 1919) allowed arrest without warrant and trial without jury, which Indians saw as a betrayal after wartime loyalty; Gandhi organised a national strike (hartal) against it, which led to protests and the Amritsar events. Other causes: the massacre itself and the Hunter Committee's weak response to Dyer; the disappointing Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms; economic hardship after the war (prices, taxes); Muslim anger over the treatment of Turkey. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking (14 marks). L1 (1–2): general statements with no relevant detail. L2 (3–6): identifies or describes relevant factors without explaining them. L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). L4 (9–13): explains factors on both sides (more developed points and accurate detail move the answer up the band). L5 (14): as L4, plus a supported judgement that answers 'how far' (or 'was it the most important'). Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point; each needs explaining, not just stating) — Rowlatt Act: March 1919, arrest without warrant, trial without jury; seen as betrayal after wartime loyalty; Gandhi's hartal; protests leading to Amritsar. Other causes: Jallianwala Bagh massacre (April 1919) and weak Hunter Committee response to Dyer; disappointing Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms; post-war economic hardship (prices, taxes); Muslim anger over the treatment of Turkey / Khilafat. A judgement must weigh the stated factor against the others, not just repeat the question.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results of the 1937 provincial elections.
parts.answer: Congress won a clear majority in five provinces and formed ministries in seven, later eight, of the eleven provinces; the Muslim League won only a small share of Muslim seats; it did not win control of any province, even Muslim-majority ones; in Punjab the Unionist Party formed the government and in Bengal Fazlul Huq's Krishak Praja Party led a coalition; the League's best results were in Muslim-minority provinces such as the UP.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Muslim League did badly in the 1937 elections.
parts.answer: It was poorly organised with few branches in the countryside; regional parties such as the Unionists in Punjab and the Krishak Praja Party in Bengal had strong local support and leaders; the League was seen as a party of landlords and the educated elite with little appeal to ordinary Muslims; it had little money and Jinnah had only recently returned to lead it.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Wardha Scheme and the Vidya Mandir Scheme introduced under Congress rule.
parts.answer: Wardha Scheme: Gandhi's education plan; teaching in Hindi; spinning and manual crafts in schools; lessons glorified Congress leaders and Hindu culture, and religious education was excluded. Vidya Mandir Scheme (Central Provinces): schools called 'temples of learning'; Hindi in Devanagari script used; Muslims saw both as attempts to convert Muslim children to Hindu culture.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4 (at least one point on each scheme for full marks).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Muslims objected to Congress rule between 1937 and 1939.
parts.answer: Bande Mataram, a song with anti-Muslim content, was made the anthem and sung in assemblies and schools; Congress flag flown on public buildings; Hindi promoted in place of Urdu; restrictions on cow slaughter and interference with Muslim worship; Muslims excluded from government jobs; Congress refused to form coalitions with the League in the UP unless League members joined Congress; the Muslim Mass Contact campaign tried to weaken the League. The Pirpur Report recorded these grievances.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Day of Deliverance (22 December 1939).
parts.answer: In October–November 1939 the Congress ministries resigned in protest because the Viceroy had declared India at war without consulting Indian leaders; Jinnah called on Muslims to celebrate 22 December 1939 as a Day of Deliverance from Congress rule; meetings were held and prayers of thanksgiving offered; some non-Muslim groups, such as many of the depressed classes, also joined.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Congress refused to form coalition governments with the Muslim League after the 1937 elections.
parts.answer: Congress had won clear majorities in most provinces, so it did not need the League's support to govern; the League's poor results let Congress claim the League did not represent Muslims, and Nehru said there were only two parties in India, Congress and the British; Congress saw itself as the national party for all Indians, including Muslims; in the UP it offered places to League members only if they merged into Congress and gave up the League's separate identity; it hoped to win Muslims directly through the Muslim Mass Contact campaign.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies reasons without explanation. L3 (4–7): explains one or more reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: Congress majorities made coalitions unnecessary; League's weak 1937 results; Nehru's 'two parties' claim / Congress as the only national party; UP terms requiring League members to join Congress; Muslim Mass Contact campaign.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes Jinnah made to the Muslim League after 1937.
parts.answer: He reorganised the party at the Lucknow session of 1937; membership fee reduced so ordinary Muslims could join; new branches set up in towns and villages; a youth and student wing (e.g. the Muslim Students Federation) and a women's wing were developed; he made agreements with provincial leaders such as Sikandar Hayat Khan.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The behaviour of the Congress ministries was the main reason for the growth of the Muslim League between 1937 and 1940.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: grievances such as Bande Mataram, the Wardha Scheme and the Muslim Mass Contact campaign drove Muslims to the League; the Day of Deliverance showed mass support. Other factors: Jinnah's leadership and reorganisation; alliances with regional leaders (Sikandar–Jinnah Pact); the outbreak of war in 1939, which made the British value Muslim support and gave the League bargaining power; the League's clearer aim, leading to the Lahore Resolution. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking (14 marks). L1 (1–2): general statements with no relevant detail. L2 (3–6): identifies or describes relevant factors without explaining them. L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). L4 (9–13): explains factors on both sides (more developed points and accurate detail move the answer up the band). L5 (14): as L4, plus a supported judgement that answers 'how far' (or 'was it the most important'). Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point; each needs explaining, not just stating) — Congress ministries: Bande Mataram; Wardha Scheme; Vidya Mandir; Muslim Mass Contact campaign; Pirpur and Shareef reports; Day of Deliverance Dec 1939 showed mass support. Other factors: Jinnah's leadership and reorganisation of the League; Sikandar–Jinnah Pact and regional alliances; outbreak of war 1939 made the British value Muslim support; clearer aim leading to the Lahore Resolution 1940. A judgement must weigh the stated factor against the others, not just repeat the question.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two mountain peaks in northern Pakistan that attract climbers and trekkers.
parts.answer: Any two of: K2; Nanga Parbat; Gasherbrum I or II; Broad Peak; Rakaposhi; Tirich Mir.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three attractions, other than mountain peaks, that bring tourists to Gilgit-Baltistan and northern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
parts.answer: Any three: lakes (e.g. Attabad, Saif-ul-Malook); glaciers (e.g. Baltoro, Passu); valleys such as Hunza, Swat, Naran-Kaghan; the Karakoram Highway; Deosai Plains / national parks and wildlife; forts such as Baltit and Altit; cool summer climate; local culture and festivals.
parts.working: 1 mark each, named or clearly described.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why it is difficult to develop tourism in the northern mountains. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Roads are narrow and often blocked by landslides or snow, so journeys are long and unsafe, which puts tourists off; the tourist season is short (mainly summer), so hotels earn little for much of the year and investors are reluctant; few modern hotels and medical facilities in remote valleys; electricity and internet supply are unreliable.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

stem:
A hill resort in the Kaghan valley recorded these numbers of visitors (thousands) in one year (hypothetical data):
Jan 2, Feb 3, Mar 6, Apr 12, May 25, Jun 48, Jul 55, Aug 41, Sep 18, Oct 10, Nov 4, Dec 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of visitors to the resort in the year.
parts.answer: 227 thousand (227,000 visitors)
parts.working: Sum of the twelve months = 227 thousand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the year's visitors who came in June, July and August. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the pattern of visitors shown in the table.
parts.answer: Very few visitors in winter (Nov–Feb, 2–4 thousand a month); numbers rise steadily from March; peak in July (55 thousand); fall sharply from September; the range is 53 thousand.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, including at least one figure from the table, up to 3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two problems that this pattern causes for people who work in tourism in the valley. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Work is seasonal, so guides, porters and hotel staff are unemployed for much of the year and must migrate or find other work; hotels are overcrowded in July, which causes high prices, water shortages and litter; hotels earn little income in winter, so it is hard to repay loans or pay staff all year.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'religious tourism'?
parts.answer: Travel to visit holy places or take part in religious festivals and pilgrimages.
parts.working: 1 mark: travel/visits; 1 mark: to holy sites / for religious reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Kartarpur Corridor was opened in 2019. State where it is and who mainly uses it.
parts.answer: It links the Gurdwara Darbar Sahib at Kartarpur in Narowal district, Punjab, to the Indian border; it is used mainly by Sikh pilgrims from India and around the world.
parts.working: 1 mark location (Kartarpur / Narowal / Punjab near Indian border); 1 mark Sikh pilgrims.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two other places in Pakistan that attract religious tourists, and state the religion linked to each.
parts.answer: Any two: Nankana Sahib (Sikh); Panja Sahib, Hasan Abdal (Sikh); Data Darbar, Lahore (Muslim / Sufi shrine); shrine of Lal Shahbaz Qalandar, Sehwan (Muslim / Sufi); Taxila or Takht-i-Bahi (Buddhist); Katas Raj temples (Hindu); Hinglaj Mata, Balochistan (Hindu).
parts.working: 1 mark each (place and religion).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two ways in which religious tourism can benefit the local economy. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Pilgrims spend on food, transport and souvenirs, which creates income and jobs for local traders; foreign pilgrims bring foreign exchange; spending leads to improved roads, hotels and services that also help local people (multiplier effect).
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which large numbers of tourists can damage the environment of mountain valleys. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Litter and plastic left at lakes and campsites pollute water and harm wildlife; trees are cut for hotel building and fuelwood, causing soil erosion and landslides; untreated sewage from hotels flows into rivers; traffic jams on narrow roads cause air and noise pollution.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Tourism in the northern areas should be expanded as fast as possible because it brings jobs and income.'
View B: 'Tourism in the northern areas must be limited because the damage it causes outweighs the benefits.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: jobs for guides, porters, drivers and hotel staff; income in poor remote areas reduces out-migration; foreign exchange; better roads and services (e.g. Karakoram Highway). View B: pollution and litter at lakes; deforestation for hotels; overcrowding and water shortages in Murree or Naran in peak season; hotels built on river banks damaged in floods (e.g. Swat in 2022); loss of local culture. A balanced judgement such as controlled (sustainable) growth.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two World Heritage Sites in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: Mohenjo-daro; Taxila; Takht-i-Bahi (with Sahr-i-Bahlol); Makli monuments, Thatta; Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens; Rohtas Fort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two facilities a heritage site needs if it is to attract more foreign tourists.
parts.answer: Any two: good road access / signposting; nearby hotels and restaurants; guides or information in English and other languages; museums or visitor centres; clean toilets and drinking water; security.
parts.working: 1 mark each; vague 'facilities' = 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which tourism can help to protect historical sites. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Entry fees raise money that can pay for repairs and conservation; tourist interest makes the government and local people value the site, so it is protected from encroachment; jobs at the site give local people a reason to look after it; international attention can bring outside funding.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the main road that links Karachi with Gwadar along the coast.
parts.answer: The Makran Coastal Highway (N-10).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the natural attractions that the Balochistan coast could offer tourists.
parts.answer: Long sandy beaches (e.g. Kund Malir); unusual rock formations shaped by wind and sea; Hingol National Park with wildlife and mud volcanoes; warm sea for swimming and fishing; a mild winter climate.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, up to 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why few tourists visit the Balochistan coast at present. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: There are very few hotels, restaurants or petrol stations along the coast, so tourists cannot stay overnight comfortably; long distances from big cities make journeys long and tiring; concerns about security discourage visitors; very hot summers and a lack of drinking water; little advertising so the coast is not well known.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.text: Explain two ways in which the growth of tourism may have affected the local people of the valley. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Positive: new jobs in hotels, transport and handicraft shops, raising incomes so fewer young people migrate to cities; better roads and electricity built for tourists also serve villages. parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the 'multiplier effect' of tourism?
parts.answer: Money spent by tourists is spent again by the people who receive it, so the total benefit to the local economy is larger than the first amount spent.
parts.working: 1 mark: tourist spending creates income; 1 mark: re-spent / creates further jobs and income.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State four types of job created directly by tourism in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any four: hotel staff; tour guides; porters; drivers / jeep operators; cooks and restaurant workers; handicraft sellers; travel agents; ticket sellers at heritage sites.

stem: A provincial tourism department earned Rs 4.8 billion from tourism in 2022 and Rs 6.3 billion in 2024 (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in tourism revenue from 2022 to 2024.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which government action can increase the number of foreign tourists visiting Pakistan.
parts.answer: Government can help: the online e-visa system and visa on arrival for some countries make entry easier; building and repairing roads (motorways, Karakoram Highway) and airports improves access; promotion abroad improves Pakistan's image; better security. Limits: foreign travel advice and perceptions of insecurity are hard to change quickly; natural hazards such as floods and landslides; private investment in hotels is needed; global events affect travel. parts.label: a
parts.text: State four factors that influence where a large factory is located.
parts.answer: Any four: raw materials; power supply; labour; market; transport links; capital; water supply; government policy / incentives; flat land.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Faisalabad is a major centre of the cotton textile industry. Explain two reasons for this. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It lies in the middle of the cotton-growing area of central Punjab, so raw cotton is close and cheap to transport; it has a large supply of skilled and cheap labour from the surrounding farming areas; it is on the motorway (M-3/M-4) and rail network, so goods reach Lahore and Karachi port easily; many related firms (ginning, spinning, dyeing) cluster there.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

stem: A sugar mill in central Sindh crushes 4,500 tonnes of sugar cane a day. On average 10.2% of the mass of the cane is recovered as sugar (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a

parts.answer: 459 tonnes

parts.answer: 55,080 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the mass of cane that is lost (not turned into sugar).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why sugar mills are located close to the sugar cane fields. You should develop your answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pakistan Steel Mills was built at Port Qasim near Karachi. Explain two reasons for this location. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Iron ore and coking coal had to be imported, so a site at a port avoided long and costly land transport; Karachi is the largest market for steel (engineering, shipbuilding, construction); a large labour force was available; flat coastal land and sea water for cooling; good rail and road links to the rest of the country.

parts.text: 'Pakistan should depend on imported steel instead of producing its own.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: For imports: Pakistan has little good iron ore or coking coal, so raw materials must be imported anyway; the state steel mill made heavy losses and stopped production in 2015; imported steel may be cheaper and of higher quality. Against: imports cost scarce foreign exchange and worsen the trade deficit; steel is needed for construction, engineering and defence, so self-reliance matters; a domestic steel industry creates jobs and linked industries; private steel re-rolling mills already exist. Judgement required.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these stages of the cotton textile industry in the correct order: weaving, ginning, garment making, spinning, dyeing and finishing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What happens during ginning?
parts.answer: The cotton fibre (lint) is separated from the seeds.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan earns more money by exporting garments than by exporting raw cotton. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Each stage of manufacturing adds value, so a kilogram of cotton made into garments sells for many times the price of raw cotton; garment making uses much labour, so it creates more jobs; exports of finished goods earn more foreign exchange; it reduces dependence on world raw cotton prices.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.text: Calculate the total value of the textile exports.
parts.answer: US$ 16,000 million
parts.working: Sum of the six values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total earned by high value-added products (knitwear, bedwear and readymade garments). Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two problems that limit the growth of Pakistan's textile exports. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: High and unreliable electricity and gas supply raises costs and stops production; strong competition from Bangladesh, China and Vietnam with lower costs; much machinery is old, so quality and productivity are lower; low cotton yields mean expensive raw material has to be imported; shortage of skilled designers and marketing.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which energy shortages affect large-scale manufacturing in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Load-shedding stops machines, so output falls and orders are delivered late, losing foreign buyers; factories must run their own generators, raising costs and making exports less competitive; gas shortages in winter close fertiliser and textile plants; investors are discouraged from setting up new factories.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'The main problem facing large-scale industry in Pakistan is the high cost of energy.'
View B: 'The main problem facing large-scale industry in Pakistan is a lack of skilled workers and modern technology.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: high electricity and gas tariffs and load-shedding raise costs for textiles, cement and fertiliser; generators expensive. View B: outdated machinery in textile mills lowers quality; low literacy and few technical institutes limit skills; little research and development; low productivity. Other factors may be mentioned (political instability, taxes). Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the main raw material used to make urea fertiliser in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Natural gas.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many fertiliser plants are located in northern Sindh and southern Punjab, for example at Daharki and Sadiqabad. Explain two reasons for this location. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: They are close to the gas fields of Sindh and Balochistan (e.g. Mari), so feedstock can be piped cheaply; they lie in major farming areas, so the market for fertiliser is close; they are on the main road and rail routes along the Indus, making distribution easy; water is available from the Indus and canals.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fertiliser industry is important to agriculture in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Fertiliser replaces nutrients in heavily used soils, raising crop yields (e.g. wheat, cotton); local production keeps fertiliser cheaper and available on time, saving foreign exchange on imports; higher yields support food security and farm incomes.
parts.working: 1 mark per point; 3 marks for a developed point plus one other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is an export processing zone (EPZ)?
parts.answer: A fenced industrial area where firms can import raw materials and machinery free of duty and manufacture goods mainly for export.
parts.working: 1 mark: designated / fenced industrial area; 1 mark: duty-free imports / goods for export.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the first EPZ set up in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Karachi Export Processing Zone.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three incentives offered to firms that set up in an EPZ.
parts.answer: Any three: duty-free import of machinery and raw materials; tax exemptions / holidays; up to 100% foreign ownership; freedom to send profits abroad; ready-built plots with power, water and roads; quick customs clearance; a single office for permissions.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two industrial estates in Pakistan and the province in which each is located.
parts.answer: Any two: SITE, Karachi (Sindh); Sundar Industrial Estate, Lahore (Punjab); Quaid-e-Azam Industrial Estate, Lahore (Punjab); Hattar, Haripur (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa); Gadoon Amazai, Swabi (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa); Hub (Balochistan).
parts.working: 1 mark each (estate and province).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to a manufacturer of setting up a factory on an industrial estate. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Plots come with roads, electricity, gas, water and drainage already provided, so the firm saves the cost and time of building these; firms are close to suppliers and customers, which cuts transport costs; shared services such as security, banks and waste treatment are cheaper; the government may give tax incentives.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage for local people of building a large industrial estate.
parts.answer: Loss of farmland / pollution of air and water / traffic congestion / pressure on housing.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are being developed under the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). Name two of them.
parts.answer: Any two: Rashakai (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa); Allama Iqbal Industrial City, Faisalabad (Punjab); Dhabeji (Sindh); Bostan (Balochistan).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rashakai SEZ is beside the M-1 motorway in Nowshera district. Explain two advantages of this location. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The motorway gives fast transport to Islamabad, Peshawar and on to Karachi port, reducing transport costs; it is on the route towards Afghanistan and Central Asia, giving access to new markets; a large labour force lives in the surrounding districts; electricity and gas networks are nearby.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one difference between an EPZ and an SEZ.
parts.answer: An EPZ produces mainly for export, while an SEZ firm may sell in the domestic market as well as export.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the government encourages industries to set up in less developed areas. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: To create jobs in poorer regions, reducing unemployment and migration to big cities such as Karachi and Lahore; to spread wealth more evenly between provinces, reducing regional inequality; to use local raw materials (minerals, crops); to reduce congestion and pollution in big cities.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Export processing zones and special economic zones are the best way to develop industry in Pakistan.'
View B: 'Export processing zones and special economic zones bring little benefit to ordinary Pakistanis.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: attract foreign investment and technology; create jobs; earn foreign exchange; ready infrastructure speeds up building (e.g. Karachi EPZ, Rashakai). View B: tax breaks reduce government revenue; many plots remain empty; jobs may go to outsiders or be low paid; profits leave the country; zones concentrated near big cities; local small firms may lose out. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

stem: A new industrial estate has 480 plots. 312 plots have working factories, 54 plots have factories under construction and the rest are empty (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of plots that are occupied by working factories.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of plots that are empty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why some plots on the estate are still empty.
parts.answer: Shortage of electricity or gas connections; high cost of plots; security concerns; long distance from ports or markets; lack of skilled labour nearby; slow government approvals.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which government policy can influence where industries are located in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Tax holidays and duty exemptions in EPZs/SEZs make certain sites cheaper, attracting firms there; government builds roads, power and gas supply to industrial estates, so firms move to those places; restrictions on new factories in crowded cities push industry elsewhere; state-owned projects (e.g. steel mill at Port Qasim) create growth centres.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which improved infrastructure, rather than tax incentives, attracts industry to an area.
parts.answer: Infrastructure: reliable electricity and gas, motorways and ports are basic needs; without them tax breaks are not enough (empty plots in remote zones). Tax incentives: lower costs and can attract export firms (EPZs) and foreign investors; matter for firms with small profit margins. Other factors: labour, markets, security. Judgement: both matter but infrastructure is usually the deciding factor.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by a 'cottage industry'?
parts.answer: Small-scale manufacturing carried out in the home, using family labour, simple tools and usually local raw materials.
parts.working: 1 mark: in the home / small scale; 1 mark: family labour / simple tools / little capital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name three products of cottage industries in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any three: hand-knotted carpets; pottery (e.g. Multan blue pottery); embroidered cloth; handloom cloth; ajrak; leather goods (e.g. khussa shoes); wooden furniture / lacquer work; baskets and mats.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one difference between cottage industry and large-scale industry.
parts.answer: Cottage industry uses hand tools and family labour at home; large-scale industry uses machines and many paid workers in factories.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why cottage and small-scale industries are important in rural Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: They give work in the off-season when there is little farm work, raising family incomes; women can earn while working at home; they need little capital, so poor families can start them; they use local raw materials such as wool, leather and clay; they keep traditional crafts alive and some goods are exported.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems faced by cottage industries. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Difficulty getting loans, so workers depend on middlemen who take most of the profit; competition from cheap factory-made goods; lack of design training and quality control limits exports; poor transport and marketing in villages.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

stem: A small workshop in Sialkot makes hand-stitched footballs. Each ball has 32 panels. It employs 25 stitchers. Each stitcher completes 4 balls a day, works 26 days a month and is paid Rs 180 per ball (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of footballs the workshop produces in one month.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of panels needed for one month's production.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate a stitcher's earnings in one month.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Sialkot has become a centre for sports goods and surgical instruments. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: A long tradition of skilled metal and leather craftsmen passed down in families; many small firms cluster together, sharing suppliers and skills; an export-processing and dry-port link (Sialkot dry port, international airport) makes exports easy; business community invested in its own infrastructure.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the government organisation that supports small and medium enterprises in Pakistan, and state one way it helps them.
parts.answer: SMEDA (Small and Medium Enterprises Development Authority); it gives business advice / training / help with finance and marketing / common facility centres.
parts.working: 1 mark name; 1 mark help.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'The government should spend more on supporting cottage and small-scale industry than on large-scale industry.'
View B: 'Large-scale industry should get priority because it does more to develop Pakistan's economy.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: cottage industry employs many people, especially women and rural workers, with little capital; reduces rural poverty and migration; uses local materials; exports such as carpets and Sialkot goods. View B: large-scale industry produces more output and exports (textiles), pays more tax, uses modern technology, supplies inputs (cement, fertiliser, steel). Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the 'informal sector'?
parts.answer: Work that is not registered with or regulated by the government, so workers pay no tax and have no legal protection such as contracts, pensions or social security.
parts.working: 1 mark: unregistered / unregulated / not taxed; 1 mark: no contracts / benefits / job security.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three examples of informal-sector jobs in a Pakistani city.
parts.answer: Any three: street vendors / hawkers; rickshaw or loader drivers; shoe-shiners; domestic workers; casual construction labourers; small roadside repair workshops; rag pickers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why many people in Pakistan's cities work in the informal sector. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rapid rural–urban migration means more workers than formal jobs; many migrants lack education or skills needed for formal jobs; informal work needs little or no capital, so it is easy to start.
parts.working: 1 mark per reason + 1 for development, max 3.

stem:
A survey of 1,250 workers in a town in Punjab found that 900 worked in the informal sector. The 900 informal workers were in these jobs (hypothetical data):
street vending 270; transport (rickshaw, loader) 225; construction labour 180; domestic work 135; small workshops 90

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the workers surveyed who work in the informal sector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the informal workers who are street vendors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which the informal sector benefits Pakistan's economy.
parts.answer: Benefits: provides jobs and income for millions who cannot find formal work, reducing poverty and crime; low-cost goods and services for poorer people; a training ground for skills; needs no government investment. Problems: no tax paid, so government revenue is low; workers have low and irregular pay, no safety rules, pensions or health cover; child labour; congestion and encroachment on pavements. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three problems faced by small farmers in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any three: small and fragmented holdings; shortage of irrigation water; waterlogging and salinity; lack of credit / dependence on money-lenders; poor-quality seed; high cost of fertiliser and pesticides; pests and diseases; low prices from middlemen; floods and droughts; lack of storage; low literacy / lack of advice.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why crop yields per hectare in Pakistan are lower than in many other countries. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Many farmers use uncertified seed, so plants are weaker and give less grain; irrigation water is wasted by flood irrigation and unlined canals, so crops at the tail end get too little; fertiliser is expensive, so poor farmers apply too little; waterlogging and salinity reduce the fertility of the soil; lack of training means modern methods are not used.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the following information about land reforms: in 1959 the ceiling on individual holdings was set at ____ acres of irrigated land; in 1972 it was reduced to ____ acres of irrigated land.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
