parts.text: By what percentage was the irrigated-land ceiling reduced between 1959 and 1972?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the land reforms had only a limited effect on the distribution of land. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Landlords transferred land into the names of relatives and servants before the reforms, so they kept control; ceilings were per individual, so families kept large estates; much of the land taken was poor, barren land; exemptions (e.g. for orchards, stud farms) and weak enforcement by officials linked to landlords.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output
stem:
Two wheat farms in the same district in one season (hypothetical data):
Farm X: 1.5 hectares, produced 4.2 tonnes
Farm Y: 3.0 hectares, produced 9.9 tonnes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the yield of wheat per hectare on each farm. Give your answers in tonnes per hectare.
parts.answer: Farm X 2.8 t/ha; Farm Y 3.3 t/ha

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three reasons why Farm Y has a higher yield than Farm X.
parts.answer: Any three: Farm Y uses certified / high-yielding seed; applies more or better-timed fertiliser; has a tube well, so a reliable water supply; uses laser land levelling; has less waterlogged or saline soil; uses machinery to sow on time; farmer has more training and credit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of mechanisation (using machines such as tractors and combine harvesters) for farmers. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Ploughing and sowing are faster, so crops are sown at the best time and yields rise; harvesting by combine reduces losses from rain and shattering; fewer labourers are needed, cutting labour costs; laser levelling saves irrigation water.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Mechanisation is the best way to increase agricultural output in Pakistan.'
View B: 'Mechanisation does more harm than good in rural Pakistan.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: timely sowing and harvesting; higher yields and less waste; allows double cropping (e.g. rice then wheat); saves water with laser levelling. View B: machines are too expensive for most small farmers, and holdings are too small and fragmented to use them; landless labourers lose jobs and migrate to cities; burning of rice stubble left by combines adds to smog; dependence on imported fuel and spare parts. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Green Revolution began in Pakistan in the 1960s. State three inputs that it introduced or increased.
parts.answer: Any three: high-yielding varieties of seed (e.g. of wheat and rice); chemical fertilisers; pesticides; tube wells for irrigation; tractors and machinery.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Green Revolution benefited large landowners more than small farmers. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The new seeds only gave high yields with plenty of fertiliser, water and pesticides, which cost money; large landowners could afford these inputs and tube wells, or get bank loans, so their yields and profits rose most; small farmers often could not afford the full package.
parts.working: 1 mark per point; 3 marks for a developed explanation.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output
stem: A farmer needs to borrow Rs 150,000 for six months to buy seed and fertiliser. A village money-lender charges simple interest of 3% per month. An agricultural bank such as ZTBL charges simple interest of 12% per year (hypothetical rates).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the interest the farmer would pay to the money-lender.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the interest the farmer would pay on a bank loan, and how much he would save by borrowing from the bank.
parts.answer: Bank interest Rs 9,000; saving Rs 18,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many small farmers still borrow from money-lenders or middlemen (arthis) rather than banks. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Banks require land titles or other collateral, which tenants and small farmers often lack; bank procedures need paperwork, which is hard for farmers with little education; banks are far away in towns, while the money-lender is in the village and lends quickly; the arthi also buys the crop, so the loan is repaid at harvest without forms.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how waterlogging and salinity reduce crop output. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Seepage from unlined canals and over-irrigation raises the water table, so roots are surrounded by water and cannot get air, and plants die; in hot weather water rises by capillary action and evaporates, leaving salt on the surface; salt makes it hard for plants to take in water and is toxic, so yields fall and land may be abandoned.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for a developed explanation of both waterlogging and salinity (max 2 if only one).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which solving water problems would increase agricultural output in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Water problems are central: most crops depend on irrigation; water shortages at canal tails; waterlogging and salinity have damaged large areas; lining canals, drainage tube wells and drip/sprinkler irrigation would raise yields. Other limits on output: small fragmented holdings, poor seed, lack of credit, pests (e.g. locusts in 2019–20), low prices and middlemen, lack of storage, floods. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output
stem:
Wheat area and production in a country over three years (hypothetical data):
Year 1: area 8.8 million hectares, production 24.0 million tonnes
Year 2: area 9.0 million hectares, production 26.2 million tonnes
Year 3: area 9.2 million hectares, production 28.0 million tonnes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the yield (tonnes per hectare) for each year. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Year 1 2.73, Year 2 2.91, Year 3 3.04 t/ha
parts.working: Production ÷ area for each year; 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in production from Year 1 to Year 3. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the data to explain whether the increase in production was mainly due to a larger area or to higher yields.
parts.answer: Area rose by only about 4.5% (8.8 → 9.2 million ha) but production rose by 16.7%, and yield rose from 2.73 to 3.04 t/ha, so higher yields were the main cause.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing area change with production change; 1 mark for using yield figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output
stem: A farmer owns 12 acres. Under inheritance, the land is divided equally among his four sons. Later each son's share is divided equally among his three children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of land each grandchild receives.
parts.answer: 1 acre
parts.working: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 acres per son; 3 ÷ 3 = 1 acre per grandchild.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by the division of land into small, scattered plots. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Plots are too small to use tractors or other machines efficiently, so costs per acre are high; time and land are wasted walking between scattered plots and on boundary ridges and paths; small plots give too little output to feed a family or produce a surplus to sell, keeping families poor; disputes over boundaries and water turns.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing the fragmentation of land holdings.
parts.answer: Consolidation of holdings (exchanging plots so each farmer has one compact block) / co-operative farming.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the floods of 2022 affected agriculture in Sindh. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Standing crops such as cotton and rice were destroyed, so farmers lost their income for the season; floodwater stayed on fields for months, delaying the sowing of the next wheat crop; livestock drowned and fodder was lost; canals, roads and storage were damaged, so inputs and crops could not be moved.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Building more dams and flood embankments is the best way to protect farming from floods.'
View B: 'Farmers must adapt to climate change, for example with new crop varieties, better forecasts and insurance.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: dams store floodwater for irrigation and electricity; embankments protect towns and fields; reduce peak flows. View B: dams are very expensive and slow to build and silt up; extreme rainfall (as in 2022) can overwhelm structures; drought- and flood-tolerant seed, changed sowing dates, early warning systems, crop insurance and keeping floodplains clear reduce losses cheaply. Judgement, possibly that both are needed.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Is wheat a rabi or a kharif crop?
parts.answer: Rabi.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State when wheat is sown and when it is harvested in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Sown October–December (mainly November); harvested April–May.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the conditions needed to grow wheat.
parts.answer: Cool, moist growing season; warm, dry and sunny weather for ripening and harvest; moderate water from rain or irrigation; fertile, well-drained loamy soil; flat land suitable for machines.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the province that produces most of Pakistan's wheat.
parts.answer: Punjab.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the conditions needed for growing rice.
parts.answer: High temperatures during growth (above about 20°C); plenty of water, as fields are flooded for much of the growing period; clay soil that holds water; flat land so water stays on the fields.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one district in Punjab famous for Basmati rice.
parts.answer: Any one: Gujranwala; Sialkot; Sheikhupura; Hafizabad; Narowal; Mandi Bahauddin.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why rice is important to Pakistan's economy. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It is a major export (especially Basmati), earning foreign exchange; it is a staple food, especially in Sindh, so it supports food security; rice milling and husking create jobs; rice-wheat rotation keeps land in use all year, raising farm incomes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two districts in the cotton-growing belt of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: Multan; Bahawalpur; Rahim Yar Khan; Vehari; Khanewal; Lodhran; Sanghar; Shaheed Benazirabad (Nawabshah); Mirpur Khas; Khairpur.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the climatic conditions needed for cotton.
parts.answer: A long frost-free growing season (about 200 days); high temperatures; plenty of sunshine, especially when the bolls open; moderate water from irrigation; dry weather during picking.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why cotton production in Pakistan has been unreliable in recent years. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Pest attacks such as pink bollworm and whitefly (cotton leaf curl virus) destroy crops; poor-quality and fake seed and pesticides; farmers have switched to sugarcane, rice or maize, which give better returns; heatwaves and floods (e.g. 2022) damage the crop; water shortages at sowing time.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many farmers choose to grow sugarcane. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Sugar mills guarantee a buyer and a government-supported price, so income is more certain; sugarcane is hardy and less affected by pests than cotton; it needs less day-to-day labour once planted; mills nearby mean low transport costs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Pakistan should grow less sugarcane because it uses too much water.'
View B: 'Sugarcane should still be grown widely because it supports farmers and industry.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: sugarcane occupies land for most of the year and needs very large amounts of irrigation water in a water-short country; it has replaced cotton in parts of the cotton belt; sugar exports earn little compared with the water used. View B: it supports sugar mills, which provide jobs; by-products (molasses for ethanol, bagasse for fuel and paper); farmers earn a reliable income; sugar is a basic food. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by a 'kharif' crop?
parts.answer: A crop sown at the start of the summer / monsoon season (around April–July) and harvested in autumn (around October–November).
parts.working: 1 mark sowing season; 1 mark harvest season.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sort these crops into rabi and kharif: wheat, rice, cotton, gram, maize, mustard.
parts.answer: Rabi: wheat, gram, mustard. Kharif: rice, cotton, maize.
parts.working: 3 marks all six correct; 2 marks four or five; 1 mark two or three.

stem:
Wheat production by province in one year, million tonnes (hypothetical data):
Punjab 21.0; Sindh 4.2; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 1.4; Balochistan 1.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle needed for each province on a pie chart of wheat production.
parts.answer: Punjab 270°, Sindh 54°, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 18°, Balochistan 18°
parts.working: Total = 28.0 million t. Value ÷ 28.0 × 360. 3 marks all correct; 1 mark method only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of wheat produced in Punjab.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why Punjab produces far more wheat than Balochistan.
parts.answer: Punjab has large areas of flat, fertile alluvial plains; it has an extensive canal irrigation system; Balochistan is mostly dry, mountainous plateau with little water and poor soils.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Match each fruit with an area where it is grown: kinnow, mango, dates, apples. Areas: Sargodha, Multan, Khairpur, Quetta.
parts.answer: Kinnow – Sargodha; mango – Multan; dates – Khairpur; apples – Quetta.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan exports only a small share of the fruit it grows. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Lack of cold storage and refrigerated transport means much fruit spoils before reaching ports; many orchards do not meet foreign quality and pest-control standards, so importers reject the fruit; poor packaging and grading lower prices; high air-freight costs; most fruit is sold in the large home market.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

stem:
Cotton production in a country (million bales) (hypothetical data):
Year A 12.0; Year B 8.4 (whitefly and pink bollworm attack); Year C 10.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in production from Year A to Year B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase from Year B to Year C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two effects of a poor cotton harvest on Pakistan's economy. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Textile mills must import raw cotton, using scarce foreign exchange and raising costs; ginning factories and farm workers lose income and jobs; cotton farmers fall into debt; lower exports of yarn and cloth widen the trade deficit; less cottonseed for edible oil.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the province where maize is an especially important food crop in the hilly districts.
parts.answer: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two uses of maize in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: human food (flour / bread); poultry feed; animal fodder (green maize); starch and cooking oil industries.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why maize production has increased in Punjab in recent years.
parts.answer: Demand from the poultry feed industry has grown; hybrid seeds give high yields; it can be grown in both spring and autumn seasons; it gives better returns than cotton in some areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'subsistence farming'?
parts.answer: Farming to produce food mainly for the farmer's own family, with little or nothing left over to sell.
parts.working: 1 mark: food for the family; 1 mark: little surplus for sale.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is meant by 'commercial farming'?
parts.answer: Farming to produce crops or livestock mainly for sale to make a profit.
parts.working: 1 mark: for sale; 1 mark: profit / market.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two examples of cash crops grown in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: cotton; sugarcane; Basmati rice; tobacco; fruit such as mangoes or kinnow.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'barani' farming?
parts.answer: Farming that depends on rainfall, not irrigation (rain-fed farming).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one area of Pakistan where barani farming is common, and two crops grown there.
parts.answer: Area: Pothwar Plateau (or Thal). Crops: any two of wheat, groundnut, gram, millet, sorghum, pulses.
parts.working: 1 mark area; 1 mark each crop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two problems faced by barani farmers. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rainfall is unreliable, so in a dry year crops fail and farmers lose income; heavy monsoon showers on sloping land cause soil erosion and gullies, reducing farmland; yields are lower than on irrigated land, so incomes are low; few water-storage facilities (small dams) to store rain.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how terraces are made and used in the northern mountains.
parts.answer: Steep hillsides are cut into a series of flat steps; each step is held up by a stone or earth wall; water from streams or glacial meltwater is led along small channels to the terraces; crops such as wheat, maize, potatoes and fruit trees are grown on them.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of terrace farming in mountain areas. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Flat steps slow down run-off, so soil erosion is reduced; water stays on the land longer, so crops get more moisture; they create flat land where there would otherwise be none, increasing the area that can be farmed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the karez system of irrigation used in Balochistan.
parts.answer: A series of vertical wells dug at the foot of the mountains connected by an underground tunnel; the tunnel slopes gently, so groundwater flows by gravity to the fields; being underground, little water is lost to evaporation in the hot, dry climate.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Subsistence farming should be replaced by commercial farming throughout Pakistan.'
View B: 'Subsistence farming is still the best choice for many farmers in Pakistan.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: commercial farming earns money and foreign exchange (cotton, rice, fruit); uses modern inputs and raises yields; feeds the growing cities. View B: small, remote holdings in mountains, deserts and barani areas cannot easily reach markets; subsistence farming spreads risk and provides food security; commercial farming needs capital and loans, which can lead to debt; a crop failure or price fall can ruin a farmer who grows one cash crop. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: A wheat farm can be seen as a system. Classify each of the following as an input, a process or an output: seed, ploughing, grain, fertiliser, harvesting, straw.
parts.answer: Inputs: seed, fertiliser. Processes: ploughing, harvesting. Outputs: grain, straw.
parts.working: 3 marks all six correct; 2 marks four or five; 1 mark two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two physical inputs and two human inputs to a farm system.
parts.answer: Physical: any two of climate (rainfall, temperature, sunshine), soil, relief / slope, water. Human: any two of labour, capital / money, machinery, seed, fertiliser, government policy, market demand.
parts.working: 1 mark for two physical; 1 mark for two human.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems
stem: A farmer grows wheat on 5 acres. Each acre gives 1,600 kg of wheat, sold at Rs 95 per kg. Costs per acre are (hypothetical data): seed Rs 9,000; fertiliser Rs 24,000; irrigation water Rs 6,000; ploughing, harvesting and labour Rs 28,000; pesticide Rs 5,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the income from selling the wheat grown on one acre.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost per acre and the profit per acre.
parts.answer: Cost Rs 72,000; profit Rs 80,000

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the profit from the whole 5-acre farm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two ways the farmer could increase this profit.
parts.answer: Use certified high-yielding seed; laser-level the land to save water and raise yields; sell directly to a government procurement centre or mill instead of a middleman; use the correct amount of fertiliser at the right time; grow a second crop in the kharif season.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one breed of buffalo and one breed of cattle found in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Buffalo: Nili-Ravi or Kundi. Cattle: Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Cholistani or Tharparkar.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three products obtained from livestock.
parts.answer: Any three: milk; meat; hides and skins (leather); wool; eggs (poultry); dung for fuel or manure; draught power.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why livestock are important to poor rural families. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Milk and meat improve the family diet; animals can be sold in an emergency, acting as savings.
parts.working: 1 mark point + 1 mark development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'transhumance'?
parts.answer: The seasonal movement of herders and their animals between summer pastures in the mountains and winter pastures in the lowlands.
parts.working: 1 mark seasonal movement; 1 mark between high and low pastures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why herders in the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan and northern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa move their animals during the year. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In winter high pastures are covered in snow and very cold, so animals are taken down to valleys and plains where there is grazing; in summer lowland grass dries up in the heat while melting snow leaves fresh grass in high alpine pastures, so herds move up; moving prevents overgrazing in one place.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one problem faced by nomadic herders today.
parts.answer: Loss of grazing land to farming or forests being protected; overgrazing; long distances from schools and health care; disputes over grazing rights; droughts.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: A dairy farm near Lahore keeps 40 buffaloes that give an average of 7 litres of milk a day each, and 20 crossbred cows that give an average of 15 litres a day each. Milk is sold at Rs 160 per litre (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the farm's total daily milk production.
parts.answer: 580 litres

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average daily milk yield per animal. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.answer: 9.67 litres

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the farm's income from milk in a 30-day month.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two reasons why milk yields per animal in Pakistan are generally low. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Animals are often underfed with poor-quality fodder, so they produce less milk; little veterinary care, so diseases such as foot-and-mouth reduce yields; most animals are of low-yielding local stock, with little use of improved breeding; heat stress in summer without shade or cooling.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems in the marketing of milk in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Most milk is sold loose through middlemen (gawalas), who pay farmers low prices; there is little cold storage or chilling, so milk spoils quickly in summer; milk is often adulterated with water or chemicals, causing health risks; long distances from villages to cities.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Large commercial dairy farms are the best way to increase milk production in Pakistan.'
View B: 'Helping small farmers with one or two animals would do more for the country.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: commercial farms use improved breeds, balanced feed, veterinary care and machines, giving much higher yields; they can supply processors with chilled, safe milk; they attract investment. View B: millions of rural families keep a few animals, so support (vaccination, training, collection centres, chilling units, microloans) would raise incomes widely and reduce poverty, especially for women; commercial farms need capital, imported breeds, and may suffer heat stress. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

stem: A broiler farmer near Rawalpindi buys 5,000 day-old chicks. 4% of them die before they are sold. The birds that survive weigh an average of 2.1 kg when sold (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of chicks that survive to be sold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of the birds sold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why commercial poultry farming has grown quickly in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Broilers are ready for market in about six weeks, so farmers get a quick return on their money; chicken is cheaper than beef or mutton, so demand from a growing urban population is high; sheds need little land, so farms can be set up near cities; feed mills and hatcheries supply chicks and feed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'deforestation'?
parts.answer: The permanent removal or clearing of forest / trees from an area, so the land is used for something else or left bare.
parts.working: 1 mark removal / cutting of trees; 1 mark large-scale / permanent / not replaced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three causes of deforestation in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any three: cutting trees for fuelwood; illegal logging for timber ('timber mafia'); clearing land for farming; building of roads, houses and towns; overgrazing of young trees by goats and sheep; forest fires; building of hotels in tourist areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Approximately what percentage of Pakistan's land area is covered by forest?
parts.answer: About 5% (accept 4–6%).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how deforestation on mountain slopes can lead to soil erosion. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Without tree cover, heavy rain hits the ground directly and loosens soil; there are no roots to bind the soil together, so it is washed downhill by run-off; on steep slopes this can cause landslides and gullies; less leaf litter means less organic matter to hold the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how deforestation in the upper Indus catchment can increase the risk of floods downstream. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Trees intercept rain and soil absorbs it; when forest is removed more rain becomes surface run-off, which reaches the rivers quickly, so river levels rise faster and higher; eroded soil is deposited in river beds, raising them and reducing their capacity, so they overflow more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

stem: A mountain district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has a total area of 12,500 km². Its forest area was 1,850 km² in 1990 and 1,295 km² in 2020 (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of forest lost between 1990 and 2020, and express it as a percentage of the 1990 forest area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average area of forest lost per year.
parts.answer: 18.5 km² per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the district covered by forest in 2020. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the forest area in this district fell.
parts.answer: Growing population needing fuelwood and timber; clearing for farmland and houses; illegal logging; new roads opening up forests; overgrazing; forest fires.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a valley in Swat, 75% of households use fuelwood as their main cooking fuel. A scheme to supply subsidised LPG cylinders is expected to make 15% of all households switch from fuelwood to LPG (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of households that would still depend on fuelwood after the scheme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many rural households in Pakistan depend on fuelwood. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Many villages are not connected to the gas pipeline network, so wood is the only fuel available; fuelwood can be collected free from nearby forests, while LPG cylinders are expensive for poor families; electricity is unreliable or too costly for cooking and heating, especially in cold mountain winters.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two alternatives to fuelwood that could reduce deforestation.
parts.answer: Any two: LPG cylinders; piped natural gas; biogas plants using animal dung; solar cookers; fuel-efficient stoves; electricity from small hydel plants.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Billion Tree Tsunami project.
parts.answer: An afforestation project in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (2014–2017); aimed to plant or regenerate about one billion trees; included new plantations, protecting areas to allow natural regeneration, and nurseries run by local people; it was later expanded nationally as the Ten Billion Tree Tsunami.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Large tree-planting campaigns such as the Billion Tree Tsunami are the best way to solve deforestation in Pakistan.'
View B: 'Tree-planting campaigns achieve little unless the causes of deforestation are tackled.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: large areas replanted or regenerated; jobs in nurseries for local people; raises public awareness; restores watersheds and reduces erosion; international recognition. View B: many saplings die without watering and protection; planted trees take decades to replace mature forest; demand for fuelwood and timber, illegal logging and overgrazing continue; enforcement of laws, alternative fuels and community management are needed. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

stem: Measurements on two nearby hill slopes of the same steepness over one monsoon season showed soil loss of 42.0 tonnes per hectare from a bare, deforested slope and 1.4 tonnes per hectare from a forested slope (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the soil loss is from the bare slope than from the forested slope.
parts.answer: 30 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how deforestation in the catchment of a reservoir such as Tarbela affects the reservoir. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Eroded soil is carried by rivers into the reservoir and settles as silt; silt reduces the volume of water that can be stored, so less water is available for irrigation in the dry season; less water also means less hydroelectricity; silt damages turbines and shortens the life of the dam.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce silt entering a reservoir.
parts.answer: Afforestation / watershed management in the catchment; check dams; terracing of slopes; controlling grazing.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the difference between 'afforestation' and 'reforestation'?
parts.answer: Afforestation is planting trees on land that has not been forest (or not for a long time); reforestation is replanting trees where forest has recently been cut down.
parts.working: 1 mark each definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is meant by 'sustainable forestry'?
parts.answer: Managing forests so that the trees cut are replaced by new growth, so that forests and their benefits continue for future generations.
parts.working: 1 mark: using / cutting trees; 1 mark: at a rate that allows replacement / for the future.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two methods of sustainable forest management.
parts.answer: Any two: replanting after felling; selective felling instead of clear-felling; fixed felling cycles / quotas; protecting areas for natural regeneration; controlling grazing; community forest management; using fuel-efficient stoves and alternative fuels.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A survey of one creek system in the Indus delta recorded 2,600 hectares of mangroves in an earlier year and 1,950 hectares twenty years later (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the mangrove area that was lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of the loss of mangrove forests in the Indus delta. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Dams and barrages upstream (e.g. Kotri) reduce the flow of fresh water and silt to the delta, so sea water becomes saltier and mangroves die; mangroves are cut for fuelwood and fed to camels and cattle; industrial and sewage pollution from Karachi damages them; land is reclaimed for ports and housing.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two benefits of mangrove forests.
parts.answer: Any two: breeding and nursery grounds for fish and shrimps; protect the coast from storm waves, cyclones and erosion; fuelwood and fodder for local people; habitat for birds and wildlife; store carbon.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A provincial forest department planted 2.4 million saplings in one season. Two years later 1.68 million were still alive. Each sapling cost Rs 40 to raise and plant (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the survival rate of the saplings as a percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total cost of the saplings and the cost per surviving tree. Give the cost per surviving tree to the nearest rupee.
parts.answer: Rs 96,000,000; about Rs 57 per surviving tree

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which poverty is the main cause of deforestation in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Poverty is important: poor rural households cannot afford gas, LPG or electricity, so they cut trees for cooking and heating fuel; poor farmers clear forest for farmland and keep goats and sheep that overgraze young trees; low incomes make villagers willing to work for the timber mafia. Other causes: illegal commercial logging by wealthy contractors for the timber trade; weak law enforcement and corruption; building of roads, hotels and housing (e.g. in tourist valleys); forest fires; rapid population growth increasing demand for wood. Judgement required, e.g. poverty drives fuelwood use but commercial logging and weak enforcement cause much of the loss.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'farm forestry'?
parts.answer: Growing trees on farmland, e.g. along field boundaries, water channels or in small woodlots, alongside crops and livestock.
parts.working: 1 mark trees on farms; 1 mark with crops / along boundaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of farm forestry to farmers. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Trees provide fuelwood and timber that can be used or sold, giving extra income; trees act as windbreaks, reducing wind erosion and protecting crops; leaves provide fodder for animals; roots bind soil and help lower a high water table, reducing waterlogging.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two fast-growing trees often planted on farms in Punjab.
parts.answer: Any two: eucalyptus (safeda); poplar; shisham; kikar; mulberry; bakain.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

stem: A forest department planted trees along both banks of a 320 km stretch of canal, at a rate of 400 trees per kilometre on each bank (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by a 'linear plantation'?
parts.answer: A line of trees planted along a road, railway, canal or river bank.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of trees planted.
parts.working: 320 km × 400 trees per km = 128,000 per bank (M1); × 2 banks = 256,000 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three benefits of planting trees along canals and roads.
parts.answer: Any three: shade for travellers; roots strengthen canal and road banks, reducing erosion; timber and fuelwood; reduce wind and dust; reduce evaporation from canals; improve the landscape; absorb vehicle pollution.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why illegal logging is difficult to control in the mountain forests of northern Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Forests are in remote, steep areas, so forest guards cannot patrol them all; there are too few guards and they are poorly paid, so some may be bribed by the timber mafia; timber is valuable, so profits are high; local people have traditional rights to use forests and laws are weakly enforced.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which local communities could be involved in protecting forests.
parts.answer: Village forest committees to manage and guard forests; sharing income from timber or tourism with villagers; employing local people as guards or in nurseries; awareness campaigns in schools and mosques.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which deforestation affects the livelihoods of people living in mountain areas. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Fuelwood becomes scarce, so women and children must walk further to collect it, losing time for school or other work, or families must buy expensive fuel; soil erosion and landslides on bare slopes destroy terraced fields and orchards, reducing food and income; loss of forest reduces fodder and grazing, so livestock numbers and milk/meat fall; fewer medicinal plants, mushrooms and pine nuts to collect and sell; damaged scenery reduces tourist income.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which deforestation is responsible for the serious floods that have affected Pakistan.
parts.answer: Deforestation contributes: more run-off and faster rises in river levels; silt raises riverbeds; landslides in the north (e.g. Swat). Other causes are often more important: extreme monsoon rainfall and climate change (e.g. 2022); melting glaciers; building on floodplains and in river beds; weak embankments and blocked drains; breaching of canal banks. Judgement required, e.g. deforestation makes floods worse but is not the main cause.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

stem: In a mountain village of 250 households, each household burns an average of 12 kg of fuelwood a day for cooking and heating. One mature tree provides about 500 kg of fuelwood (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of fuelwood one household uses in a year (365 days).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of fuelwood used by the whole village in a year, in tonnes.
parts.answer: 1,095 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of trees that must be cut each year to supply this fuelwood.
parts.answer: 2,190 trees

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why fuelwood collection is a major cause of deforestation in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Even one village needs thousands of trees each year, far more than can regrow naturally; multiplied over thousands of villages without gas, forests are cleared faster than they are replaced.
parts.working: 1 mark use of figures; 1 mark link to rate of regrowth / many villages.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A fire in the pine forests of a hill forest reserve in northern Pakistan burnt 1,200 hectares of the reserve’s 16,000 hectares (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the reserve that was burnt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three causes of forest fires in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any three: very hot, dry weather / heatwaves; lightning; carelessly thrown cigarettes or campfires left by visitors; burning of grass or crop residue spreading into forests; deliberate fires (e.g. to clear land or hide illegal logging); dry pine needles that burn easily.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two effects of forest fires.
parts.answer: Any two: loss of trees and timber; death of wildlife and loss of habitat; soil left bare and eroded; air pollution / smoke; damage to homes and villages; release of carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'overgrazing'?
parts.answer: Keeping too many animals on an area of grazing land for too long, so that vegetation is eaten faster than it can regrow.
parts.working: 1 mark too many animals; 1 mark vegetation cannot recover.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how overgrazing can lead to desertification in Balochistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Goats and sheep eat young shoots and seedlings, so trees and bushes cannot regenerate; bare soil is exposed to strong winds and occasional heavy rain, so the topsoil is eroded; the land loses fertility and moisture, so it becomes desert-like; low and unreliable rainfall means recovery is very slow.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two national parks in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: Khunjerab; Margalla Hills; Ayubia; Hingol; Lal Suhanra; Deosai; Kirthar; Chitral Gol; Central Karakoram.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which national parks and protected areas can conserve Pakistan's forests.
parts.answer: Can help: legal protection stops logging and grazing within park boundaries; protects wildlife and biodiversity; tourism earns income that can pay for guards; research and education. Limits: too few staff and little funding, so illegal cutting continues; local people lose access to fuelwood and grazing, causing conflict; protected areas cover only a small part of forest land; fires and pressure from tourism. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

stem:
Total area and forest area of four districts (hypothetical data):
District A: 6,000 km², forest 1,500 km²
District B: 8,400 km², forest 588 km²
District C: 3,200 km², forest 96 km²
District D: 12,000 km², forest 300 km²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage forest cover of each district. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.working: Forest area ÷ total area × 100 for each. 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage forest cover of the four districts together.
parts.working: Forest 2,484 km² ÷ total 29,600 km² × 100 = 8.4%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Many experts suggest that about 25% of a country's land should be forest. Which district meets this level, and suggest why the others fall short.
parts.answer: District A (25%). The others fall short because they are drier (lowland plains or desert) with little natural forest, because land is used for farming and towns, and because trees have been cut for fuelwood.
parts.working: 1 mark for A; 2 marks for two reasons.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why planting trees in desert areas such as Thar and Cholistan is difficult. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Very low and unreliable rainfall, so saplings need irrigation that is expensive or unavailable; very high summer temperatures and evaporation cause young trees to dry out; sandy soils hold little water or nutrients; shifting sand dunes and strong winds bury or uproot saplings; grazing animals eat them.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read these two views:
View A: 'Providing alternative fuels is the best way to reduce deforestation in Pakistan.'
View B: 'Planting more trees is the best way to reduce deforestation in Pakistan.'
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to examples you have studied.
parts.answer: View A: fuelwood is the main use of cut trees, so gas, LPG, biogas or solar cookers tackle the main cause; protects existing mature forests, which are more valuable than young plantations. View B: tree planting increases forest cover (e.g. Billion Tree Tsunami, mangrove planting in Sindh); provides future fuelwood and timber; restores watersheds; alternative fuels are expensive and gas supplies are limited. Judgement, possibly that both are needed.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Match each forest type with an area where it is found: coniferous forest, mangrove forest, riverine forest, tropical thorn forest. Areas: the Indus delta, the banks of the Indus in Sindh, the plains of Punjab, the mountains around Murree.
parts.answer: Coniferous – mountains around Murree; mangrove – Indus delta; riverine – banks of the Indus in Sindh; tropical thorn – plains of Punjab.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two trees found in coniferous forests in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: deodar; chir pine; blue pine (kail); fir; spruce; chilghoza pine.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two uses of coniferous forests.
parts.answer: Any two: timber for buildings and furniture; fuelwood; resin and turpentine (from chir pine); pine nuts (chilghoza); attracting tourists; protecting watersheds.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the conditions in which coniferous forests grow in Pakistan.
parts.answer: In the northern mountains at altitudes of roughly 1,000–4,000 m; cool to cold temperatures with snow in winter; fairly high rainfall / precipitation from the monsoon and western depressions; on steep slopes with thin soils.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which coniferous trees are adapted to their environment. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Needle-shaped leaves with a waxy coat lose little water, which helps when the ground is frozen; conical shape and flexible branches let snow slide off, so branches do not break; evergreen leaves allow photosynthesis to start as soon as it is warm enough in the short growing season; thick bark protects against cold and fire.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the location of riverine (bela) forests in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Along the banks and floodplains of rivers, especially the Indus in Sindh and southern Punjab.
parts.working: 1 mark rivers / floodplains; 1 mark Indus / Sindh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two trees found in riverine forests.
parts.answer: Any two: babul / kikar; shisham; tamarisk (lai); poplar (bahan).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why riverine forests have declined. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Dams and barrages have reduced the summer floods that these forests need for water and new silt, so trees die and fewer seedlings grow; land along rivers has been cleared for farming as population grows; trees are cut for fuelwood and timber; areas are used to grow crops after floods recede.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

stem:
A transect up a mountainside in northern Pakistan recorded these vegetation zones (hypothetical data):
900–1,800 m: chir pine forest
1,800–3,000 m: deodar and blue pine forest
3,000–3,600 m: fir, spruce and birch
above 3,600 m: alpine grassland and shrubs
The temperature at the valley floor (1,200 m) was 24°C on a summer afternoon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a fall in temperature of 6.5°C for every 1,000 m rise in height, calculate the expected temperature at 3,700 m when it is 24°C at 1,200 m. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data and your answer to explain why vegetation changes as you go up the mountain. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Temperature falls with height, so the growing season becomes shorter higher up; broadleaved and chir pine trees need warmer conditions and grow lower down, while fir and spruce tolerate cold; above about 3,600 m it is too cold and windy, with frozen soils, for trees, so only grasses and small plants (alpine pasture) grow.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which mangrove trees are adapted to grow in coastal swamps.
parts.answer: Breathing roots (pneumatophores) stick up out of the mud to take in air; they can tolerate salt water / get rid of salt through their leaves; stilt or prop roots anchor them in soft mud.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the most common mangrove species in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Avicennia marina (grey / white mangrove, locally 'timar').
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two places on Pakistan's coast where mangroves are found.
parts.answer: Any two: the Indus delta (Sindh); creeks near Karachi (e.g. Sandspit / Korangi creek); Miani Hor (Sonmiani); Kalmat Khor; Jiwani.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Changa Manga is an irrigated plantation in Punjab. Describe what is meant by an 'irrigated plantation'.
parts.answer: A forest planted by people on land in the plains where natural rainfall is too low, and watered from canals.
parts.working: 1 mark planted / man-made; 1 mark watered by canal irrigation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two trees grown in irrigated plantations.
parts.answer: Any two: shisham; mulberry; eucalyptus; kikar; poplar; bakain.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two benefits of irrigated plantations such as Changa Manga. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: They supply timber and fuelwood to nearby cities, reducing pressure on natural forests; mulberry wood is used for sports goods and furniture, supporting local industries; they are used for recreation and tourism; they provide wildlife habitat and help reduce wind erosion in the plains.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two trees or shrubs found in tropical thorn forests in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: kikar (Acacia); ber; jand (khejri); karir; frash.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which plants in tropical thorn forests are adapted to dry conditions. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Long tap roots reach water deep underground, so plants survive months without rain; small leaves or thorns reduce the surface area for transpiration, so less water is lost; thick bark and waxy leaves reduce water loss; thorns also protect plants from grazing animals.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one use of these forests to local people.
parts.answer: Fuelwood; fodder for goats and camels; timber for tools and fencing; fruit (ber); shade.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the juniper forest at Ziarat in Balochistan.
parts.answer: One of the largest juniper forests in the world; contains very slow-growing trees, some of which are thousands of years old; grows on mountain slopes in a cold, dry climate; protected as a biosphere reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which the juniper forest at Ziarat is under threat.
parts.answer: Threats: cutting for fuelwood in very cold winters; overgrazing of seedlings by goats and sheep, so few young trees grow; very slow growth means losses cannot be replaced quickly; droughts and climate change; disease (e.g. dwarf mistletoe) and pests; pressure from tourism and roads. Protection: legal status as a protected area, conservation projects, gas supply to some villages, awareness. Judgement required.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points, one side or generic. L2 (3–4): developed points on one side, or simple points on both sides. L3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with a named Pakistani example and a reasoned judgement.

stem:
Area of forest in a country by type, thousand hectares (hypothetical data):
coniferous 2,000; scrub and thorn 1,000; mangrove 400; riverine 300; irrigated plantations 300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle for each forest type on a pie chart.
parts.answer: coniferous 180°, scrub and thorn 90°, mangrove 36°, riverine 27°, irrigated plantations 27°
parts.working: Total = 4,000. Area ÷ 4,000 × 360. 3 marks all correct; 2 marks three or four; 1 mark method only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the forest area that is coniferous.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why most of Pakistan's natural forest is found in the north.
parts.answer: The northern mountains receive more rainfall and snowfall; cooler temperatures reduce evaporation; the plains and south are too dry and the land is used for farming.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two points.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe where alpine pastures are found in Pakistan.
parts.answer: High in the northern mountains above the tree line (roughly above 3,500 m), e.g. in Gilgit-Baltistan, Chitral and upper Swat or Kaghan; the Deosai Plains.
parts.working: 1 mark altitude / above tree line; 1 mark named area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why trees cannot grow in alpine areas. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Temperatures are very low and the growing season is too short for trees; strong winds, frozen and thin soils and snow cover for much of the year.
parts.working: 1 mark point + 1 mark development.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which alpine pastures are used by people. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Herders take sheep, goats and yaks up to graze in summer (transhumance), which provides meat, milk and wool; medicinal herbs are collected and sold; tourists visit for trekking and camping, bringing income; summer settlements make butter and cheese.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two trees found in the sub-tropical dry broadleaved forests of the Pothwar Plateau and Margalla Hills.
parts.answer: Any two: wild olive (kahu); phulahi; sanatha (shrub); kikar; ber.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why these forests are often thin and scattered. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rainfall is moderate and falls mainly in the monsoon, so there is a long dry season; the hills have thin, stony soils that are easily eroded; heavy grazing by goats and cutting for fuelwood near towns such as Islamabad and Rawalpindi; frequent fires in the dry season.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two reasons + 1 mark each for development (a consequence or 'which leads to').

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way these forests are important to nearby cities.
parts.answer: They protect water catchments (e.g. for Rawal / Simly dams); recreation and tourism (e.g. Margalla Hills National Park); reduce soil erosion and flooding; improve air quality.
parts.working: 1 mark.

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Battle of Plassey (1757).
parts.answer: Fought in Bengal in 1757 between the East India Company under Robert Clive and the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. Clive's force was much smaller, but Mir Jafar, the Nawab's commander, had been promised the throne and kept his troops out of the fight. Siraj-ud-Daulah was defeated and later killed. Mir Jafar became Nawab under Company control.
parts.working: 1 mark per accurate point, max 4: Siraj-ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal; Company army led by Clive; Company heavily outnumbered; Mir Jafar's treachery / bribed to stay out of battle; Nawab defeated and killed; Mir Jafar made a puppet Nawab; Company gained control of Bengal's trade and wealth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the East India Company won the Battle of Plassey.
parts.answer: Mir Jafar's betrayal meant a large part of the Nawab's army did not fight, so the Company did not need to beat the full force. The Company's troops were better trained and disciplined and had effective artillery, so they held firm when the Nawab's attack faltered.
parts.working: Level-style: 1 mark per reason identified, +1 for each explained (max 2 reasons x 2). Reasons: treachery of Mir Jafar / other nobles; superior discipline and training; artillery and firepower; Clive's leadership; Nawab's unpopularity with Hindu bankers (Jagat Seth).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Battle of Buxar (1764) and the settlement that followed it.
parts.answer: The Company, led by Hector Munro, defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim (former Nawab of Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daulah (Nawab of Awadh) and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) Shah Alam granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, the right to collect their land revenue.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4: date/place in Bihar; Munro; the three allies named (1 mark for any two); allies defeated; Treaty of Allahabad 1765; Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; Shah Alam given a pension / Allahabad and Kora.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Buxar was a more important victory for the Company than Plassey.
parts.answer: At Plassey the Company won largely by bribery against one ruler; at Buxar it defeated the Mughal emperor and two Nawabs in open battle, showing its military power. Buxar also brought the Diwani, giving the Company legal right to Bengal's revenue, which paid for its army and further expansion.
parts.working: 2 explained points, 2 marks each: open military victory, not treachery; defeated the emperor himself, ending Mughal authority in the east; Diwani gave legal revenue rights; revenue funded armies for further conquest.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a Subsidiary Alliance required of an Indian ruler.
parts.answer: The ruler had to accept a force of Company troops in his state and pay for them (in cash or by giving up territory). A British Resident was placed at his court. He could not employ other Europeans, especially the French, and could not make war or treaties without Company permission.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: British troops stationed in state; ruler pays for them / cedes land; British Resident at court; no other Europeans employed; foreign policy controlled by Company; introduced by Lord Wellesley (1798); Hyderabad first to accept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the Subsidiary Alliance system helped the British to expand their control.
parts.answer: Rulers lost control of their armies and foreign policy, so they became dependent on the Company without a war. If a ruler failed to pay for the troops the Company took his land, so territory grew cheaply; the Company also had an army paid for by Indians in the heart of each state.
parts.working: 2 explained points x 2: control without fighting; land ceded when payments fell behind; Indian rulers paid for British troops; French influence removed; Resident interfered in internal affairs.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Who was Tipu Sultan?
parts.answer: Ruler of Mysore in southern India (from 1782), son of Haider Ali, who fought the East India Company in the Anglo-Mysore wars.
parts.working: 1 for ruler of Mysore; 1 for son of Haider Ali / fought the British in the Mysore wars.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Tipu Sultan was defeated by the British in 1799.
parts.answer: Tipu could not get real help from the French, who were busy with wars in Europe and Egypt. The Nizam of Hyderabad and the Marathas allied with the British instead of with him. The Company had greater resources and men, and some of Tipu's own officials betrayed him; he was killed defending his capital, Seringapatam.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per explained reason, max 5: lack of French help; neighbouring rulers (Nizam, Marathas) sided with the British; Company's superior resources / Wellesley's determination; treachery within his court; siege and fall of Seringapatam.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Doctrine of Lapse.
parts.answer: Introduced by Lord Dalhousie (Governor-General 1848–56): if a ruler of a dependent state died without a natural male heir, his state passed (lapsed) to the Company; adopted sons were not accepted as heirs. Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur were taken this way.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Dalhousie; no natural male heir → state annexed; adopted heir not recognised; example (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Doctrine of Lapse caused anger among Indians.
parts.answer: Adoption of an heir was an accepted Hindu custom, so refusing to recognise adopted sons was seen as an attack on religion and tradition. Ruling families lost their thrones and pensions (for example the Rani of Jhansi), and their soldiers and servants lost jobs, creating powerful enemies who later joined the 1857 rising.
parts.working: 2 explained points x 2: against custom of adoption; rulers dispossessed; loss of jobs for courtiers/soldiers; fear that no state was safe; link to leaders of 1857.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the British took control of Sindh and the Punjab in the 1840s.
parts.answer: Sindh: Charles Napier defeated the Talpur Amirs at the Battle of Miani (1843) and Sindh was annexed. Punjab: after Ranjit Singh's death (1839) the Sikh state became unstable; the British won the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46) and took land and control, then annexed the Punjab in 1849 after the Second Anglo-Sikh War.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: Napier; Talpur Amirs; Miani 1843; Ranjit Singh's death and instability; two Anglo-Sikh wars; Punjab annexed 1849 (Dalhousie).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the British wanted to control Sindh.
parts.answer: Sindh controlled the Indus River and the route to Afghanistan, which mattered after the First Afghan War, and the British feared Russian advance from Central Asia. The Indus and the port of Karachi also offered trade routes into the interior.
parts.working: 2 explained points x 2: strategic route to Afghanistan / fear of Russia; control of the Indus for trade and transport; port of Karachi; wish to restore prestige after Afghan defeat.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the Governor-General who introduced the Subsidiary Alliance and the one who introduced the Doctrine of Lapse.
parts.answer: Lord Wellesley (Subsidiary Alliance); Lord Dalhousie (Doctrine of Lapse).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Military strength was the most important reason why the British were able to take control of much of the subcontinent by 1850.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: victories at Plassey, Buxar, the Mysore, Maratha and Sikh wars depended on disciplined, well-armed troops. Disagree: much was won by diplomacy and policy (Subsidiary Alliance, Doctrine of Lapse), by treachery (Mir Jafar) and because Indian rulers were divided and the Mughal empire was weak; Company wealth from Bengal's revenue paid for armies. Judgement: military power mattered, but disunity among Indian rulers made it effective.
parts.working: Level marking (14 marks). L1 (1–2): general statements with no relevant detail. L2 (3–6): identifies or describes relevant factors without explaining them. L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). L4 (9–13): explains factors on both sides (more developed points and accurate detail move the answer up the band). L5 (14): as L4, plus a supported judgement that answers 'how far' (or 'was it the most important'). Content points (credit any relevant, accurate point; each needs explaining, not just stating) — Military strength: disciplined, well-armed troops; victories at Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764, Mysore, Maratha and Sikh wars; naval power. Other reasons: divisions among Indian rulers; Mughal decline; Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley) and Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie); bribery and treachery (Mir Jafar); Company wealth from Bengal revenue paid for armies. A judgement must weigh the stated factor against the others, not just repeat the question.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main changes made by the Regulating Act (1773) and Pitt's India Act (1784).
parts.answer: Regulating Act: the Governor of Bengal became Governor-General (Warren Hastings), with a council of four, and a Supreme Court was set up at Calcutta; the British government began to supervise the Company. Pitt's India Act: a Board of Control in London, appointed by the government, oversaw the Company's political affairs, giving dual control by Company and Crown.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4 (at least one per Act for full marks): Governor-General of Bengal; council of four; Supreme Court at Calcutta; Board of Control; dual control; Company kept trade.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the British government passed laws to control the East India Company in this period.
parts.answer: Company officials were becoming rich through corruption and private trade while the Company itself was near bankruptcy and asked Parliament for loans. Parliament also felt that ruling millions of people was too important to leave to a trading company, so it wanted political oversight.
parts.working: 2 explained points x 2: corruption of officials; Company's financial crisis / loans; ruling territory is a government matter; misrule in Bengal / famine 1770.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company
stem: Source A (written for this question): 'After the 1760s the Company's servants no longer acted only as merchants. They collected taxes, kept armies and decided who sat on the throne of Bengal. A Nawab who tried to stop them, such as Mir Qasim, soon found himself at war with them.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to Source A, identify three ways in which the Company acted as more than a trading company.
parts.answer: It collected taxes; it kept armies; it decided who ruled Bengal (chose the Nawab).
parts.working: 1 mark each, from the source only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Mir Qasim came into conflict with the East India Company.
parts.answer: Mir Qasim tried to rule independently: he moved his capital to Monghyr and built up his own army. He objected to Company officials misusing dastaks (duty-free trade permits) for private trade, which ruined Indian merchants and cut his revenue, and when he abolished duties for everyone the Company went to war (1763).
parts.working: 2 explained points x 2: misuse of dastaks; loss of revenue; abolished all duties; independent army/capital; led to war and Buxar.

parts.answer: After 1857 Muslims were distrusted by the British and lacked English, so they could not get government jobs that Hindus were taking. Sir Syed believed learning English and science would let Muslims compete, regain status and show loyalty, while keeping their faith.
