parts.answer: Deforestation in the catchments of the northern hills means less rain is intercepted and more runs off quickly, so river levels rise faster. Building houses and roads on floodplains and in old river beds puts more people and property in the path of floods and blocks the natural flow of water.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: deforestation; building on floodplains/riverbeds; blocked drains/encroachment; poorly maintained embankments; climate change from emissions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Building more embankments is the best way to reduce flood damage in Pakistan.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: Embankments protect towns and farmland from normal floods and are relatively cheap, but they can fail in extreme floods (as in 2010 and 2022), give a false sense of safety and move the problem downstream. Other methods such as early-warning systems, planting trees in catchments, storage dams and keeping people off high-risk floodplains may be more effective. A balanced answer reaches a judgement.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) both sides developed with a conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the sea into which the Indus flows and the landform it has built at its mouth.
parts.answer: The Arabian Sea; a delta (the Indus Delta).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the Indus Delta is shrinking.
parts.answer: Dams and barrages upstream trap silt and take water for irrigation, so little water or sediment reaches the delta to build it up. With less river flow, sea water pushes inland (sea intrusion), eroding the coast and making land saline.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: less freshwater below Kotri; silt trapped behind dams; sea-water intrusion / coastal erosion; mangrove loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the Indus rises.
parts.answer: In Tibet (near Lake Mansarovar / Mount Kailash), China.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the river on which Mangla Dam is built.
parts.answer: The Jhelum.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the course of the Indus through Pakistan.
parts.answer: It enters Pakistan in Gilgit-Baltistan and flows through deep gorges in the northern mountains, then southwards past Tarbela and Attock (where the Kabul joins). It crosses the Punjab plains, receives the Panjnad near Mithankot, then flows through Sindh past Sukkur and Hyderabad to the Arabian Sea.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3: north (Gilgit-Baltistan, gorges); flows south; Attock / Kabul River; Panjnad near Mithankot; through Sindh to Arabian Sea / delta.

stem: On a map with a scale of 1 : 2,000,000, the straight-line distance between Taunsa Barrage and Guddu Barrage on the Indus measures 12.9 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many kilometres does 1 cm on this map represent?
parts.answer: 20 km.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the straight-line distance between the two barrages in kilometres.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the distance along the river is greater than the straight-line distance.
parts.answer: The river meanders across its floodplain, so it follows a winding course that is longer than a straight line.
parts.working: 1 for meanders/bends; 1 for development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a natural levee forms.
parts.answer: When a river floods it spreads out over its floodplain and slows down suddenly at the edge of the channel. The coarsest, heaviest sediment is dropped first, closest to the channel. Repeated floods build these deposits into raised banks (levees).
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why rivers in the plains of Pakistan change their course from time to time.
parts.answer: The rivers carry huge loads of silt from the mountains, which are deposited on the river bed, raising it above the surrounding plain. In a large flood the river can break through its banks and take a new, lower route, as the Indus and its tributaries have done in the past.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3: heavy silt load; bed raised; breaks levees in floods; flat land / gentle gradient lets channel shift; meanders migrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems that heavy silt loads in rivers cause for people in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Silt settles in reservoirs such as Tarbela, reducing the amount of water they can store for irrigation and power. Silt also fills canals, so they must be cleaned regularly, which is costly, and river beds rise, increasing flood risk.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: reservoir capacity loss; canal desilting cost; raised riverbeds/flooding; damage to turbines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce the amount of silt entering rivers.
parts.answer: Plant trees / terrace slopes in the catchment areas to reduce soil erosion (or check dams).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the desert found in south-east Sindh.
parts.answer: The Thar Desert.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the desert in the Bahawalpur region of Punjab.
parts.answer: The Cholistan Desert.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the desert that lies between the Indus and the Jhelum rivers.
parts.answer: The Thal Desert.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the sandy desert found in western Balochistan.
parts.answer: The Kharan Desert.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem:
Average monthly rainfall (mm) at a weather station in the Thar Desert (figures approximate, for this question):
Jan: 2
Feb: 3
Mar: 2
Apr: 1
May: 4
Jun: 18
Jul: 95
Aug: 82
Sep: 26
Oct: 3
Nov: 1
Dec: 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total annual rainfall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the annual rainfall that falls in July and August. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Thar Desert receives so little rain.
parts.answer: The monsoon winds reach it last, after losing much of their moisture, and there are no mountains to force the air to rise and cool. Winds blowing from the dry west / high pressure in winter bring no rain, and high temperatures cause rapid evaporation.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3: far from moisture source / end of monsoon track; no relief to cause uplift; dry winds; high evaporation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two physical features of the Thar Desert.
parts.answer: Sand dunes (some moving); sandy soils; very low, unreliable rainfall; high summer temperatures and large daily temperature range; scrub vegetation; few permanent rivers (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which people in the Thar Desert make a living.
parts.answer: Many keep goats, sheep, cattle and camels because animals can graze sparse scrub and move to find pasture. Some grow millet and other drought-tolerant crops in the rainy season when the monsoon brings enough rain; others work in handicrafts (embroidery, weaving) or in the Thar coalfield.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: livestock herding; rain-fed crops (millet, guar); handicrafts; coal mining; migration for work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'desertification'.
parts.answer: The process by which land in dry areas becomes desert-like, losing its vegetation and soil fertility, as a result of human activity and/or climate change.
parts.working: 1 for land becoming desert/ degraded; 1 for causes (human activity or climate) / dry areas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two human causes of desertification in Cholistan.
parts.answer: Overgrazing by large herds removes the grass and shrubs that hold the soil, so wind blows the soil away. Cutting trees and shrubs for fuelwood has the same effect, and over-pumping groundwater lowers the water table so plants die.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: overgrazing; fuelwood collection; overuse of groundwater; poor farming practices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how canal irrigation changed the Thal Desert.
parts.answer: Canals from the Jinnah Barrage (the Thal Canal) brought river water to the desert, so land that had only sparse grazing could grow wheat, cotton, sugarcane and gram. Settlements, roads and markets grew up and dunes were levelled for fields, although some areas later suffered waterlogging and salinity.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each, max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why irrigation has not been extended to most of the Thar Desert.
parts.answer: The Thar is far from large river barrages / canal systems in parts; shifting sand dunes would fill canals; high evaporation and porous sand mean water losses would be huge; high cost compared with likely returns (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is a 'toba' in Cholistan?
parts.answer: A natural or dug hollow / pond that collects rainwater for people and animals.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems faced by people living in the Cholistan Desert.
parts.answer: Water is scarce because rain is low and unreliable; tobas dry up in long droughts, forcing families to migrate with their animals. Services are few because people are scattered and roads are poor, so access to schools and health care is limited.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: water shortage; drought kills livestock; poor transport; few services; extreme heat.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to improve the water supply for these people.
parts.answer: Lining tobas / building covered tanks; solar-powered tube wells; pipelines from canals; desalination of saline groundwater (any one).
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: In June, the average daytime maximum at a station in the Kharan Desert is about 44 °C and the night-time minimum about 23 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the daily (diurnal) temperature range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why deserts have a large diurnal range of temperature.
parts.answer: Clear skies with few clouds let strong sunshine heat the ground quickly by day. At night there is no cloud cover to trap heat, so it is lost rapidly by radiation. Dry air and sand / bare rock heat and cool quickly.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a barchan (crescent-shaped dune) forms.
parts.answer: Wind blowing mainly from one direction drives sand into a heap. Sand is blown up the gentle windward slope and falls down the steep leeward (slip) face. The edges move faster than the higher middle, so the 'horns' point downwind, giving a crescent shape.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The deserts of Pakistan have more advantages than disadvantages for the country.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: Advantages: Thar coal reserves; potential for solar power; tourism (Derawar Fort, jeep rallies in Cholistan); livestock and handicrafts; land that can be irrigated (Thal). Disadvantages: water shortage, droughts and famine; poverty and poor services; desertification spreading; difficult transport. A judgement is needed.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) both sides developed with a judgement.

stem: K2 in the Karakoram is about 8611 m high and Nanga Parbat in the Himalayas about 8126 m high.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much higher K2 is than Nanga Parbat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the mountain range in which Tirich Mir is found.
parts.answer: The Hindu Kush.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two mountain ranges in the western mountains of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: Sulaiman, Kirthar, Safed Koh, Toba Kakar, Waziristan Hills, Chagai Hills, Makran Coast Ranges.
parts.working: 1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the Potwar Plateau.
parts.answer: An upland area between the Jhelum and Indus rivers, south of the northern mountains and north of the Salt Range; height roughly 300–600 m; land deeply cut by gullies (badland topography) from soil erosion; contains oil and gas fields.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why soil erosion is a serious problem on the Potwar Plateau.
parts.answer: Rain falls in heavy monsoon downpours on soft soils, so running water cuts deep gullies. Natural vegetation has been removed by grazing and fuelwood cutting, leaving the soil unprotected.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: heavy rain; soft soils; sloping land; deforestation; overgrazing.

stem: Air temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for every 1000 m rise in height. On a June afternoon the temperature at a town in the plains (near sea level) is 32 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the temperature at the same time at a hill station 2400 m higher. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 fall of 15.6 °C; A1 16.4 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hill stations such as Murree attract visitors in summer.
parts.answer: Their height makes them much cooler than the hot plains, so people go there to escape the heat; they also have forests and scenery.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the pass on the Karakoram Highway at the border with China.
parts.answer: Khunjerab Pass.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the pass between Peshawar and Afghanistan.
parts.answer: Khyber Pass.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the pass that links Sibi with Quetta.
parts.answer: Bolan Pass.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why mountain passes have been important in the history and trade of Pakistan.
parts.answer: They are gaps through otherwise high mountain barriers, so they have been the routes taken by traders, travellers and invaders entering the subcontinent. Today roads and railways use them, for example the Karakoram Highway for trade with China and the Khyber route to Afghanistan.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the northern mountains are important to the rest of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Glaciers and snowfields in the Karakoram and Himalayas feed the Indus and its tributaries, which supply irrigation water to the plains. The steep rivers in the mountains give sites for hydroelectric power such as Tarbela and the planned Diamer-Bhasha Dam.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: water source; HEP; tourism; forests/timber; barrier to cold winds from Central Asia; minerals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two natural hazards found in the northern mountains.
parts.answer: Any two: landslides blocking roads such as the Karakoram Highway; avalanches; earthquakes (e.g. 2005); glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs); flash floods.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Salt Range.
parts.answer: A line of hills in northern Punjab at the southern edge of the Potwar Plateau, running roughly east–west between the Jhelum and the Indus; height up to about 1,500 m; contains large rock-salt deposits, mined at Khewra, as well as gypsum, limestone and coal.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Balochistan Plateau is thinly populated.
parts.answer: It is very dry with low, unreliable rainfall and few permanent rivers, so there is little water for farming. The land is rugged and rocky with poor soils, and summers are very hot and winters cold, making transport and services difficult to provide.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape and direction of the western mountains.
parts.answer: They run roughly north to south along the western border (from the Safed Koh down to the Kirthar near the coast), lower than the northern ranges, in parallel ridges with valleys between.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The mountains of Pakistan are more of a barrier than a resource.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: Barrier: rugged relief makes roads and railways expensive and dangerous; landslides cut communities off; few people can farm the steep slopes. Resource: water from glaciers and snow for irrigation; HEP; tourism (K2, Hunza, Swat); forests; minerals; defensive barrier. Judgement required.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) both sides developed with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the country that borders Pakistan to the north-east.
parts.answer: China.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two countries that border Pakistan to the west.
parts.answer: Afghanistan and Iran.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the province whose capital is Peshawar.
parts.answer: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the provincial capital of Balochistan.
parts.answer: Quetta.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: Approximate areas (km²): Balochistan 347,190; Punjab 205,344; Sindh 140,914; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 101,741; Islamabad Capital Territory 906.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total area of these five units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Balochistan's area as a percentage of this total. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Balochistan has the largest area but the smallest population of the four provinces. Suggest two reasons for this.
parts.answer: Dry climate with little water for farming; rugged mountains and plateaus; poor transport links; few job opportunities (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's position in the world using latitude and neighbouring regions.
parts.answer: Pakistan lies roughly between 24° N and 37° N, in South Asia, north of the Arabian Sea. It is close to the Middle East (Gulf) to the west and Central Asia to the north, with China to the north-east and India to the east.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3: approximate latitude; South Asia; Arabian Sea coastline; links to Middle East / Central Asia / China.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of Pakistan's location for trade.
parts.answer: Its ports (Karachi, Gwadar) on the Arabian Sea are near the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf, so it can serve major shipping routes and oil-producing countries. It can act as a land route for landlocked Afghanistan and Central Asian states and for western China (CPEC) to reach the sea, earning transit income.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: coastline and ports; near Gulf; transit for Afghanistan/Central Asia; CPEC link with China.

stem: Pakistan stretches from about 24° N to about 37° N. One degree of latitude is about 111 km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the north–south extent of Pakistan in kilometres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this north–south extent and the range of relief lead to a variety of climates within Pakistan.
parts.answer: The south is closer to the tropics and near sea level, so it is hot all year, with the coast moderated by the sea. The north is further from the Equator and much higher, so it has cold winters with snow and mild summers, and the mountains also block or receive monsoon rain differently.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: latitude; altitude; distance from sea; relief and rainfall.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the narrow strip of Afghan territory that separates Pakistan from Tajikistan.
parts.answer: The Wakhan Corridor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the largest city of Sindh, which is also Pakistan's main seaport.
parts.answer: Karachi.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the deep-sea port on the Makran coast developed with Chinese help.
parts.answer: Gwadar.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two reasons why Punjab has the largest population of the provinces.
parts.answer: Fertile, flat plains watered by five rivers and canals; large irrigated farming; many industries and large cities (Lahore, Faisalabad); good transport links (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

stem: In an illustrative example, a country has about 230 billion m³ of renewable water a year and a population of about 250 million. Countries with less than 1,000 m³ per person per year are said to face water scarcity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water available per person per year.
parts.answer: 230 billion ÷ 250 million = 920 m³ per person.
parts.working: M1 correct division with units; A1 920 m³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this country faces water scarcity, giving a reason.
parts.answer: Yes: 920 m³ is below 1,000 m³ per person.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why water available per person is falling in Pakistan.
parts.answer: The population is growing rapidly, so the same water is shared among more people. Reservoirs are losing storage to silt and little new storage has been built, while groundwater is being over-pumped faster than it is recharged.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: population growth; silting of reservoirs; limited new dams; over-pumping of groundwater; wastage; climate change and reduced glacier flows.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of drinking water for people in Pakistan's cities.
parts.answer: Any two: rivers/canals (e.g. Indus via Keenjhar Lake for Karachi); reservoirs/dams (Simly, Khanpur, Hub); groundwater from tube wells; bottled or tanker water.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of water pollution in rivers near large cities.
parts.answer: Untreated sewage from homes is emptied straight into rivers and drains because there are few treatment plants. Factories such as tanneries and textile mills discharge chemicals and dyes without treatment, poisoning the water.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: raw sewage; industrial effluent; solid waste dumping; agricultural run-off (fertilisers, pesticides).

stem: A survey of 400 households in a village in southern Punjab found that 136 had piped water at home, 212 used a hand pump or tube well and the rest collected water from a canal or pond.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of households with piped water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many households collected water from a canal or pond.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two health risks for the households that use canal or pond water.
parts.answer: The water may carry bacteria and viruses from sewage and animals, causing diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid, especially in children. Standing water also breeds mosquitoes, spreading malaria and dengue.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: water-borne diseases; mosquito-borne disease; chemical contamination from farm run-off.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many people in Karachi suffer from water shortages.
parts.answer: The city's population has grown faster than its water supply, which depends mainly on the Indus (via Keenjhar Lake) and Hub Dam. Much water is lost through leaking pipes and illegal connections, and a 'tanker mafia' sells water at high prices.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: population growth; limited sources / dependence on Indus and Hub; leakage and theft; unequal distribution; low rainfall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to improve water supply to a large city like Karachi.
parts.answer: Any two: repair leaking pipes; stop illegal connections; build new supply schemes (e.g. bulk water projects); desalination plants; recycle treated waste water for industry; rainwater harvesting.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) affects water supply in Pakistan.
parts.answer: The treaty gave the three eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India and the three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan. To replace the eastern river water, Pakistan built link canals, Mangla and Tarbela dams and barrages under the Indus Basin Project; the Ravi and Sutlej now carry little water through Pakistan except in floods.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each, max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Pakistan's water shortage is caused more by poor management than by a lack of water.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: Management: large losses from unlined canals; flood irrigation wastes water; little storage (only about a month of river flow); low water charges encourage waste; pollution makes water unusable. Natural/limited supply: arid climate, low rainfall in most of the country, dependence on one river system, variable monsoon and glacier melt, rising population. Judgement required.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) both sides developed with judgement.

stem: A school in Islamabad collects rainwater from a roof of area 120 m². The annual rainfall is taken as 500 mm, and about 80% of the water falling on the roof can be stored.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water the school can collect in a year, in m³.
parts.working: M1 area × rainfall in metres; A1 48 m³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits of rainwater harvesting in Pakistan.
parts.answer: It reduces demand on piped supply and groundwater, so water tables fall more slowly. It stores monsoon water that would otherwise run off, which can be used for gardens, toilets or recharging aquifers, and it reduces urban flooding.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'groundwater'.
parts.answer: Water stored underground in the soil and in permeable rocks (aquifers).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the water table under Lahore has fallen.
parts.answer: A growing city pumps large amounts of water from tube wells for homes and industry, faster than rain and rivers recharge it. The Ravi now carries little water and paved surfaces stop rain soaking into the ground, so recharge is reduced.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: over-pumping; population growth; reduced Ravi flow; less recharge from paved surfaces.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one problem caused by a falling water table.
parts.answer: Wells and hand pumps dry up / deeper, more expensive pumping / poorer-quality (saline or arsenic-rich) water drawn up.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two effects of polluted water on farming and fishing in the Indus Delta and lower Sindh.
parts.answer: Any two: crops irrigated with contaminated water give lower yields or unsafe food; fish stocks fall in lakes such as Manchar; fishermen lose income; mangroves damaged.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which industrial water pollution could be reduced.
parts.answer: Factories could be made by law to install treatment plants before releasing waste, with fines for breaking the rules. Industrial estates could share combined effluent treatment plants, which are cheaper for small firms.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: laws/enforcement (EPA); treatment plants; combined plants in estates; recycling water; relocating polluting industry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rural women and children are most affected by water shortages.
parts.answer: In many villages it is their task to fetch water, so they walk long distances carrying heavy loads. This takes time from school and paid work, and lack of clean water at home increases illness among children.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which climate change may affect Pakistan's future water supply.
parts.answer: Higher temperatures are melting glaciers faster, giving more water at first but less in the long term as glaciers shrink. Rainfall is becoming more variable, with more droughts and more intense floods, making supply less reliable.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: glacier melt; changes to monsoon; higher evaporation; more floods/droughts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of water in Pakistan other than for irrigation.
parts.answer: Any two: drinking/domestic use; industry (cooling, processing); hydroelectric power; fishing; transport; recreation/tourism.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Agriculture uses about nine-tenths of the water taken from rivers and groundwater in Pakistan. Suggest two reasons why.
parts.answer: Pakistan's climate is mainly arid or semi-arid, so most crops need irrigation; thirsty crops such as rice and sugarcane are widely grown; flood irrigation wastes much water (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

stem: A town's water board pumps 1200 thousand litres a day into its pipes, but meters show only 780 thousand litres a day reach homes and businesses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of water lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two causes of this loss and one way to reduce it.
parts.answer: Causes: leaking, old pipes; illegal connections / theft; unmetered use. Reduction: replace or repair pipes; detect and remove illegal connections; install meters.
parts.working: 1 each for two causes; 1 for a matching solution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a karez works.
parts.answer: A karez is an underground channel dug into the foot of a hill or alluvial fan. It carries groundwater by gravity to the surface at a lower level. Vertical shafts at intervals are used for digging and cleaning; water is used in fields and villages, for example in Balochistan.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of the karez system in Balochistan.
parts.answer: Because the water flows underground, little is lost by evaporation in the hot, dry climate. It works by gravity, so no fuel or electricity is needed and it can supply water all year.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: low evaporation; no pumping cost; reliable supply; community-managed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the difference between a perennial canal and an inundation canal?
parts.answer: A perennial canal takes water from a barrage or dam and flows all year; an inundation canal flows only when the river is high in summer floods.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of inundation canals.
parts.answer: They have no water in winter when the river is low, so rabi crops cannot be irrigated. Their supply depends on the size of the flood: a poor flood brings too little water and a big flood can damage fields.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

stem: In a canal command area, 25% of the water entering the main canal is lost by seepage and evaporation before reaching the watercourses, and a further 20% of what remains is lost in the watercourses before reaching the fields.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For every 100 units of water entering the canal, calculate how many units reach the fields.
parts.working: M1 successive reductions; A1 60.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to reduce these losses.
parts.answer: Line canals and watercourses with bricks or concrete; cover/pipe watercourses; remove weeds and repair banks; level fields (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A farmer near Multan irrigates orchards using flooding, which uses about 6000 m³ of water per hectare per season. Drip irrigation would use 40% less water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water used per hectare with drip irrigation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total water saved on 15 hectares in one season.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why few farmers in Pakistan use drip irrigation.
parts.answer: High cost of pipes and equipment; small farms and poor farmers; lack of knowledge/training; canal water is cheap so there is little reason to save it; electricity/power needed for pumps (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two traditional methods of lifting water from wells in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: Persian wheel; shaduf; charsa (leather bag pulled by animals); hand pump.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tube wells have become a common method of irrigation.
parts.answer: They can supply water whenever the farmer needs it, including when canals are closed. They supplement canal water in areas at the tail end of canals and also help lower high water tables. Cheap diesel and electric pumps and government schemes encouraged them.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

stem: A tube well pumps water at 0.03 m³ per second and runs for 8 hours a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water pumped in one day.
parts.working: M1 convert hours to seconds; A1 864 m³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by the rapid growth in the number of private tube wells.
parts.answer: Over-pumping lowers the water table, so wells must be deepened and pumping costs rise. In some areas the deeper water is saline, and using it damages soil; high fuel and electricity costs also burden farmers.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: falling water table; saline groundwater; energy cost/load-shedding; inequality between rich and poor farmers.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe sprinkler irrigation.
parts.answer: Water is pumped through pipes and sprayed over crops through nozzles, like rain.
parts.working: 1 for pipes/pump; 1 for spraying like rain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare sprinkler irrigation with flood irrigation.
parts.answer: Sprinklers use less water and spread it more evenly, giving less waterlogging and salinity; they suit uneven land. Flood irrigation is cheap and simple and needs no energy, but wastes water through run-off and seepage. Sprinklers cost more and need power and maintenance.
parts.working: 1 per valid comparison, max 4; must refer to both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Indus Basin irrigation system is important to Pakistan's economy.
parts.answer: Most of Pakistan's crops, including wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane, are grown on irrigated land because rainfall is too low. These crops feed the population and supply raw materials to industries such as textiles and sugar, which earn much of Pakistan's export income and provide many jobs.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: food security; raw materials for industry; exports; employment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Modern irrigation methods should replace traditional methods everywhere in Pakistan.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: For: drip and sprinkler save water and raise yields; lined canals reduce waterlogging. Against: modern methods are costly and need power; traditional methods such as karez are sustainable and suit local conditions, cost little and are community-run; small farmers cannot afford equipment. Judgement required.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2); L2 (3–4) both sides developed with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two cropping seasons in Pakistan and give one crop grown in each.
parts.answer: Kharif (summer) – e.g. rice, cotton, sugarcane, maize; Rabi (winter) – e.g. wheat, gram, mustard.
parts.working: 1 each for season names; 1 each for correct crop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why rabi crops in the Indus Plain depend heavily on canal or tube-well irrigation.
parts.answer: Winter rainfall in the plains is low and unreliable, while river flow is low in winter, so water must be supplied from storage reservoirs through perennial canals or pumped from groundwater.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the river on which Tarbela Dam is built.
parts.answer: The Indus.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between a dam and a barrage.
parts.answer: A dam is a high wall that stores large amounts of water in a reservoir (for irrigation and HEP); a barrage is a lower structure with gates that raises the river level to divert water into canals and stores little water.
parts.working: 1 per difference, max 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two barrages on the Indus.
parts.answer: Any two: Jinnah, Chashma, Taunsa, Guddu, Sukkur, Kotri.
parts.working: 1 each.

stem: A reservoir in northern Pakistan could originally store 9.0 km³ of water. Silt reduces its storage by about 0.09 km³ each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the storage after 20 years.
parts.working: B1 7.2 km³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of original storage lost in that time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which loss of storage affects Pakistan.
parts.answer: Less water can be stored from the summer floods for use in the dry winter, so canals receive less water for rabi crops. Lower water levels also mean less hydroelectric power, increasing the use of expensive imported fuel.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: less irrigation; less HEP; less flood control.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits of large multi-purpose dams such as Tarbela and Mangla.
parts.answer: They store monsoon and snow-melt water and release it through the year to canals, allowing two crops a year. Water flowing through turbines generates cheap hydroelectricity; they also help control floods and support fishing and tourism.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: irrigation; HEP; flood control; fishing/recreation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems of building large dams.
parts.answer: Any two: high cost and long construction time; people and villages displaced; farmland and forests drowned; silting; sites in earthquake zones; disputes between provinces.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the building of new large dams in Pakistan is often controversial.
parts.answer: Downstream provinces, especially Sindh, fear that new dams upstream will reduce the water reaching their canals and the Indus Delta. Large dams displace thousands of people and drown land, and their huge cost and debts make governments hesitate.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Pakistan should build more small dams instead of large dams.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: Small dams: cheaper, quicker, fewer people displaced, serve local farms in barani areas, less controversy. Large dams: store far more water, generate much more HEP, give greater flood control and serve the whole Indus system. Judgement required.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2); L2 (3–4) both sides developed with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the river on which Warsak Dam is built.
parts.answer: The Kabul River.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the barrage at Sukkur by its other name.
parts.answer: Lloyd Barrage.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a barrage helps irrigation.
parts.answer: Gates across the river hold back water and raise its level. This lets water flow by gravity into canals that start just above the barrage. Canal flow can be controlled by opening or closing the gates.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is a link canal?
parts.answer: A canal that carries water from one river to another.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why link canals were built in Pakistan after 1960.
parts.answer: Under the Indus Waters Treaty the water of the eastern rivers went to India, so canals in Punjab that had been fed by the Ravi and Sutlej would have run dry. Link canals carry water from the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) eastwards to keep these canals supplied.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: treaty context; transfer water from west to east; keep existing canals and farmland in use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'waterlogging'.
parts.answer: When the water table rises to (or near) the surface so the soil is saturated and roots cannot breathe.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how salinity develops in irrigated areas.
parts.answer: When the water table is high, water rises to the surface through the soil by capillary action. In the hot climate it evaporates quickly, leaving the dissolved salts behind as a white crust (kallar) on the surface, which harms crops.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 4: high water table; capillary action; evaporation; salts left / crust; reduced fertility.

stem: On a farm in Sindh, wheat yields fell from 3.2 tonnes per hectare to 2.4 tonnes per hectare as salinity increased.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of waterlogging in the Indus Plain.
parts.answer: Water seeps from unlined canals and watercourses into the ground, raising the water table. Farmers over-irrigate with flood methods and the flat land has poor natural drainage, so excess water cannot drain away.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: canal seepage; over-irrigation; poor drainage; flat land; heavy monsoon/floods.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What do the letters SCARP stand for?
parts.answer: Salinity Control and Reclamation Project(s).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which waterlogging and salinity can be reduced.
parts.answer: Tube wells (as in SCARP) pump out groundwater to lower the water table, and the water can be reused for irrigation. Lining canals stops seepage; drains such as the Left Bank Outfall Drain carry saline water away to the sea.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: tube wells; canal lining; drainage; leaching with extra water; salt-tolerant crops; gypsum; tree planting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of waterlogging and salinity on farmers.
parts.answer: Crop yields fall and some land becomes too salty to farm, so farmers' incomes drop and some must leave the land. Treating the land (gypsum, drainage, extra water) is costly, and houses and roads can be damaged by the high water table.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Waterlogging and salinity are caused more by people than by nature.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: People: unlined canals, over-irrigation, poor drainage design, cutting trees, poor maintenance. Nature: flat land with little natural drainage, hot climate with high evaporation, saline rocks and groundwater, heavy rain/floods. Judgement required.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2); L2 (3–4) both sides developed with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two coastal provinces of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Sindh and Balochistan.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between marine fishing and inland fishing.
parts.answer: Marine fishing takes place in the sea (Arabian Sea) and inland fishing in rivers, lakes, reservoirs and fish ponds; marine catches are larger and include shrimp, tuna and pomfret, while inland catches are mainly freshwater species such as rohu and other carp.
parts.working: 1 per difference, max 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why fishing is important to people living on the Makran coast.
parts.answer: There is little farmland or industry in this dry area, so fishing is the main source of jobs, income and food for coastal villages.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'overfishing'.
parts.answer: Catching fish faster than the stock can reproduce, so numbers fall.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two causes of overfishing in Pakistan's coastal waters.
parts.answer: Many more boats and modern trawlers now fish the same area, so the total catch has grown too large. Fine-mesh nets catch young fish before they breed, and regulations on mesh size and closed seasons are poorly enforced.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: too many boats/trawlers; fine-mesh nets / juvenile catch; weak enforcement; rising demand for export and fishmeal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why mangrove forests in the Indus Delta are important for fishing.
parts.answer: Mangrove roots give shelter and food to young shrimp, crabs and fish, acting as nurseries before they move out to sea. Their loss therefore reduces future catches; mangroves also protect the coast from storms and erosion, protecting fishing villages.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: breeding/nursery grounds; food supply; coastal protection; filter pollutants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the area of mangroves has decreased.
parts.answer: Any two: less fresh water and silt reaching the delta because of dams and barrages; cutting for fuelwood and fodder; camel grazing; pollution from Karachi; land reclamation for ports and housing.
parts.working: 1 each.

stem: A fishing cooperative in Keti Bandar recorded an average catch of 640 kg per boat per trip ten years ago and 480 kg per boat per trip this year (invented figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in the catch per trip.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons for this fall.
parts.answer: Overfishing and the use of fine-mesh nets have reduced the number of fish reaching breeding age. Less fresh water and silt reaching the delta, together with mangrove loss and pollution, have damaged breeding grounds.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which water pollution affects fishing near Karachi.
parts.answer: Any two: untreated sewage and industrial waste kill fish or drive them away; contaminated fish are unsafe to eat or export; oil spills damage marine life; lower catches near the coast force boats to travel further.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two measures that could make fishing in Pakistan more sustainable.
parts.answer: Enforce a closed season during the main breeding months so that stocks can recover. Set and check a minimum mesh size so young fish escape, and limit the number of trawler licences.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: closed seasons; mesh size; licences/quotas; protect/replant mangroves; marine protected areas; treat pollution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why many small-scale fishermen in Pakistan remain poor.
parts.answer: They often borrow money from middlemen to buy boats, nets and fuel and must then sell their catch to them at low prices. Small boats without ice or cold storage cannot travel far or keep fish fresh, so they catch less and sell lower-quality fish.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: debt to middlemen; low prices; small boats/poor equipment; lack of ice/cold storage; falling stocks; little education/alternative work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The fishing industry could make a much bigger contribution to Pakistan's economy.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: For: long coastline and large exclusive economic zone with unused deep-sea stocks; exports could grow with better hygiene and processing; aquaculture can expand inland; new harbours (Gwadar). Against: stocks already overfished near the coast; poor infrastructure; export markets demand strict standards; pollution and mangrove loss; limited investment. Judgement required.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2); L2 (3–4) both sides developed with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is aquaculture?
parts.answer: The farming of fish or shellfish in ponds, tanks or cages.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of fish farming in Punjab.
parts.answer: Fish ponds can use land that is too waterlogged or saline for crops, giving farmers another source of income. Farmed fish provide a regular supply of protein for nearby cities without reducing wild stocks.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: uses poor land; extra income; reliable supply to cities; reduces pressure on rivers; uses canal/tube-well water.

stem: A boat owner in Pasni sells a catch of shrimp for Rs 2,200 per kg at the harbour. The same shrimp, once processed and frozen, are sold for export at a value equivalent to Rs 3,400 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in value from harbour sale to export.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Pakistan of processing more seafood before export.
parts.answer: Processed products sell at a higher price, so Pakistan earns more foreign exchange from the same catch. Processing plants create jobs in packing, freezing and transport in coastal towns.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the building of dams and barrages on the Indus has affected inland and delta fisheries.
parts.answer: Barrages block the upstream migration of fish such as the palla (hilsa), which swims from the sea up the Indus to breed, so catches have fallen sharply. Reduced flow below Kotri brings less fresh water and nutrients to the delta, increasing salinity and harming mangroves and shrimp breeding.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each. Credit reservoir fisheries (Tarbela, Mangla) as a positive point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to protect river fish stocks.
parts.answer: Any two: fish ladders/passes at barrages; closed seasons in rivers; ban on poisoning and dynamite fishing; stocking rivers from hatcheries; reducing pollution.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the fishing industry provides employment other than catching fish.
parts.answer: Any two: boat building and repair; net making; ice factories; processing (freezing, canning, drying); transport and marketing; fishmeal plants.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why fish consumption per person in Pakistan is low compared with many countries.
parts.answer: Many people live far from the coast and fresh fish is hard to transport without cold chains, so it is expensive inland. Meat and chicken are traditional preferences, and much of the best catch (shrimp, tuna) is exported.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: distance from coast; poor cold chain; food preference; high price; exports take the best catch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'by-catch'?
parts.answer: Unwanted fish and other sea creatures caught accidentally while fishing for target species.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by by-catch in Pakistani waters.
parts.answer: Young fish of valuable species are caught and turned into fishmeal for poultry feed, so they never grow to breed and future catches fall. Turtles, dolphins and sharks caught in gill nets may die, harming marine ecosystems.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name Pakistan's main fish harbour.
parts.answer: Karachi Fish Harbour (West Wharf).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two fishing harbours on the Balochistan coast.
parts.answer: Any two: Gwadar, Pasni, Ormara, Jiwani, Sonmiani (Damb).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why most of the catch is landed at Karachi.
parts.answer: Best facilities (auction halls, ice, cold storage, processing plants); large local market; good road, rail and air links for distribution and export (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a trawl net is used.
parts.answer: A large cone-shaped net is dragged behind a boat, through the water or along the sea bed, catching fish and shrimp in its narrow end.
parts.working: 1 for net dragged by boat; 1 for detail (sea bed / cone shape).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of bottom trawling.
parts.answer: Dragging heavy nets along the sea bed destroys habitats such as coral, sea grass and breeding grounds. Trawls catch everything in their path, including young fish and other species, so there is a large wasteful by-catch.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe gill-net fishing.
parts.answer: A wall of net is hung in the water; fish swim into it and are trapped by their gills in the mesh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the methods used by traditional small-scale fishermen with those used by modern commercial fleets.
parts.answer: Small-scale fishermen use small wooden boats (often with outboard engines), hand-hauled gill nets, cast nets and lines close to the shore, catching small amounts. Commercial fleets use large trawlers or long-liners with echo sounders, GPS and freezers, fishing further out for longer and catching much larger quantities.
parts.working: 1 per valid comparison, max 4; both sides needed.

stem: Fish begin to spoil within hours in Pakistan's hot climate. A rule used on some boats is to carry about 1 kg of ice for every 1 kg of fish expected to be caught, plus 50% extra for a trip of more than two days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much ice a boat should carry for a three-day trip if it expects to catch 1,800 kg of fish.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which better handling and storage would increase fishermen's incomes.
parts.answer: Fish kept on ice stay fresh and fetch higher prices, especially for export. Less fish is wasted or sold cheaply as fishmeal, so more of the catch earns money.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which fish are preserved or processed in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any three: icing/chilling; freezing; canning; sun-drying; salting; smoking; making fishmeal or fish oil.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sun-drying of fish is common on the Makran coast.
parts.answer: The hot, dry, sunny climate dries fish quickly, and villages are far from ice plants and markets, so drying is a cheap way to preserve fish without electricity.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why some export markets have rejected Pakistani seafood in the past.
parts.answer: Fish was often handled in unhygienic conditions on boats and at harbours, with dirty decks and too little ice, so bacteria levels were high. Processing plants did not always meet the strict food-safety and traceability standards demanded by importers such as the European Union.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each: poor hygiene on boats; poor harbour conditions; lack of cold chain; standards/traceability not met.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements at fish harbours that would help increase exports.
parts.answer: Any two: clean, covered auction halls; more ice and cold-storage plants; clean water supply and drainage; training for fishermen; quality testing laboratories; better roads to processing plants.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Gwadar has potential to become an important fishing port.
parts.answer: It lies on the Makran coast, close to rich fishing grounds of the Arabian Sea, and already has a fishing community. Investment in its deep-sea port and road links under CPEC could provide modern harbours, processing plants and transport for exports.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two problems that limit the fishing industry in Gwadar today.
parts.answer: Any two: shortage of fresh water and electricity; limited cold storage and processing; distance from large markets; competition from large trawlers; limited local skills/investment.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two methods used for inland fishing in rivers and lakes.
parts.answer: Any two: cast nets; gill nets; hook and line; traps; seine nets from small boats.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one large lake in Sindh important for inland fishing.
parts.answer: Manchar Lake (or Keenjhar or Haleji).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why fishing in Manchar Lake has declined.
parts.answer: Polluted, saline drainage water flowing into the lake has killed fish and plants, so catches fell and many fishing families left.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development.

stem: A small company in Ormara operates 12 boats. In one month each boat makes 18 trips and lands an average of 350 kg of mixed fish per trip, sold at an average of Rs 260 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total monthly catch in tonnes.
parts.working: M1; A1 75.6 tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the company's total monthly income from the catch.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why income may vary greatly from month to month.
parts.answer: Rough seas/storms during the south-west monsoon stop boats going out; closed season; fish migrate; prices change (any one).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe long-line fishing.
parts.answer: A very long main line with many baited hooks on short branch lines is set from a boat and left in the water, then hauled in.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fishing activity off the Pakistan coast is reduced in June and July.
parts.answer: The south-west monsoon brings strong winds and very rough seas, making it dangerous for small boats to go out. It is also the main breeding season for shrimp and many fish, so a closed season is declared to protect stocks.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of using modern technology such as echo sounders and GPS on fishing boats.
parts.answer: Echo sounders locate shoals of fish under the boat, so less time and fuel are wasted searching. GPS lets crews find good fishing grounds again and navigate safely back to harbour in bad weather.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Modern fishing technology is a threat to fish stocks in Pakistan.' Do you agree? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: Threat: larger catches with less effort; bottom trawling damages habitats; freezers allow long trips and more fishing. Not a threat if managed: technology can monitor boats, help enforce zones and closed seasons, and select target species to reduce by-catch; the real problem is weak regulation. Judgement required.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2); L2 (3–4) both sides developed with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two marine species that are important for Pakistan's seafood exports.
parts.answer: Any two: shrimp/prawns; tuna; pomfret; lobster; crab; squid/cuttlefish; mackerel.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two freshwater fish caught or farmed in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: rohu; thaila (catla); mori (mrigal); mahseer; trout; tilapia; palla (hilsa) in the lower Indus.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name Pakistan's national fish.
parts.answer: The mahseer.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: The marine catch landed by one harbour in a year was made up as follows (percentage by weight, invented figures): Shrimp 18%; Tuna and mackerel 24%; Sardines 30%; Pomfret and croakers 12%; Others 16%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle of the sector for shrimp if the data were drawn as a pie chart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Shrimp is a small part of the catch by weight but the largest part by value. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Shrimp sells at a much higher price per kg than other fish; there is strong export demand; it is processed (frozen) for overseas markets.
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why sardines make up a large share of the catch by weight.
parts.answer: They live in large shoals near the surface and are easily caught in large quantities by purse seine nets (much used for fishmeal).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In which parts of Pakistan is trout found?
parts.answer: In cold, fast-flowing, clear streams and rivers of the northern mountains, e.g. Swat, Kaghan, Chitral, Gilgit.
parts.working: 1 for cold mountain streams; 1 for named area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why trout cannot live in the rivers of the plains.
parts.answer: Trout need cold, clear water with plenty of dissolved oxygen; river water in the plains is too warm and muddy in summer.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development.

stem: A fish pond in Muzaffargarh produced 1,450 kg of carp per hectare per year using traditional methods. After the farmer added aerators and better feed, production rose to 2,340 kg per hectare per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two kinds of carp commonly farmed in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: rohu, thaila (catla), mori (mrigal), silver carp, grass carp, common carp.
parts.working: 1 each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the life cycle of the palla (hilsa) that makes it vulnerable.
parts.answer: It lives in the sea but migrates up the Indus into fresh water to breed, so it must pass through the river delta and barrages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why palla catches in Sindh have fallen.
parts.answer: Kotri Barrage and reduced river flow block the fish's migration route, so far fewer can reach breeding areas upstream. Low freshwater flow, pollution and overfishing of fish before they spawn have also reduced the population.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why is shrimp catching concentrated off the Sindh coast near the Indus Delta?
parts.answer: The shallow waters and creeks of the delta, with mangrove forests, provide breeding and nursery grounds for shrimp; nutrients brought by the river support food for them; the continental shelf is wide there.
parts.working: 1 per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one fish product made from small, low-value fish.
parts.answer: Fishmeal (for poultry/animal feed) or fish oil.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why tuna is caught mainly in deeper offshore waters, while shrimp is caught close to the shore.
parts.answer: Tuna are large, fast-swimming fish that migrate through the open ocean, so they are found in deep offshore waters and are caught by gill nets and long lines from larger boats. Shrimp live on the shallow sea bed and in creeks near the delta, so they are caught by trawling in coastal waters.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development for each species.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the value of Pakistan's fish exports can change greatly from year to year.
parts.answer: Changes in catch size (weather, stock levels); changes in world prices or demand; export bans or rejections on quality grounds; exchange-rate changes (any two).
parts.working: 1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Bhutto's policy of nationalisation between 1972 and 1976.
parts.answer: In January 1972 the government took over about 30 large firms in basic industries such as iron and steel, heavy engineering, chemicals, cement and public utilities; life insurance companies were nationalised in 1972; banks were nationalised in 1974; in 1976 cotton-ginning, rice-husking and flour mills were taken over; a Board of Industrial Management was set up to run the units.
parts.working: 1 mark per accurate point up to 4: about 30 large units / ten basic industries (1972); named industries (steel, engineering, chemicals, cement, utilities); insurance 1972; banks 1974; ginning, rice-husking and flour mills 1976; Board of Industrial Management; owners given limited compensation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto introduced land reforms in 1972.
parts.answer: Bhutto's PPP had promised 'roti, kapra aur makaan' and needed to keep the support of poor peasants who voted for it in 1970; a small number of landlords owned huge estates and held great political power, which Bhutto wanted to reduce; lowering the ceiling (to 150 acres irrigated / 300 unirrigated) was meant to release land for landless tenants; giving tenants security against eviction and making landlords pay water rates and seed costs aimed to raise farm output and reduce rural poverty.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: election promise / Islamic socialism; reduce power of big landlords (feudals); give land to landless peasants; tenants' rights against eviction; raise agricultural productivity; reduce rural inequality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the 1973 Constitution.
parts.answer: Pakistan became the Islamic Republic of Pakistan with Islam as the state religion; it set up a federal parliamentary system with the Prime Minister as head of government and the President as a largely ceremonial head of state; Parliament had two houses, the National Assembly and the Senate; the President and Prime Minister had to be Muslims; it listed fundamental rights and an independent judiciary; Urdu was the national language.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: Islamic Republic / Islam the state religion; federal; parliamentary – PM holds power; President ceremonial; bicameral (National Assembly and Senate); PM and President Muslim; Council of Islamic Ideology; fundamental rights; Urdu national language, English official for a time; passed April 1973, in force 14 August 1973.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto was removed from power in July 1977.
parts.answer: The opposition parties, united in the Pakistan National Alliance (PNA), accused the PPP of rigging the March 1977 elections, which it won by a very large margin; mass protests and strikes followed and many people were killed, so the country became hard to govern; Bhutto used the army and the Federal Security Force against protesters, which made him look authoritarian; rising prices and the failure of nationalisation had lost him support among industrialists and the middle class; talks with the PNA dragged on, and on 5 July 1977 General Zia-ul-Haq took over in 'Operation Fair Play', saying he would restore order and hold elections.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: alleged rigging of 1977 elections; PNA movement / strikes and violence; harsh use of FSF and army; economic problems (inflation, nationalisation); loss of support of religious groups and businessmen; army intervention, Operation Fair Play.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Simla Agreement of 1972.
parts.answer: It was signed in July 1972 by Bhutto and the Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi after the 1971 war; both sides agreed to settle their disputes peacefully through bilateral talks; troops were to withdraw to their own side of the international border and India gave back the West Pakistan territory it had occupied; in Kashmir both agreed to respect the new Line of Control; the return of prisoners of war was left to later talks (they came home by 1974).
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: July 1972, Simla; Bhutto and Indira Gandhi; disputes to be settled peacefully and bilaterally; withdrawal to international border / territory returned; Line of Control in Kashmir respected; POW issue settled later; restore communications and trade.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto's industrial reforms did not achieve all that he hoped.
parts.answer: Many nationalised units were run by civil servants and political appointees rather than experienced managers, so efficiency fell and many made losses; private investors lost confidence and moved their money abroad or stopped investing, so industrial growth slowed; the take-over of small ginning and rice mills in 1976 upset small businessmen who had supported the PPP; the oil price rise of 1973–74 and floods raised costs and inflation, which hid any gains from the reforms; labour laws raised wages, but strikes and low productivity continued.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: poor management / political appointments; loss of investor confidence / capital flight; small businesses angered (1976); world oil crisis and inflation; labour unrest; corruption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Bhutto's policy towards the Muslim world between 1972 and 1977.
parts.answer: He hosted the second Islamic Summit Conference of the OIC at Lahore in February 1974, attended by leaders such as King Faisal and Colonel Gaddafi; at the summit Pakistan recognised Bangladesh; he built close links with Saudi Arabia, Libya, Iran and the Gulf states, which gave loans and aid; thousands of Pakistani workers went to the Gulf states, sending back remittances.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: Lahore Islamic Summit 1974; named leaders; recognition of Bangladesh at the summit; financial help from oil-rich states; jobs for Pakistani workers in the Middle East / remittances; support for Arab states over Palestine / 1973 war.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Bhutto's domestic policies between 1971 and 1977 were successful.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: the 1973 Constitution was passed with the support of all parties and is still the basis of government; land reforms and labour laws gave some help to tenants and workers; health reforms (rural health centres) and education reforms (free schooling to class 8, new schools, Allama Iqbal Open University 1974) widened opportunities; the Qadiani issue was settled to the satisfaction of religious groups. Disagree: nationalisation made industry inefficient and scared off investors; land reforms were evaded by landlords who transferred land to relatives; the Federal Security Force was used against opponents; the military action in Balochistan (1973–77) caused resentment; the 1977 election rigging allegations led to his fall. Judgement: e.g. the constitution was a lasting success, but economic and political methods weakened his government.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the problems faced by refugees arriving in Pakistan in 1947.
parts.answer: Millions of Muslim refugees (about seven million) crossed into Pakistan, many on foot or in packed trains; trains and columns were attacked and many people were killed; they arrived with few possessions and needed food, shelter and medical care; camps such as the Walton camp in Lahore were overcrowded and disease spread; many had no jobs or land, so resettling them was slow.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: about seven million refugees; violence / attacks on trains and caravans; arrived with nothing; lack of shelter / camps (e.g. Walton, Lahore); disease and lack of medicine; unemployment / need for land and housing; Jinnah's Relief Fund.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the canal water dispute was a serious problem for Pakistan between 1947 and 1960.
parts.answer: The Radcliffe Award left the headworks at Ferozepur and Madhopur in India although the canals they fed irrigated land in Pakistan's Punjab; in April 1948 India cut off the water, threatening crops at sowing time and the farm economy on which most Pakistanis depended; Pakistan feared India could do this whenever it chose, which added to bitterness between the two countries; a 1948 temporary agreement made Pakistan pay for water, which it saw as unfair; the dispute was only settled by the Indus Waters Treaty in 1960 through the World Bank, which gave the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) to India and the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: headworks in India; water stopped April 1948; agriculture / food supply threatened; insecurity – India controlled supply; payment demanded; long dispute until 1960 treaty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Objectives Resolution of 1949.
parts.answer: It was moved by Liaquat Ali Khan and passed by the Constituent Assembly in March 1949; it said sovereignty belongs to Allah and is exercised by the people through their elected representatives as a sacred trust; the state would follow the principles of democracy, freedom, equality, tolerance and social justice as laid down by Islam; Muslims would be able to live according to Islam; minorities would be free to profess and practise their religions; Pakistan would be a federation with fundamental rights and an independent judiciary.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: March 1949; Liaquat Ali Khan; sovereignty of Allah; authority exercised by elected representatives; Islamic principles of democracy, equality, tolerance, justice; minority rights; federal system; fundamental rights; independent judiciary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it took Pakistan nine years to produce its first constitution.
parts.answer: Politicians disagreed about the balance of power between East and West Pakistan, because East Pakistan had the larger population and wanted representation by population while the West feared domination; there was a dispute about the national language (Urdu or Bengali as well); there was disagreement about the place of Islam in the state; leading figures died early – Jinnah in 1948 and Liaquat assassinated in 1951 – leaving weak leadership; governors-general such as Ghulam Muhammad dismissed governments and dissolved the Constituent Assembly in 1954, delaying the work; provincial jealousies and frequent changes of Prime Minister made agreement hard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the 1956 Constitution.
parts.answer: It came into force on 23 March 1956 and named the country the Islamic Republic of Pakistan; the President had to be a Muslim; it set up a parliamentary system with a Prime Minister; there was a single-house National Assembly of 300 seats with parity, 150 each for East and West Pakistan; Urdu and Bengali were both national languages; Iskander Mirza became the first President.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: 23 March 1956; Islamic Republic; President a Muslim; parliamentary / PM; unicameral National Assembly 300; parity between wings; Urdu and Bengali national languages; federal; Iskander Mirza President.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the One Unit scheme was introduced in 1955.
parts.answer: Merging the provinces and states of the west into a single province of West Pakistan created two units of equal standing, so parity could be used in the National Assembly and East Pakistan's larger population would not give it a permanent majority; the government argued it would reduce administrative costs by replacing several provincial governments with one; it was meant to reduce provincialism and build national unity; it made it easier to plan development such as irrigation for the whole western wing.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: create parity with East Pakistan; reduce the influence of the Bengali majority; save administrative cost / efficiency; reduce provincial rivalry / unity; easier development planning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of the war over Kashmir in 1947–1948.
parts.answer: Muslims in Poonch rebelled against the Maharaja Hari Singh, and Pashtun tribesmen entered Kashmir in October 1947 in support; the Maharaja signed the Instrument of Accession to India and Indian troops were flown into Srinagar; fighting followed and the Pakistani army joined in 1948; India took the issue to the UN, which arranged a ceasefire from 1 January 1949 and called for a plebiscite, which was never held.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Dealing with the refugee crisis was Jinnah's greatest achievement as Governor-General.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: he set up the Quaid-e-Azam Relief Fund, moved temporarily to Lahore to oversee the work, appealed for calm and visited camps, and millions of refugees were fed and slowly resettled. Disagree: other achievements were as important – he set up a working central government in Karachi from almost nothing, building a civil service; he founded the State Bank of Pakistan (1948) so Pakistan had its own currency; he negotiated with the princely states, bringing many (e.g. Bahawalpur, Khairpur, Kalat) into Pakistan; he dealt with the division of assets and the Kashmir war; he gave the nation a sense of unity in its first year. Judgement: e.g. setting up a working state was the greater achievement because without it refugees could not have been helped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the domestic policies of Nawaz Sharif's first government (1990–1993).
parts.answer: He followed a policy of privatisation, selling state-owned industries and banks; he deregulated the economy and encouraged foreign investment; the Yellow Cab scheme gave loans to young people to buy taxis; work began on the Lahore–Islamabad motorway (M-2); the Shariat Bill (1991) declared the Quran and Sunnah the supreme law.

parts.text: Explain why Benazir Bhutto's first government was dismissed in 1990.
parts.answer: President Ghulam Ishaq Khan used the Eighth Amendment (Article 58(2)(b)) to dismiss her in August 1990; he and the army leadership distrusted her and she clashed with them over appointments; her government was accused of corruption, including charges against her husband Asif Zardari; law and order in Sindh broke down, with ethnic violence in Karachi and Hyderabad after her alliance with the MQM ended; her opponents in the IJI controlled the Punjab government and blocked her policies, so she passed almost no laws.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the nuclear tests carried out by Pakistan in 1998.
parts.answer: India carried out nuclear tests on 11 and 13 May 1998; Nawaz Sharif's government responded with tests on 28 May 1998 in the Ras Koh hills of Chagai, Balochistan, followed by a further test on 30 May; Pakistan became the first Muslim country to show nuclear weapons capability; the USA, Japan and others imposed economic sanctions; 28 May is marked as Youm-e-Takbeer.

parts.text: Explain why General Musharraf took power in October 1999.
parts.answer: Relations between Nawaz Sharif and the army had broken down after the Kargil conflict of 1999, when Sharif withdrew under US pressure and blamed the army; on 12 October 1999 Sharif tried to dismiss Musharraf while he was flying back from Sri Lanka and to stop his plane landing, so the army took over; Sharif had built up a lot of personal power through the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments and had clashed with the judiciary and the President, which made many see him as autocratic; the economy was weak after the 1998 sanctions and foreign debt was high, so many people welcomed the change.
