parts.text: Describe the main events of Benazir Bhutto's second government (1993–1996).
parts.answer: Farooq Leghari, a PPP member, became President; the government ran the Lady Health Workers programme and set up women's police stations; a military operation was conducted against violence in Karachi; her brother Murtaza Bhutto was killed in a police encounter in Karachi in September 1996; Leghari dismissed the government in November 1996 for corruption and misrule.

parts.text: 'The Eighth Amendment was the main cause of political instability in Pakistan between 1988 and 1999.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: Article 58(2)(b) let the President dismiss elected governments, and it was used against Benazir (1990, 1996) and Nawaz Sharif (1993), so no government finished its term; every elected government knew it could be removed, so it spent its time defending itself. subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results of the general election of December 1970.
parts.answer: It was Pakistan's first general election held on adult franchise (one person, one vote); the Awami League led by Mujib won 160 of the 162 general seats in East Pakistan, giving it an overall majority in the National Assembly; the PPP led by Bhutto won 81 of the 138 seats in West Pakistan; neither party won any seats in the other wing.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: first election on adult franchise; Awami League 160 of 162 East Pakistan seats; overall majority; PPP 81 seats in the West; no party won seats in both wings; country divided along regional lines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why East Pakistan separated from Pakistan in 1971.
parts.answer: East Pakistanis felt economically exploited because more development money, industry and jobs went to the West although jute from the East earned much of the foreign exchange; Bengalis were under-represented in the army and civil service, so they felt they had little power; the Urdu–Bengali language dispute made Bengalis feel their culture was not respected; after the 1970 election the Awami League was not allowed to form a government, and the military crackdown of March 1971 turned demands for autonomy into a war for independence; India supported the Mukti Bahini and invaded in late 1971, so Pakistani forces surrendered at Dhaka on 16 December 1971.

Reasons: economic disparity; under-representation in army and civil service; language and culture; Six Points / Awami League; denial of power after 1970 election; military action 1971; Indian intervention; geographical distance.

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Legal Framework Order of 1970.
parts.answer: It was issued by Yahya Khan in March 1970 to set the rules for the coming election; One Unit was ended and the four western provinces restored; parity was replaced by representation by population, one person one vote, in a National Assembly of 313 seats; the new Assembly had 120 days to write a constitution; the constitution had to protect Pakistan's Islamic ideology, federal system and territorial unity, and the President could reject it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Was the Six Points programme the most important reason for the separation of East Pakistan? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Yes: Mujib's Six Points (1966) demanded a loose federation in which the centre controlled only defence and foreign affairs and each wing had its own currency and taxes; this gave Bengali grievances a clear programme and made the Awami League the dominant party, and West Pakistani leaders saw it as a step towards separation, so they would not hand over power. Other reasons: economic disparity built up resentment over many years; Bengalis were under-represented in the army and bureaucracy; the language dispute from 1948–52; Bhutto's refusal to attend the Assembly in Dhaka and Yahya's postponement of it in March 1971; the army crackdown (Operation Searchlight); Indian military intervention which decided the outcome. Judgement: e.g. the Six Points expressed the demand, but the military crackdown and Indian intervention made separation happen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the military events in East Pakistan between March and December 1971.
parts.answer: On 25 March 1971 the army began Operation Searchlight to crush the Awami League and Mujib was arrested and flown to West Pakistan; Bengali fighters formed the Mukti Bahini and waged a guerrilla war with Indian help; millions of refugees fled into India; India attacked in November–December 1971 and full war followed on both fronts; Pakistani forces under General Niazi surrendered at Dhaka on 16 December 1971 and about 90,000 became prisoners of war.

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's relations with the USA between 1954 and 1965.
parts.answer: Pakistan signed a mutual defence agreement with the USA in 1954 and joined the US-backed alliances SEATO (1954) and the Baghdad Pact/CENTO (1955); in return it received large amounts of military and economic aid; it allowed the USA to use an air base at Badaber near Peshawar, from which the U-2 spy plane shot down over the USSR in 1960 had flown; relations cooled when the USA gave arms to India after 1962 and stopped aid to both sides in the 1965 war.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: 1954 defence agreement; SEATO 1954; Baghdad Pact / CENTO 1955; military and economic aid; Badaber base / U-2 incident 1960; US arms to India 1962; aid suspended in 1965 war.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan's relations with the USSR were often poor between 1947 and 1979.
parts.answer: Pakistan joined US-led alliances (SEATO and CENTO) against communism, so the USSR saw it as part of the Western camp; Liaquat Ali Khan visited the USA in 1950 rather than the USSR, which was seen as a snub; the U-2 incident of 1960 led the USSR to threaten Pakistan; the USSR supported India over Kashmir, using its veto in the UN Security Council, and signed a treaty of friendship with India in 1971 before the war; it also supported Afghanistan's claims over Pakhtunistan. There were better moments, such as the Tashkent talks of 1966 and Soviet help with the Karachi steel mill in the 1970s.

Reasons: Pakistan in Western alliances; Liaquat's US visit 1950; U-2 1960; Soviet support for India / veto on Kashmir; 1971 Indo-Soviet treaty; support for Afghanistan. Credit balancing points (Tashkent 1966, Pakistan Steel Mills).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's membership of the Commonwealth since 1947.
parts.answer: Pakistan joined the Commonwealth at independence in 1947; it left in 1972 when Britain and other members recognised Bangladesh; it rejoined in 1989 under Benazir Bhutto; it was suspended from the Commonwealth's councils after the military takeover of October 1999; membership gave it access to scholarships, trade links and a forum to raise issues such as Kashmir.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: joined 1947; left 1972 over recognition of Bangladesh; rejoined 1989; suspended after 1999 coup; benefits (scholarships, trade, conferences).

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Pakistan has had good relations with the UK since 1947.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: the UK was the former colonial power and many British officers served in Pakistan's army and civil service in the early years; Pakistan was a Commonwealth member and joined Western alliances with the UK; the UK is a major trading partner and source of aid and investment; a large Pakistani community lives in Britain and sends remittances; many Pakistani students study in the UK. Disagree: Pakistan felt the UK did not support it over Kashmir; Pakistan left the Commonwealth in 1972 because Britain recognised Bangladesh; the UK criticised the 1998 nuclear tests and the 1999 military takeover; immigration controls caused tension. Judgement: e.g. relations have mostly been good because of trade and the large British-Pakistani community, despite periods of tension.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's relations with the USA during the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan (1979–1989).
parts.answer: After the Soviet invasion of December 1979 Pakistan became a frontline state; the Reagan administration agreed a large aid package (about US$3.2 billion over six years from 1981) including F-16 fighter aircraft; US weapons and money for the Afghan mujahideen were channelled through Pakistan's ISI; the USA overlooked Pakistan's nuclear programme and military rule; Pakistan took in about three million Afghan refugees.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: frontline state after 1979; large aid package (1981, about $3.2 billion); F-16s; arms to mujahideen via ISI; refugees hosted; US silence on nuclear programme / military rule; Geneva Accords 1988.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why relations between Pakistan and the USA became worse during the 1990s.
parts.answer: With the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan in 1989 and the end of the Cold War, Pakistan was less important to the USA; in 1990 the USA applied the Pressler Amendment because it could not certify that Pakistan had no nuclear weapons, so aid was cut and F-16s already paid for were not delivered; Pakistan's nuclear tests in 1998 led to further US sanctions; the Kargil conflict of 1999 and the military takeover in October 1999 brought more criticism and restrictions; the USA built closer ties with India.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: end of Cold War / Afghan war; Pressler Amendment 1990; F-16 issue; 1998 nuclear tests and sanctions; Kargil 1999; 1999 coup; closer US–India relations.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's relations with China between 1950 and 1972.
parts.answer: Pakistan was one of the first countries to recognise the People's Republic of China (1950) and diplomatic relations began in 1951; the 1963 border agreement settled the frontier between Xinjiang and the northern areas; China gave diplomatic and military support to Pakistan in the 1965 war; work began on the Karakoram Highway to link the two countries; Pakistan helped arrange the secret visit of US adviser Henry Kissinger to Beijing in 1971.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: early recognition 1950; diplomatic relations 1951; 1963 border agreement; support in 1965 war; aid / military equipment; Karakoram Highway; Kissinger visit 1971 / role as bridge to USA; support in 1971 crisis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan's relations with Afghanistan were difficult between 1947 and 1979.
parts.answer: Afghanistan was the only country to vote against Pakistan joining the UN in 1947; it refused to accept the Durand Line as the border and claimed that Pashtun areas of Pakistan should form 'Pakhtunistan'; Pakistan's embassy in Kabul was attacked in 1955 and relations were broken off from 1961 to 1963, with the border closed and trade disrupted; Afghanistan received Soviet aid and was close to India, while Pakistan was in Western alliances; there were border clashes and support for rebels on both sides.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: UN vote 1947; Durand Line; Pakhtunistan; embassy attacked 1955 / relations broken 1961–63; Soviet and Indian links; border incidents.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the war between Pakistan and India in 1965.
parts.answer: It began after clashes in the Rann of Kutch earlier in 1965 and Operation Gibraltar, when Pakistan sent fighters into Indian-held Kashmir in August; India attacked across the international border towards Lahore on 6 September 1965; there was heavy tank fighting, for example around Chawinda and Sialkot; after about 17 days a UN-backed ceasefire came into effect on 23 September 1965; the war ended with the Tashkent Declaration in January 1966.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: Rann of Kutch clashes; Operation Gibraltar, August 1965; Indian attack towards Lahore, 6 September; tank battles (Chawinda / Sialkot); air battles; ceasefire 23 September; Tashkent Declaration 1966.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why relations between Pakistan and Bangladesh improved after 1974.
parts.answer: Pakistan recognised Bangladesh in February 1974 at the time of the Lahore Islamic Summit, and Mujib attended the summit, which opened the way to talks; both were Muslim-majority countries and members of the OIC, so they had shared interests; full diplomatic relations were set up in 1976 after changes of government in Bangladesh; trade agreements and air links followed; both were founding members of SAARC in 1985, which gave regular contact; leaders exchanged visits in the 1980s and 1990s. Problems such as the stranded Biharis and division of assets remained.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: recognition 1974 / Lahore Summit; shared Islamic identity and OIC; new governments in Bangladesh after 1975; diplomatic relations 1976; trade and air links; SAARC 1985; official visits.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Tashkent Declaration of 1966.
parts.answer: It was signed in January 1966 by Ayub Khan and the Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri at talks arranged by the Soviet Prime Minister Kosygin; both sides agreed to withdraw their forces to the positions held before the 1965 war; they agreed to settle disputes by peaceful means and not interfere in each other's affairs; diplomatic relations, trade and communications were to be restored and prisoners exchanged; Kashmir was not settled.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: January 1966; Soviet mediation (Kosygin); Ayub and Shastri; withdrawal to pre-war positions; peaceful settlement / non-interference; restore diplomatic and trade relations; exchange of POWs; no solution on Kashmir / Shastri died in Tashkent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The Kashmir issue has been the main reason for poor relations between Pakistan and India since 1947.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: Kashmir led to wars in 1947–48 and 1965 and the Kargil conflict of 1999; the promised plebiscite was never held; it has blocked many attempts at friendship, for example the talks after Lahore in 1999. Disagree: other issues caused hostility – the division of assets and the refugee violence of 1947; the canal water dispute until 1960; India's role in the separation of East Pakistan in 1971; the nuclear arms race and tests of 1974 and 1998; disputes over Siachen and Sir Creek. There were also periods of improvement: the Indus Waters Treaty, the Simla Agreement, the 1988 agreement not to attack nuclear facilities and the 1999 Lahore Declaration. Judgement: e.g. Kashmir is the most lasting cause, but 1971 and the nuclear race made relations worse.

L3 (7–10): explains factors on one side only (7–8 for one explained point, 9–10 for two or more). author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the system of Basic Democracies introduced by Ayub Khan in 1959.
parts.answer: It created 80,000 elected Basic Democrats, 40,000 from each wing; they were elected by adult voters in union councils at the lowest level; above these were tehsil (thana), district and divisional councils, partly made up of officials; the councils handled local matters such as roads, sanitation and schools; the Basic Democrats formed the electoral college which elected the President and the assemblies.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: introduced 1959; 80,000 Basic Democrats (40,000 per wing); union councils elected; tiered system – tehsil/thana, district, divisional councils; officials nominated to higher tiers; local development duties; electoral college for President (1960 referendum, 1965 election).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Ayub Khan was able to take power in 1958.
parts.answer: Between 1951 and 1958 there were many Prime Ministers, so government was unstable and politicians were seen as self-seeking; the economy was weak, with food shortages, smuggling and rising prices; President Iskander Mirza declared martial law on 7 October 1958 and appointed Ayub as Chief Martial Law Administrator, but Ayub removed Mirza on 27 October; the army was the most organised institution and Ayub was its commander, so there was little resistance; many people hoped the army would end corruption and restore order before the planned 1959 elections.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: political instability / frequent changes of PM; corruption; economic crisis; Mirza's martial law, October 1958; strength of the army; public support for order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the agricultural reforms of Ayub Khan's government.
parts.answer: The 1959 land reforms set a ceiling of 500 acres of irrigated or 1,000 acres of unirrigated land per person, with the surplus given to tenants; high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice were introduced in the 'Green Revolution'; farmers were encouraged to use fertilisers, pesticides and tube-wells, with loans from the Agricultural Development Bank; the Indus Basin works built dams such as Mangla and link canals.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: land reform 1959 / ceilings; surplus land to tenants; Green Revolution – HYV seeds; fertilisers and pesticides; tube-wells; loans; Mangla dam / link canals; mechanisation (tractors).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Ayub Khan's government fell in 1969.
parts.answer: Many people saw the Tashkent Declaration of 1966 as a betrayal of the gains of the 1965 war, and Bhutto left the government and formed the PPP (1967) to oppose Ayub; economic growth had mainly benefited a few rich families (the '22 families'), while workers faced rising prices, for example of sugar; the 'Decade of Development' celebrations of 1968 annoyed people who had not benefited; in East Pakistan the Agartala conspiracy case against Mujib increased anger; student and worker protests spread across both wings and Ayub, also in poor health, handed power to General Yahya Khan in March 1969.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements. L2 (2–4): identifies or describes reasons. L3 (4–7): explains reasons, 5 marks for one well-explained reason, 7 for two or more. Reasons: Tashkent; Bhutto and the PPP; inequality / 22 families; inflation; 'Decade of Development' resentment; East Pakistan unrest / Agartala case; mass protests; ill health.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the 1962 Constitution.
parts.answer: It set up a presidential system in which the President held most power and there was no Prime Minister; the President was elected indirectly by the Basic Democrats acting as an electoral college; the President could veto laws and dissolve the National Assembly, and appointed ministers and governors; there was a single-house National Assembly; it introduced a federal system with two provinces; the country was first called the 'Republic of Pakistan', with 'Islamic' restored by amendment in 1963.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Ayub Khan's economic reforms were more successful than his political reforms.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: GDP grew quickly in the 1960s (about 6% a year); industry expanded with the help of foreign aid and the Pakistan Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation; the Green Revolution raised wheat and rice output; the Indus Waters Treaty and the Mangla and Tarbela projects improved irrigation. Disagree: the gains were unevenly shared, with wealth concentrated in a few families and East Pakistan falling behind; inflation rose in the late 1960s. Political reforms: Basic Democracies brought some local development and the 1962 Constitution gave stability for a time, and Islamabad was built as a new capital; but indirect elections were seen as undemocratic, the 1965 election against Fatima Jinnah was seen as unfair, and the system collapsed in 1969. Judgement: e.g. the economic reforms achieved more, but their unequal results contributed to his fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Zia-ul-Haq's Islamisation policies.
parts.answer: The Hudood Ordinances (1979) introduced Islamic punishments for crimes such as theft and adultery; the Zakat and Ushr Ordinance (1980) made the state deduct zakat from bank accounts; a Federal Shariat Court was set up in 1980 to check laws against Islamic teachings; the Majlis-e-Shoora was set up as an advisory council; Islamiyat and Arabic were encouraged in schools and the Qanun-e-Shahadat (law of evidence, 1984) was introduced.

parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq was able to stay in power for eleven years.
parts.answer: Martial law gave him control of the army and courts, and the Provisional Constitutional Order of 1981 made judges swear loyalty to him; Bhutto, his main rival, was executed in 1979 and the Movement for the Restoration of Democracy (1983) was crushed; the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan made Pakistan important to the USA, which gave large aid and ignored his rule; Islamisation won the support of religious parties; remittances from the Gulf helped the economy grow; the 1984 referendum and the non-party elections of 1985, with the Eighth Amendment, gave him legal cover.

Reasons: martial law / control of army and judiciary; Bhutto removed; MRD suppressed; US support after 1979; religious support; economic growth / remittances; 1984 referendum, 1985 elections, Eighth Amendment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Eighth Amendment of 1985.
parts.answer: It was passed by the National Assembly elected in the non-party elections of 1985, under Prime Minister Junejo; it gave legal protection (indemnity) to all actions of the martial law government since 1977; Article 58(2)(b) allowed the President to dismiss the Prime Minister and dissolve the National Assembly; the President could appoint the Prime Minister, provincial governors and the chiefs of the armed forces; it changed the system into a mix of presidential and parliamentary rule.

Judgement: e.g. Islamisation had the most lasting effect on society, though the Eighth Amendment had the greater political effect.

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's part in United Nations peacekeeping.
parts.answer: Pakistan joined the UN on 30 September 1947; its troops first served in a UN mission in the Congo in 1960; Pakistani soldiers have since served in many missions, for example in Somalia, Bosnia, Sierra Leone and Liberia; Pakistan has been one of the largest providers of troops to UN peacekeeping; many Pakistani peacekeepers have lost their lives on duty.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: UN member 1947; first mission Congo 1960; named later missions (Somalia, Bosnia, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Haiti etc.); among the largest troop contributors; casualties / medals; police and medical units too.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan has wanted close relations with other Muslim countries since 1947.
parts.answer: Pakistan was created as a homeland for Muslims, so Islamic unity is part of its ideology; it has supported Muslim causes such as Palestine and wanted Muslim support over Kashmir; oil-rich states such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE have given loans, cheap oil and aid, especially in crises; millions of Pakistanis work in the Gulf and send remittances home; through the OIC, of which Pakistan is a founding member, it gains a stronger voice in world affairs, as at the 1974 Lahore Summit.

Reasons: Islamic ideology; Palestine and Kashmir; financial help / oil; jobs and remittances; OIC voice / Lahore Summit; defence links and training.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's membership of SAARC and the ECO.
parts.answer: SAARC was founded at Dhaka in 1985 by seven South Asian countries including Pakistan, India and Bangladesh, to encourage economic and social co-operation; Pakistan hosted its summit at Islamabad in 1988; the ECO was set up in 1985 by Pakistan, Iran and Turkey, replacing the earlier RCD of 1964; in 1992 it was expanded to ten members including Afghanistan and the Central Asian republics.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: SAARC 1985, Dhaka; seven founding members; aims – regional co-operation; Islamabad summit 1988; India–Pakistan rivalry limits it; ECO 1985 (Pakistan, Iran, Turkey); successor to RCD 1964; expanded 1992 to ten members.

parts.text: 'Pakistan's membership of world organisations has brought it more benefits than problems since 1947.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Benefits: the UN arranged the 1949 ceasefire in Kashmir and passed resolutions for a plebiscite; UN agencies such as UNICEF, WHO and UNHCR have helped with health, refugees and disasters; the World Bank arranged the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 and the IMF has given loans; the OIC has supported Pakistan diplomatically; the Commonwealth and SAARC give trade and education links. Problems: the UN resolutions on Kashmir have not been carried out; SEATO and CENTO did not help Pakistan in 1965 or 1971; IMF loans come with conditions such as tax rises and subsidy cuts; Pakistan was suspended from the Commonwealth (1999); SAARC has been held back by India–Pakistan rivalry. Judgement: e.g. benefits outweigh problems because of aid and diplomatic support, even though Kashmir remains unresolved.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the language movement in East Pakistan between 1948 and 1956.
parts.answer: In March 1948 Jinnah said in Dhaka that Urdu alone would be the state language, which upset Bengali speakers; in 1952 Prime Minister Khawaja Nazimuddin repeated this, and students protested; on 21 February 1952 police fired on protesting students in Dhaka and several were killed; the movement continued, and in 1954 the Constituent Assembly accepted Bengali; the 1956 Constitution made both Urdu and Bengali national languages.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: Jinnah's 1948 speech; Bengali speakers' opposition; Nazimuddin 1952; student protests; 21 February 1952 shootings; martyrs remembered (Shaheed Minar); 1954 acceptance; 1956 Constitution – Urdu and Bengali.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Urdu was chosen as the national language of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Urdu had been the language of the Pakistan Movement and was associated with Muslim identity across the subcontinent, since it is written in the Persian–Arabic script and contains many Persian and Arabic words; it was understood in most parts of the country, so it could unite people who spoke different regional languages such as Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto and Balochi; it had a rich literature, including the poetry of Iqbal; Sir Syed and the Aligarh Movement had defended it during the Urdu–Hindi controversy, so it had become a symbol of Muslim rights; choosing a regional language would have favoured one province over the others.

Reasons: symbol of Muslim identity / Pakistan Movement; script and vocabulary; widely understood – unifying; rich literature (Iqbal, Ghalib); Urdu–Hindi controversy; neutral between provinces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how regional languages have contributed to the culture of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Punjabi has a strong tradition of Sufi poetry, such as Waris Shah's Heer Ranjha and the poems of Bulleh Shah; Sindhi literature includes Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai's Shah jo Risalo; Pashto poets include Khushal Khan Khattak and Rahman Baba; Balochi has a long tradition of oral ballads and folk poetry; regional languages are used in radio, television, music and newspapers.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4, with a named language and accurate example: Punjabi (Waris Shah, Bulleh Shah); Sindhi (Shah Abdul Latif); Pashto (Khushal Khan Khattak, Rahman Baba); Balochi (folk ballads, poets such as Jam Durrak); media and music in regional languages; academies / boards promoting them.

parts.text: 'Pakistan's governments were successful in improving education between 1947 and 1999.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Agree: the number of schools, colleges and universities grew greatly; Bhutto made schooling free up to class 8 and founded the Allama Iqbal Open University (1974) for distance learning; Zia promoted adult literacy and Islamic education; many new universities and technical institutes were opened, and the Social Action Programme of the 1990s targeted primary schools. Disagree: literacy rose only slowly and was still well under half the population by the end of the 1990s; spending on education stayed low, around 2% of GDP; girls and rural children had far fewer chances, and many schools lacked teachers or buildings; nationalisation of private schools in 1972 lowered standards in some places; frequent policy changes and the gap between English-medium and Urdu-medium schools continued. Judgement: e.g. access expanded, but low spending meant quality and literacy improved only slowly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the foreign policy of Benazir Bhutto's first government (1988–1990).
parts.answer: She hosted the SAARC summit in Islamabad in December 1988, when Rajiv Gandhi visited and the two countries agreed not to attack each other's nuclear facilities; Pakistan rejoined the Commonwealth in 1989; she visited the USA in 1989 and addressed the US Congress; the Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan was completed in February 1989, and her government supported the mujahideen's attempt to take Jalalabad; tension rose with India over Kashmir in 1990.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 4: SAARC summit 1988; Rajiv Gandhi visit / nuclear facilities agreement; rejoined Commonwealth 1989; visit to USA and Congress; Soviet withdrawal / Jalalabad; Kashmir tension 1990.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq's foreign policy made Pakistan more important to the USA.
parts.answer: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979, Pakistan became the frontline state against Soviet expansion, so the USA needed its co-operation; Zia allowed weapons and money for the Afghan mujahideen to pass through Pakistan, which was the only practical route into Afghanistan; Pakistan hosted about three million Afghan refugees, showing it was carrying a heavy burden for the West; its links with China and the Muslim world made it a useful partner; in return the USA gave large aid packages and F-16 aircraft and did not press Zia over democracy or the nuclear programme.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the annual range of temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total annual rainfall.
parts.answer: 525 mm
parts.working: M1 adding the twelve months; A1 525 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why most of the rain at this station falls in July and August. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Moist monsoon winds from the Bay of Bengal, arriving from the east and south-east, reach northern Punjab in July, bringing humid air that rises and gives heavy showers; intense summer heating causes air to rise by convection, so it cools and condenses into thunderstorms; nearness to the foothills forces the moist air to rise (relief rain).
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: arrival of monsoon winds (moist air from the sea); convectional uplift from summer heating; relief uplift by nearby hills; low pressure over the heated land draws in moist air.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Climate data for a highland valley station at about 1,700 m in northern Balochistan (rounded figures):
Mean temperature (°C): Jan 4, Feb 6, Mar 11, Apr 16, May 21, Jun 25, Jul 27, Aug 25, Sep 20, Oct 14, Nov 9, Dec 5
Precipitation (mm): Jan 50, Feb 52, Mar 40, Apr 22, May 6, Jun 2, Jul 10, Aug 8, Sep 2, Oct 3, Nov 8, Dec 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual range of temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many months have a mean temperature below 10 °C.
parts.answer: 4 months (Nov, Dec, Jan, Feb)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the annual precipitation that falls from December to March. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this station receives most of its precipitation in winter rather than in the monsoon season. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In winter, western depressions from the Mediterranean move east over Iran and Afghanistan and bring rain and snow to the north-western highlands; the monsoon winds come from the east and south-east and have lost most of their moisture before they reach Balochistan, and the mountains to the east block them, so summer is dry.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: western depressions in winter (origin, path); snowfall at altitude; monsoon weak / exhausted by the time it reaches the west; rain shadow of ranges to the east; distance from the Bay of Bengal.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean monthly temperatures (°C) for two stations in southern Pakistan (rounded figures). Station A is on the Arabian Sea coast; Station B is about 450 km inland in upper Sindh.
Station A: Jan 19, Feb 20, Mar 24, Apr 28, May 30, Jun 31, Jul 30, Aug 29, Sep 29, Oct 28, Nov 24, Dec 20
Station B: Jan 15, Feb 18, Mar 25, Apr 31, May 36, Jun 38, Jul 35, Aug 33, Sep 32, Oct 28, Nov 22, Dec 16

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual temperature range for Station A and for Station B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much hotter Station B is than Station A in June.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Station A has a smaller temperature range than Station B. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Station A is on the coast, and the sea heats up and cools down more slowly than land, so it keeps the coast cooler in summer and warmer in winter; the daily sea breeze brings cooler, moist air on land in summer afternoons; Station B is far inland, where dry land heats strongly under clear skies in summer and loses heat quickly in winter nights (continentality).
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: maritime influence – sea heats/cools slowly; sea breezes; higher humidity / cloud at coast reduces extremes; continental interior – dry air, clear skies, rapid heating and cooling.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Monthly rainfall (mm) at a station at the foot of the Margalla Hills (rounded figures):
Rainfall: Jan 55, Feb 70, Mar 75, Apr 50, May 35, Jun 70, Jul 300, Aug 290, Sep 110, Oct 30, Nov 15, Dec 35

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total annual rainfall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the annual rainfall that falls in July, August and September. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: This station has a second, smaller rainfall peak. State the months in which it occurs and the weather system that causes it.
parts.answer: February–March; western depressions (winter disturbances from the west).
parts.working: B1 Feb–Mar; B1 western depressions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe one way in which the timing of rainfall at this station helps farmers.
parts.answer: Winter rain falls when rabi crops such as wheat are growing, so less irrigation is needed (or monsoon rain waters kharif crops).
parts.working: B1 any valid link of rainfall season to crop season.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean monthly temperatures (°C) for a station in the central Punjab plain (rounded figures):
Temperature: Jan 10, Feb 13, Mar 18, Apr 24, May 30, Jun 33, Jul 32, Aug 31, Sep 29, Oct 24, Nov 17, Dec 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean annual temperature. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of months in which the mean temperature is 30 °C or more.
parts.answer: 4 months (May to August)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the pattern of temperature through the year.
parts.answer: Cool winter with the lowest mean in January (10 °C); temperatures rise steadily from February to a maximum in June (33 °C); they stay high (31–32 °C) in July and August, then fall from September to December; annual range 23 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3; at least one figure needed for full marks.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Data for three stations in Pakistan (rounded figures):
Station X: January mean −2 °C, July mean 17 °C, annual precipitation 650 mm, mostly falling as snow and rain in winter and spring
Station Y: January mean 18 °C, July mean 30 °C, annual rainfall 180 mm
Station Z: January mean 14 °C, July mean 37 °C, annual rainfall 90 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the climatic region of each station, choosing from: highland, lowland, coastal, arid. Use each region no more than once. Give one piece of evidence from the data for each.
parts.answer: X – highland (very cold winter, −2 °C in January, cool summer of 17 °C, much winter snow/precipitation); Y – coastal (small range of 12 °C, mild winter of 18 °C); Z – arid (very low total rainfall of 90 mm and very hot summer of 37 °C).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct station with evidence (3); +1 for explaining that Z's very low rainfall makes it arid rather than lowland.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why Station Y receives less rain than many places further north in Pakistan, even though it is next to the sea.
parts.answer: The monsoon winds reach this coast after crossing dry land / they blow parallel to the coast, and there are no mountains to force the air to rise, so little condensation happens; a temperature inversion over the coast stops air rising.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two points: no relief to lift air; winds parallel to coast / weakened monsoon; inversion layer / dry air above.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the four seasons of Pakistan's climate and give the approximate months of each.
parts.answer: Cold season – about mid-November to February; hot season – March to May/June; monsoon (rainy) season – about late June/July to September; post-monsoon (retreating monsoon) season – October to mid-November.
parts.working: 1 mark per season with roughly correct months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the weather of the northern plains during the cold season.
parts.answer: Mainly dry, sunny days with cool to mild temperatures (about 10–20 °C by day); cold nights, sometimes with frost; dense fog in the plains, especially December–January; some light rain from western depressions.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

stem:
Mean April temperatures at four places along a valley in the northern mountains (rounded figures):
500 m: 22 °C
1500 m: 15 °C
2500 m: 9 °C
3500 m: 2 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, describe the relationship between altitude and temperature.
parts.answer: Temperature falls as altitude rises; it drops by about 6–7 °C for every 1,000 m (from 22 °C at 500 m to 2 °C at 3500 m).
parts.working: B1 inverse relationship; B1 use of data / rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average fall in temperature per 1,000 m between 500 m and 3500 m. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the climate of the northern mountains affects the people who live there. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Heavy snow in winter blocks passes and roads such as the Karakoram Highway, so villages are cut off and supplies must be stored; the short growing season allows only one crop a year, so farming is limited; many people practise transhumance, moving livestock to high pastures in summer and down in winter; cold winters raise fuel use, leading to cutting of trees for firewood.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: snow blocks transport; short growing season; transhumance / seasonal migration; demand for firewood / deforestation; tourism in summer.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Climate data for a station in the Potwar Plateau (rounded figures):
Mean temperature (°C): Jan 10, Feb 12, Mar 17, Apr 23, May 28, Jun 31, Jul 29, Aug 28, Sep 27, Oct 23, Nov 17, Dec 12
Rainfall (mm): Jan 60, Feb 70, Mar 80, Apr 60, May 40, Jun 60, Jul 230, Aug 220, Sep 90, Oct 30, Nov 15, Dec 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using figures from the data, describe the climate of this station.
parts.answer: Hot summer, highest temperature in June (31 °C); cool winter, lowest in January (10 °C), range 21 °C; total rainfall 995 mm; wettest month July (230 mm) and August, so a clear monsoon maximum; driest month November (15 mm); a smaller winter–spring peak (70–80 mm in Feb–Mar).
parts.working: 1 mark per accurate point using data up to 4; must mention both temperature and rainfall for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of rainfall in the wettest month to rainfall in the driest month. Give your answer in the form n : 1, with n to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why June is hotter than July at this station although the sun is high in the sky in both months.
parts.answer: In July the monsoon brings thick cloud cover and rain, which reflect and block incoming sunshine and cool the ground by evaporation; June is mostly cloudless with dry air, so heating is stronger.
parts.working: B1 cloud cover in July reduces insolation; B1 rain/evaporation cooling or clear skies in June.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the term monsoon?
parts.answer: A seasonal reversal of wind direction that brings a wet season; in Pakistan, moist winds from the sea in summer (July–September) bring most of the year's rain.
parts.working: B1 seasonal change of wind direction; B1 brings heavy rain in summer / wet season.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction from which the summer monsoon winds reach the northern Punjab.
parts.answer: From the east / south-east (from the Bay of Bengal).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why monsoon rainfall decreases from north-east to south-west across Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The monsoon winds come from the Bay of Bengal across India, so they lose moisture as rain on the way and are driest when they reach the south-west; the north-east has the Himalayan foothills, which force air to rise and give heavy relief rain, while Sindh and Balochistan are low and flat or in rain shadow; the south-west is furthest from the source of moist air.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: distance from Bay of Bengal / moisture lost on the way; relief rain in the north-east foothills; flat lowland / rain shadow in the south-west; Arabian Sea branch blows parallel to the coast.

stem:
Approximate mean annual rainfall at five places, from north-east to south-west (rounded figures):
Murree: 1700 mm
Islamabad: 1150 mm
Lahore: 650 mm
Multan: 190 mm
Jacobabad: 110 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in annual rainfall between the wettest and driest places in the table.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in annual rainfall from Murree to Jacobabad. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Murree and Islamabad are about 40 km apart. Explain why Murree receives much more rain.
parts.answer: Murree is about 2,000 m up in the hills, so moist monsoon air is forced to rise over the hills, cools and condenses, giving heavy relief rain; Islamabad is lower, at the foot of the hills.
parts.working: B1 altitude / hills; B1 forced uplift → cooling → condensation (relief rain).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe western depressions, including where they come from and when they affect Pakistan.
parts.answer: They are low-pressure weather systems that form over the Mediterranean Sea region and move eastwards over Iran and Afghanistan; they reach Pakistan mainly from December to March; they bring rain to the north and west, and snow to the mountains.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: low-pressure systems; origin Mediterranean; move east over Iran/Afghanistan; season (winter, Dec–Mar); rain/snow in north and west. Max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which winter rainfall from western depressions is important for farming in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It falls while rabi crops such as wheat and gram are growing, so it reduces the need for canal or tubewell water, which saves costs; in barani (rain-fed) areas of the Potwar Plateau it is the main water for wheat, so a dry winter means a poor harvest; snowfall in the mountains melts in spring and summer, feeding the rivers and canals used for irrigation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: waters rabi crops (wheat); barani farming dependent on it; snow store feeds rivers; reduces irrigation cost / pumping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how relief rainfall forms over the Himalayan foothills during the monsoon. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Moist monsoon winds blow towards the foothills and are forced to rise over the high ground; as the air rises it expands and cools, and when it reaches its dew point the water vapour condenses to form clouds; the droplets grow and fall as heavy rain on the windward slopes, while the leeward side is drier (rain shadow).
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: moist air forced to rise by mountains; cools on rising; condensation at dew point / clouds form; rain on windward side; rain shadow on leeward side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Monsoon rainfall brings more benefits than problems to Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Benefits: monsoon rain fills reservoirs such as Tarbela and Mangla, used for irrigation and hydel power; it waters kharif crops such as rice, cotton and sugar cane; it recharges groundwater for tubewells; it cools temperatures after the hot season. Problems: heavy rain causes floods, as in 2010 and 2022, destroying crops, homes and roads; urban flooding in cities such as Karachi and Lahore; landslides in the northern areas; standing water spreads malaria and dengue; rainfall varies from year to year, so a weak monsoon causes drought. Judgement: e.g. the benefits outweigh the problems because farming and power depend on it, provided flood management improves.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement. Use named examples (e.g. 2022 floods, Tarbela, kharif crops).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these stages of the formation of convectional rain in the correct order:
P  Water vapour condenses into towering cumulonimbus clouds
Q  The sun heats the ground strongly
R  Heavy showers and thunderstorms fall in the afternoon
S  Warm air rises and cools
parts.answer: Q, S, P, R
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 if two adjacent stages are swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why convectional rain is most common in the plains of Punjab in the summer afternoons. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In summer the sun is high and days are long, so the ground heats most strongly by the afternoon, causing warm air to rise rapidly; during the monsoon the air is humid, so rising air quickly reaches dew point and produces cumulonimbus clouds and thunderstorms; in winter heating is weaker and air drier, so convection rarely produces rain.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: maximum heating in summer afternoons; humid monsoon air; rapid rising and cooling; contrast with winter.

stem:
Annual rainfall (mm) at a rain-fed (barani) farming area for five years:
Year 1: 512, Year 2: 680, Year 3: 395, Year 4: 840, Year 5: 448

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean annual rainfall for the five years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate by what percentage the wettest year was above the mean. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.working: M1 difference ÷ mean × 100; A1 46.1%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two problems that this variability of rainfall causes for farmers who depend on rain. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In dry years such as Year 3 crops fail and fodder is scarce, so farmers lose income and may have to sell animals or borrow money; in very wet years such as Year 4 floods and waterlogging damage crops and soil; farmers cannot plan which crops to sow or how much seed and fertiliser to buy, so they choose low-risk, low-yield crops.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: drought years – crop failure, debt; wet years – flooding / soil erosion; uncertainty in planning; migration to cities in bad years.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A town at 250 m has a mean July temperature of 33 °C. Temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m of height. Estimate the mean July temperature of a hill resort at 2250 m.
parts.working: M1 height difference 2000 m → 6.5 × 2 = 13 °C; A1 20 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why temperature falls as altitude increases.
parts.answer: The air is heated mainly from the ground, so air further from the ground is cooler; at higher altitudes the air is thinner (lower pressure), holds less heat and less water vapour, so it absorbs and keeps less heat.
parts.working: B1 heating from the ground surface; B1 thinner air holds less heat.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two factors other than altitude that affect temperatures in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: latitude; distance from the sea; cloud cover; aspect (direction a slope faces); winds.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why Jacobabad in upper Sindh is one of the hottest places in Pakistan in May and June.
parts.answer: It is far from the sea, so there is no cooling sea breeze (continentality); the sky is cloudless and the air very dry, so the sun heats the ground strongly; the sun is almost overhead and days are long in early summer; it is on a low flat plain surrounded by dry land and hot winds (loo) blow across it.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3: distance from sea; clear skies / dry air; high sun angle and long days; low altitude; hot dry winds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why places in the far north of Pakistan are colder in winter than places in the far south. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The north is at a higher latitude, so the winter sun is lower in the sky and its energy is spread over a larger area, and days are shorter, so less heating; most of the north is also at high altitude, where the air is thinner and holds less heat; cold air from Central Asia can reach it, while the south is moderated by the warm Arabian Sea.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: latitude / angle of the sun; shorter winter days; altitude; distance from the warm sea; cold northerly air.

stem:
Mean temperatures for a coastal city and an inland city in Balochistan (rounded figures):
Coastal city: coolest month 17 °C, hottest month 30 °C
Inland city at 1,600 m: coolest month 3 °C, hottest month 27 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual temperature range for each place.
parts.answer: Coastal: 13 °C; inland: 24 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the sea breeze keeps coastal areas cooler on summer afternoons. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: By day the land heats up faster than the sea, so warm air rises over the land and creates lower pressure; cooler, denser air moves in from the higher pressure over the sea to replace it, lowering temperatures on the coast; the moist sea air also adds cloud and humidity, which limits further heating.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: land heats faster than sea; low pressure over land; cool air flows in from the sea; moist air / cloud limits heating.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
July mean temperatures at three stations in the same mountain district (rounded figures):
Station P: altitude 150 m, July mean 34 °C
Station Q: altitude 1350 m, July mean 27 °C
Station R: altitude 2350 m, July mean 21 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a fall of 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, calculate the temperature expected at Q and at R from the temperature at P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the actual and the expected temperature at Q and at R.
parts.answer: Q: 27 − 26.2 = +0.8 °C (actual warmer); R: 21 − 19.7 = +1.3 °C (actual warmer)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two factors, other than altitude, that could explain these differences.
parts.answer: Aspect – the stations may be on south-facing slopes that receive more direct sunshine; sheltered valley sites trap heat; less cloud cover or less forest; local winds (e.g. warm dry winds descending into valleys).
parts.working: B1 each for two valid factors with brief explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the term latitude?
parts.answer: The distance of a place north or south of the Equator, measured in degrees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how cloud cover affects temperatures in Pakistan by day and by night. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: By day, cloud reflects and absorbs sunlight, so less reaches the ground and daytime temperatures are lower (e.g. during the monsoon); by night, cloud acts like a blanket and traps heat radiated from the ground, so nights are warmer; with clear skies in deserts days are very hot and nights cold, giving a large daily range.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: day – reflects insolation, cooler; night – traps outgoing radiation, warmer; clear skies – large daily range in deserts; example monsoon / Thar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the aspect of a slope affects temperature in the northern mountains.
parts.answer: South-facing slopes receive more direct sunshine, so they are warmer (snow melts earlier) than north-facing slopes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the term drought?
parts.answer: A long period with much less rainfall than normal, so that there is a serious shortage of water.
parts.working: B1 long period / prolonged; B1 below-normal rainfall / water shortage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of drought on people living in the Thar Desert. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Wells and ponds dry up, so women and children walk long distances for water, which may be unsafe to drink and spreads disease; grazing and fodder fail, so cattle, goats and sheep die and families lose their main source of food and income; food shortages lead to malnutrition, especially among children; many families migrate to barrage areas or towns to find work.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: water shortage; livestock deaths; crop failure and hunger / malnutrition; disease; migration; debt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the causes of the severe floods in Pakistan in 2022.
parts.answer: Monsoon rainfall from June to August was several times the normal amount in Sindh and Balochistan; very high temperatures earlier in the year increased glacier melt in the north; much of the lower Indus plain is very flat, so water could not drain away; embankments were breached and hill torrents flooded towns.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3: exceptional monsoon rain (Sindh, Balochistan); heatwave / glacier melt; flat land, poor drainage; breaches / hill torrents; deforestation or climate change accepted with explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two impacts of floods such as those of 2022 on farming in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Standing crops such as cotton, rice and dates were destroyed, so farmers lost income and the country lost export earnings; livestock drowned, removing a source of milk and income; floodwater stood for months, so wheat could not be sown on time for the next rabi season; irrigation canals and roads were damaged, increasing costs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: crop losses; livestock deaths; delayed sowing; damaged canals / roads; food prices rise; soil damage or silt.

stem:
Daily maximum temperatures (°C) during a heatwave in a coastal city:
Day 1: 41, Day 2: 43, Day 3: 44, Day 4: 42, Day 5: 39, Day 6: 38, Day 7: 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of days on which the maximum temperature was 40 °C or above.
parts.answer: 5 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean daily maximum temperature for the seven days. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why heatwaves cause more deaths in large cities such as Karachi than in rural areas. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Concrete buildings and roads absorb heat by day and release it at night, so cities stay hot at night (urban heat island) and people get no relief; power cuts during peak demand stop fans and air-conditioners; many poor people live in crowded, poorly ventilated housing; outdoor workers such as labourers and street vendors cannot avoid the heat; water shortages make dehydration worse.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: urban heat island; power and water shortages; crowded housing; outdoor workers; humidity at coast; lack of shade / trees.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two periods of the year when tropical cyclones are most likely to affect Pakistan's coast.
parts.answer: May–June (before the monsoon) and October–November (after the monsoon).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two coastal areas of Pakistan that are at risk from tropical cyclones.
parts.answer: Any two: Karachi; Thatta / Keti Bandar (Indus delta); Badin; the Makran coast (Gwadar, Pasni, Ormara).
parts.working: B1 for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which authorities can reduce the impact of a tropical cyclone on coastal communities. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Early warning systems using satellite tracking by the Meteorological Department give time to evacuate people from low-lying villages to shelters; fishermen can be told not to go to sea, so boats and lives are not lost; planting and protecting mangrove forests in the Indus delta absorbs storm surges and waves; building raised shelters and stronger houses reduces damage.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: forecasting and early warning; evacuation and shelters; fishing ban; mangroves; embankments / building codes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF)?
parts.answer: A sudden flood caused when water stored in a lake formed by a melting glacier breaks through the ice or moraine (rock debris) that dams it.
parts.working: B1 lake formed by glacier melt; B1 sudden release when dam of ice/moraine fails.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the risk of GLOFs is increasing in Gilgit-Baltistan and Chitral. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rising temperatures are making glaciers melt faster, so more and larger glacial lakes are forming; these lakes are held back by loose moraine or ice, which can give way suddenly; heavy rain or heatwaves can raise lake levels quickly; more people now live and build in narrow valleys below the glaciers, so more are exposed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: global warming / faster melting; more lakes forming; weak moraine dams; heatwaves and heavy rain; settlement in valleys.

stem:
Air quality index (AQI) readings at one monitoring station in Lahore on six days in November:
180, 245, 310, 420, 390, 260

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of readings that were above 300 ('hazardous').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why smog is worst in Lahore between November and January. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In winter cold, calm air near the ground is trapped under a layer of warmer air (temperature inversion), so pollutants cannot rise and spread; winds are light, so smoke builds up; at this time farmers burn rice straw after the harvest and smoke drifts over the city; emissions from vehicles, brick kilns and factories add to the pollution, and fog mixes with the smoke.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: temperature inversion; calm winds; crop residue burning; vehicles, kilns, industry; fog.

parts.label: c
parts.text: 'Smog in Lahore can only be reduced by controlling crop burning.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: crop residue burning in Punjab after the rice harvest produces large amounts of smoke exactly when smog peaks; offering farmers machines such as happy seeders or buying straw could cut this quickly. Against: vehicles are a major year-round source, so better fuel, emission checks and public transport (e.g. Lahore Metro Bus and Orange Line) are needed; brick kilns can switch to zig-zag technology; factories and burning of rubbish also contribute; planting trees and banning open burning in the city help. Judgement: e.g. controlling crop burning is important but not enough on its own, because traffic and industry pollute every day.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the hot, dry, dusty wind that blows across the plains of Punjab and Sindh in May and June.
parts.answer: The loo.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two effects of dust storms and hot winds on people in the plains.
parts.answer: Heatstroke and dehydration, especially among outdoor workers; breathing problems and eye infections from dust; damage to crops and fruit; poor visibility disrupts road and air transport; power lines brought down.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two effects.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which people in the plains adapt their daily lives to very hot summers.
parts.answer: Working outdoors early in the morning or evening and resting at midday; thick-walled houses with small windows and flat roofs for sleeping on at night; drinking more water and traditional drinks; planting shade trees.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two adaptations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pakistan produces less than 1% of the world's greenhouse gas emissions but is one of the countries most affected by climate change. Explain two reasons why Pakistan is very vulnerable to climate change. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Its rivers depend on glaciers in the Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush, so faster melting first raises flood and GLOF risk and later threatens water supply; most of the country is arid or semi-arid with high temperatures, so heatwaves and droughts become more extreme; farming, which employs a large share of the workforce, depends on irrigation and monsoon rain; many people are poor and live in flood-prone areas, so they cannot easily recover.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: glacier dependence; heat and aridity; agriculture-dependent economy; flood-prone plains / coast; poverty and weak infrastructure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Pakistan should spend more on adapting to climate change than on reducing its own emissions.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For adaptation: Pakistan's emissions are small, so cutting them will hardly change world temperatures; its people are already suffering floods, heatwaves and droughts, so money for flood defences, early warning, heat action plans, drought-resistant crops and water storage saves lives now. For reducing emissions: cleaner energy such as solar, wind and hydel reduces costly oil imports and air pollution (smog); reforestation such as large tree-planting programmes both stores carbon and reduces floods and soil erosion; showing action helps Pakistan gain international climate finance. Judgement: e.g. adaptation should come first, but many actions (solar power, trees) do both.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

stem:
River levels (m above normal) at a gauge on the Chenab during a monsoon flood:
Day 1: 3.2, Day 2: 3.9, Day 3: 4.6, Day 4: 5.1, Day 5: 4.8, Day 6: 4.1, Day 7: 3.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: The danger level at the gauge is 4.5 m. State the number of days on which the river was above the danger level.
parts.answer: 3 days (Days 3, 4 and 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rise in river level from Day 1 to the peak.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two methods used in Pakistan to reduce the damage caused by river floods. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Embankments (bunds) along the Indus and its tributaries keep high water within the river channel, protecting farmland and towns; large dams such as Tarbela and Mangla store monsoon floodwater and release it slowly; flood forecasting and early warnings from gauges and satellites give people time to move to safety; spurs and diversion channels protect barrages and cities.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: embankments / bunds; dams and reservoirs; forecasting and warning; diversion channels; banning building on floodplains; afforestation upstream.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Rainfall (mm) at a station in Sindh in a flood year compared with normal:
July: normal 60, flood year 210
August: normal 70, flood year 330
September: normal 40, flood year 150

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total rainfall for the three months in the flood year as a percentage of the normal total. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rainfall in August of the flood year as a percentage of normal. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why floods in the lower Indus plain of Sindh often last much longer than floods in the mountain valleys. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The lower Indus plain is very flat with a gentle gradient, so water spreads out and drains away slowly; embankments, roads and canal banks trap water on the land side, so it cannot return to the river; the soil is fine and often already saturated, so little water soaks in; in the mountains steep slopes carry water away quickly although floods there are more sudden and destructive.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: flat land / low gradient; obstructions (embankments, roads, canals); saturated or clay soils; high water table; contrast with steep mountain valleys.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the term death rate?
parts.answer: The number of deaths in a year for every 1,000 people in the population.
parts.working: B1 deaths per 1,000 per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A district has a birth rate of 27 per 1,000 and a death rate of 7 per 1,000. Calculate its rate of natural increase as a percentage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why death rates in Pakistan have fallen since 1950. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Vaccination programmes against diseases such as measles, tuberculosis and polio mean fewer children die young; more hospitals, basic health units and Lady Health Workers give people access to treatment; cleaner drinking water and better sanitation reduce diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea; improved food supply since the Green Revolution reduces malnutrition.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: vaccination; medical facilities and medicines; clean water and sanitation; better nutrition; health education.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to birth rates and death rates in Stage 2 of the demographic transition model.
parts.answer: Birth rates stay high; death rates fall rapidly, so the population grows quickly.
parts.working: B1 birth rate high; B1 death rate falls rapidly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Pakistan is often described as being between Stage 2 and Stage 3 of the model. Explain why its birth rate is now falling slowly. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: More girls are going to school and women who are educated tend to marry later and have fewer children; family planning services and contraception are more widely available, especially in cities; as child death rates fall, parents no longer need many children to make sure some survive; in towns children are costly to raise and educate rather than helping on the farm.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: female education / later marriage; family planning; lower infant mortality; urbanisation / cost of children; women working outside the home.

stem:
Approximate population (millions) of a province by age group:
0–14: 8.6
15–64: 13.1
65+: 0.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the province's population aged 0–14. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The dependency ratio = (population aged 0–14 + population aged 65+) ÷ population aged 15–64 × 100. Calculate the dependency ratio. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the population pyramid you would expect for this province.
parts.answer: A wide base because of the large number of children, narrowing steadily upwards (triangular / concave sides), with a very narrow top because few people live beyond 65.
parts.working: B1 wide base; B1 narrow top / tapering shape.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Population of Pakistan at four censuses (approximate, millions):
1981: 84.3
1998: 132.4
2017: 207.7
2023: 241.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in population between 1998 and 2023.
parts.working: B1 109.1 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in population between 1998 and 2023. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan's population has continued to grow rapidly. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Birth rates remain high, especially in rural areas, because many families want sons to work on the land and support parents in old age; early marriage gives women a long child-bearing period; death rates have fallen because of better health care, so natural increase is high; a very young population means many people are entering child-bearing age (population momentum); use of contraception remains low.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: high birth rate (rural, sons, old-age security, religious or cultural beliefs); early marriage; falling death rate; young population / momentum; low contraceptive use; limited female education.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A useful estimate of the time a population takes to double is 70 ÷ (annual growth rate in %). Pakistan's population grew at about 2.5% a year between 2017 and 2023. Estimate how many years it would take to double at this rate.
parts.working: B1 28 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems that rapid population growth causes for the government of Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It must provide more schools, teachers and hospitals every year just to keep up, so quality falls and class sizes rise; millions of young people enter the labour market each year, and not enough jobs are created, so unemployment and underemployment rise; demand for food, water and housing rises, putting pressure on irrigation water and causing growth of katchi abadis.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: services (education, health); jobs; food and water; housing; budget pressure / debt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: 'Pakistan's large and young population is an asset rather than a problem.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Asset: a large young workforce can raise production and attract investment if it is educated and skilled (demographic dividend); a big home market helps industries such as textiles and food; young workers abroad send remittances; young people quickly adopt technology, supporting the IT sector and freelancing. Problem: many young people lack education and skills, so they cannot find good jobs; high dependency ratio strains family incomes; pressure on schools, hospitals, water and housing; unemployment can lead to social unrest. Judgement: e.g. it can be an asset only if the government invests in education, skills and job creation.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two measures the government has used to reduce the birth rate in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Family planning centres and free or cheap contraceptives; Lady Health Workers visiting homes to advise families; media campaigns on small families; encouraging girls' education; involving religious leaders to support birth spacing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two measures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why birth rates are higher in rural areas than in cities in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Children help with farm work and looking after animals from a young age, so large families are seen as an economic benefit; rural women have lower literacy and marry younger, so they have more children; family planning services and clinics are fewer and further away; infant mortality is higher, so parents have more children to make sure some survive; traditional and religious attitudes against contraception are stronger.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: children as farm labour; old-age security; low female literacy / early marriage; poor access to family planning; higher infant mortality; traditions.

stem:
Percentage of the population in three age groups in two districts:
District A: 0–14 years 42%, 15–64 years 54%, 65+ years 4%
District B: 0–14 years 30%, 15–64 years 63%, 65+ years 7%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the dependency ratio for each district, using (% aged 0–14 + % aged 65+) ÷ % aged 15–64 × 100. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which district is more likely to be a large city. Give two reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: District B: it has fewer children (lower birth rate, typical of cities with more education and family planning) and more people aged 15–64 because young adults migrate to cities for work; it also has more elderly people because of better health care.
parts.working: B1 District B with one reason; B1 second reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two consequences for District A of having such a high proportion of children. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Many more school places and teachers are needed, and if they are not provided many children will not attend school; each worker must support more dependants, so family incomes are stretched and poverty continues; in future a large number of young people will need jobs, putting pressure on the labour market; demand for child health care and vaccination is high.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: demand for schools; demand for child health care; high dependency on workers / poverty; future job demand; future high birth rate (momentum).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of these jobs as primary, secondary or tertiary:
(i) a fisherman at Gwadar
(ii) a worker in a cement factory
(iii) a teacher in Multan
(iv) a cotton farmer in Sanghar
parts.answer: (i) primary; (ii) secondary; (iii) tertiary; (iv) primary
parts.working: B2 all four correct; B1 two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is meant by tertiary employment?
parts.answer: Jobs that provide services rather than goods, e.g. teaching, banking, transport, health care.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many people in Pakistan still work in primary activities. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Most people live in rural areas where farming is the main source of work, so they work on family land or as tenants; many have low levels of education and skills, so they cannot get factory or office jobs; agriculture is labour-intensive, with crops such as cotton and wheat still often picked or harvested by hand; there are few factories or services in many villages.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: rural population / farming main activity; low education and skills; labour-intensive farming; lack of other jobs in rural areas; family tradition / land ownership.

stem: Employment by sector in a district of southern Punjab (% of workers): Agriculture 45, Industry 21, Services 34

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle needed for each sector if this information is drawn as a pie chart.
parts.answer: Agriculture 162°, Industry 75.6°, Services 122.4°
parts.working: M1 % × 3.6; A1 all three angles correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sector in which most people in the district work.
parts.answer: Agriculture (45%)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which this employment structure is likely to change as the district develops. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The share in agriculture is likely to fall because machines such as tractors and harvesters replace farm workers; new factories (e.g. textiles, food processing) and industrial estates would create secondary jobs, attracting workers from farms; as incomes rise people demand more services such as schools, shops, banks, transport and IT, so tertiary employment grows.
