parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: mechanisation reduces farm jobs; industrialisation increases secondary; rising incomes increase services; education / skills allow movement to services; rural–urban migration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by underemployment?
parts.answer: When people work fewer hours than they want, or in jobs that do not use their skills and qualifications.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many educated young people in Pakistan's cities are unemployed. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The number of graduates is growing faster than the number of new jobs, because economic growth has been slow; many degrees do not match the skills employers need, such as technical and IT skills, so graduates cannot find suitable work; job seekers often prefer government or office jobs and wait for them rather than take lower-status work; recruitment can depend on contacts, so those without connections struggle.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: slow job creation / low investment; skills mismatch; preference for government jobs; nepotism; energy shortages closing factories; rapid population growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way in which the government could reduce unemployment among young people.
parts.answer: Technical and vocational training (e.g. TEVTA courses) linked to industry needs; IT and freelancing training; cheap loans for young entrepreneurs; attract investment to SEZs.
parts.working: B1 any valid suggestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by seasonal unemployment?
parts.answer: Unemployment that happens at certain times of the year when work is not available, e.g. between farming seasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of seasonal work in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: cotton picking (autumn); wheat harvesting (April–May); sugar cane cutting and crushing (winter); work in hill tourist resorts in summer; fishing seasons.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which rural families in Pakistan cope with seasonal unemployment. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Family members migrate temporarily to cities to work as labourers, sending money home; they take up cottage industries such as weaving, embroidery or pottery during slack seasons; they keep livestock, which provides milk and income all year; they borrow from landlords or shopkeepers until the next harvest, which can lead to debt.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: temporary migration; cottage industries; livestock; borrowing / debt; working in the informal sector.

stem:
A country's employment structure (% of workers) at two dates (approximate figures):
Year 1: Agriculture 51, Industry 20, Services 29
Year 2: Agriculture 37, Industry 25, Services 38

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the percentage of workers in each sector between Year 1 and Year 2.
parts.answer: Agriculture −14 percentage points, Industry +5 percentage points, Services +9 percentage points
parts.working: M1 subtraction; A1 all three correct with sign.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the share of workers in agriculture has fallen. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Farm mechanisation (tractors, threshers, combine harvesters) means fewer workers are needed; land holdings are divided between heirs until they are too small to support a family, so young people leave farming; low and uncertain farm incomes push people to look for work in towns; growth of industry and services in cities offers better-paid jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: mechanisation; fragmentation of land; low farm incomes; pull of urban jobs; education leading to non-farm jobs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem caused by this change for the cities that receive the workers.
parts.answer: Many rural migrants cannot find formal jobs, so they work in the informal sector with low pay, and live in katchi abadis without proper water and sanitation.
parts.working: B1 problem; B1 development.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a smaller proportion of women than men work outside the home in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Cultural traditions in many areas expect women to look after the home and children, so families may not allow them to take paid work; lower female literacy and fewer technical skills limit the jobs available; lack of safe, affordable transport and fear of harassment make travelling to work difficult; few workplaces offer day-care or flexible hours.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: cultural expectations; lower education; transport / safety; lack of childcare; discrimination in hiring or pay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to Pakistan of increasing the number of women in paid work. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It would add more workers and skills to the economy, raising production and national income; women earning money increase family incomes, which can pay for children's education and health; working women tend to marry later and have fewer children, reducing population growth; industries such as garments and IT gain skilled workers.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: bigger workforce / higher GDP; family income and child welfare; lower birth rate; skills for industries; women's independence and status.

stem:
Labour force figures for a province (millions):
Age 15–24: unemployed 1.9, employed 18.2
Age 25–34: unemployed 1.4, employed 23.5
Age 35–54: unemployed 0.7, employed 20.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: The unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ (employed + unemployed) × 100. Calculate the unemployment rate for each age group. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.working: B1 each correct rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The best way to reduce unemployment in Pakistan is to expand large-scale manufacturing.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: factories such as textiles, cement and food processing employ large numbers of semi-skilled workers; industry adds value to raw materials such as cotton and earns export income; industrial estates and SEZs (e.g. under CPEC) can attract foreign investment. Against: modern factories are increasingly mechanised and need fewer workers; energy shortages and high costs limit industrial growth; services such as IT, freelancing, tourism and retail can create jobs faster and need less capital; agriculture and agro-based industries employ more people in rural areas; small and cottage industries and the informal sector create many jobs for low-skilled workers. Judgement: e.g. manufacturing helps, but a mix including IT, services and small businesses with skills training will do more.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the term emigration?
parts.answer: Leaving one's own country to live in another country.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two push factors and two pull factors that cause people to move from villages to cities in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Push (any two): lack of jobs in farming / mechanisation; low incomes; few schools or hospitals; floods or drought; land disputes. Pull (any two): jobs in factories and services; higher wages; better schools, hospitals and electricity; relatives already in the city.
parts.working: B1 two push factors; B1 two pull factors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two effects of rural–urban migration on the villages that people leave. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Young men leave, so there are fewer workers for farming and women, children and the elderly take on more work; migrants send money home, which pays for better houses, education and farm inputs; the village loses its most educated and energetic people, slowing its development; families are separated for long periods.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: loss of labour; remittances; loss of skilled / educated people; ageing population; family separation; ideas brought back.

stem:
Remittances sent home by Pakistanis working abroad in one year (hypothetical figures, US$ billion):
Saudi Arabia: 7.4
UAE: 5.5
UK: 4.5
USA: 3.5
Other: 6.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total remittances received.
parts.answer: US$ 27.0 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total that came from Saudi Arabia and the UAE together. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which remittances benefit Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Remittances bring in foreign exchange, which helps pay for imports such as oil and reduces the trade deficit; families spend the money on education, health care and housing, raising living standards; money invested in land, shops or small businesses creates local jobs; they reduce poverty in areas with many migrants.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: foreign exchange / balance of payments; household living standards; investment and jobs; poverty reduction; construction boom.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by seasonal migration?
parts.answer: Moving away from home for part of the year and returning, e.g. for harvest work or to find grazing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the seasonal movement of herders and their animals in the northern mountains (transhumance).
parts.answer: In summer herders take sheep, goats and cattle up to high mountain pastures as the snow melts; in autumn they bring them down to the valleys or plains, where it is warmer and fodder is stored for winter.
parts.working: B1 upward in summer to high pastures; B1 downward in autumn/winter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why families from the Thar Desert migrate for part of the year. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: When the monsoon fails, wells and ponds dry up and grazing disappears, so families move with their animals to the irrigated barrage areas where water and fodder are available; there is little paid work in the desert, so they move to work as labourers at harvest time (e.g. wheat, cotton, sugar cane) in irrigated districts; drought causes food shortages, so they move to be near markets and relief.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: drought / lack of water; grazing for livestock; harvest work in irrigated areas; food shortage; return after rains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by 'brain drain'?
parts.answer: The emigration of highly educated and skilled people (e.g. doctors, engineers, IT experts) to other countries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many skilled Pakistanis emigrate to countries such as the UK, Canada and the Gulf states. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Salaries for doctors, engineers and IT specialists are many times higher abroad, so they can support their families better; there are more opportunities for training, research and promotion; economic and political uncertainty, inflation and power cuts at home push people out; relatives already abroad help them settle and find work.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: higher wages; career opportunities; better living standards / services; instability at home; family networks; demand for skills abroad.

parts.label: c
parts.text: 'Emigration of skilled workers does more harm than good to Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Harm: Pakistan loses doctors, nurses and engineers that cost the country a lot to train, so hospitals and universities are short of staff; it reduces the skills needed for development and new businesses; families are separated. Good: emigrants send large remittances (Pakistan receives tens of billions of US dollars a year), which support the balance of payments and families; some return with new skills, savings and contacts and start businesses; it reduces unemployment among graduates; the diaspora invests in property and projects in Pakistan. Judgement: e.g. it does more good while remittances are high, but Pakistan should encourage return and train more professionals.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the country from which Pakistan received the largest number of refugees after 1979.
parts.answer: Afghanistan.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two provinces of Pakistan where most of these refugees settled.
parts.answer: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.
parts.working: B1 both.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two effects of the arrival of large numbers of refugees on the areas where they settled. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Demand for water, fuel wood and grazing increased, leading to deforestation and overgrazing around camps; competition for jobs and housing pushed down wages and raised rents for local people; schools and hospitals became overcrowded; refugees also brought trade and businesses, such as transport and carpet weaving, and received international aid that improved some services.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: pressure on resources / environment; job competition and wages; pressure on services; housing and rents; new businesses / skills; aid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by urbanisation?
parts.answer: An increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At the 2023 census Pakistan had a population of about 241.5 million, of whom about 93.8 million lived in urban areas. Calculate the percentage living in urban areas. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by rapid urban growth in a city such as Karachi or Lahore. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Housing cannot be built fast enough, so many people live in katchi abadis without piped water or sewerage, causing disease; traffic congestion increases journey times and air pollution; water supply and electricity cannot meet demand, so there are shortages and load-shedding; there are not enough formal jobs, so many work in the low-paid informal sector.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: housing / katchi abadis; traffic and pollution; water, sewerage and power; unemployment / informal sector; crime; waste disposal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the living conditions in a typical katchi abadi.
parts.answer: Houses built of mud, scrap or unbaked bricks on land without legal title; narrow unpaved lanes; open drains and little or no sewerage; few water taps, so water is bought or collected; illegal electricity connections; overcrowding with large families in one or two rooms.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which living conditions in katchi abadis can be improved. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Self-help schemes like the Orangi Pilot Project in Karachi help residents build low-cost sewers lane by lane, reducing disease; giving residents legal ownership (regularisation) encourages them to invest in better houses; the government can provide piped water, electricity and paved roads; low-cost housing schemes can rehouse people from the most dangerous sites.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: self-help (Orangi Pilot Project); regularisation / ownership; provision of services; low-cost housing; health and school facilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the population of large cities in Pakistan is growing faster than the national population. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Cities grow from both natural increase and rural–urban migration, as people move in for jobs, education and health care; many migrants are young adults, so they add to births in the city; city boundaries expand and absorb surrounding villages; people displaced by floods or conflict often move to cities.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: rural–urban migration (pull factors); young migrants raise births; boundary expansion; displacement by disasters/conflict.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The best way to reduce the problems of Pakistan's large cities is to develop rural areas.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: if villages had more jobs (agro-based industry, small businesses), schools, clinics and electricity, fewer people would migrate, reducing pressure on city housing, transport and water; developing small towns spreads growth. Against: cities need direct investment anyway – mass transit (e.g. Lahore Orange Line, Karachi Green Line BRT), water schemes, sewerage and low-cost housing; rural development is slow and expensive and people may still be attracted by city wages; urban planning and regularisation of katchi abadis help those already in cities. Judgement: e.g. both are needed – rural development slows migration, but city infrastructure must still improve.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

stem: The population of a large city in Pakistan grew from about 7.1 million to about 13.0 million in 20 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the city's population over the 20 years. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average number of people added to the city each year.
parts.answer: 5.9 million ÷ 20 = about 295,000 people a year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two problems this growth causes for public transport in the city. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The number of commuters rises faster than buses and roads are added, so buses and vans are overcrowded and unsafe; more private cars and motorbikes cause traffic jams and long journey times, raising fuel use and air pollution; building mass transit systems is very expensive and takes years, so services lag behind demand.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: overcrowded buses; congestion; pollution; cost and time of new systems; long commutes from outer settlements.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Approximate figures from the 2023 census:
Punjab: population 127.7 million, area 205,344 km²
Balochistan: population 14.9 million, area 347,190 km²

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by population density?
parts.answer: The average number of people living in each square kilometre of an area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the population density of each province to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Punjab: 127.7 million ÷ 205,344 km² ≈ 622 people per km²; Balochistan: 14.9 million ÷ 347,190 km² ≈ 43 people per km²
parts.working: B1 Punjab 622; B1 Balochistan 43.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Balochistan has a much lower population density than Punjab. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Balochistan is mostly mountains, plateaus and desert, so there is little flat land for farming or building; rainfall is very low and there are few permanent rivers, so irrigation is limited and few crops can be grown; there are fewer industries and jobs, so people move away; poor roads and services make settlement difficult. Punjab has fertile alluvial plains watered by the Indus and its tributaries and a dense canal network.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: relief (mountains/plateau); arid climate / lack of water; little irrigation; few jobs / industry; poor communications; contrast with fertile, irrigated Punjab plains.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by population distribution?
parts.answer: The way in which people are spread out across an area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the distribution of population in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Most people live in the Indus plain, especially in central and northern Punjab and along the Indus in Sindh; large concentrations in cities such as Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad and Rawalpindi–Islamabad; the Peshawar valley is densely populated; the western plateaus of Balochistan, the deserts (Thar, Cholistan, Kharan) and the high northern mountains are thinly populated.
parts.working: 1 mark per point up to 3; must include both dense and sparse areas for full marks.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two physical factors that encourage high population densities in parts of Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Flat land in the Indus plain makes farming, building and transport easy; fertile alluvial soils deposited by rivers give high crop yields; reliable water from rivers and canals allows irrigation; a moderate climate with monsoon rain in northern Punjab supports farming.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: flat relief; fertile soil; water supply / irrigation; favourable climate; coastal access (Karachi).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mountain valley in Swat has an area of 340 km² of usable land and a population of 156,400. Calculate its population density.
parts.answer: 156,400 ÷ 340 = 460 people per km²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some valleys in the northern mountains have high population densities, even though mountain areas overall are sparsely populated. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Valley floors are flatter and have fertile alluvial soil, so terraced and irrigated farming is possible; rivers and glacier-fed streams give a reliable water supply; roads and settlements follow the valleys, so trade, services and tourism are concentrated there; the surrounding steep slopes are unsuitable, so people crowd into the small usable area.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: flat valley floors; fertile soils; water supply; routes / roads along valleys; tourism and services; people concentrated in limited usable land.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem caused by high densities in such valleys.
parts.answer: Building on floodplains increases flood risk; pressure on forests for fuel and timber; small farm sizes.

stem:
Population and area of two districts (hypothetical figures):
District A: population 2.3 million, area 3,410 km²
District B: population 0.25 million, area 18,000 km²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the population density of each district to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: District A: 2.3 million ÷ 3,410 km² ≈ 674 people per km²; District B: 0.25 million ÷ 18,000 km² ≈ 14 people per km²

parts.label: b
parts.text: District A is in the canal-irrigated plain of central Punjab and District B is in the Cholistan Desert. Explain two reasons for the difference in density. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: District A has perennial canal water, so crops such as wheat, cotton and sugar cane can be grown all year and support many people, while District B has very low rainfall and almost no surface water, so only nomadic herding is possible; District A has towns, roads, industries and services offering jobs; District B has sandy soils and extreme temperatures, making settlement difficult.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: irrigation vs no water; fertile soils vs sand; jobs / industry / towns; transport; climate extremes in desert.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a district, 4.6 million of the 7.2 million people aged 10 and over can read and write. Calculate the literacy rate. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why female literacy is lower than male literacy in many rural areas of Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: There are fewer girls' schools in villages and they may be far away, so parents do not allow girls to travel for safety reasons; many families value boys' education more because sons are expected to earn; girls are kept at home to help with housework, fetching water or looking after siblings; early marriage ends girls' education; there is a shortage of female teachers.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: few or distant girls' schools; safety and travel; family preference for boys; domestic work; early marriage; lack of female teachers; poverty.

stem:
Health data for two districts (hypothetical):
Rural district: population 1,250,000, doctors 410
City district: population 3,600,000, doctors 3,900

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of people per doctor in each district, to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Rural district: 3,049; city district: 923

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which health care in rural areas of Pakistan has been improved. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Lady Health Workers visit homes to give advice on family planning, mother and child care and vaccination, reaching women who cannot travel; Basic Health Units and Rural Health Centres provide first-level treatment closer to villages; the Expanded Programme on Immunisation and polio campaigns vaccinate children door to door; health insurance schemes (e.g. Sehat Card) help poor families pay for hospital treatment.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: Lady Health Workers; BHUs / RHCs; vaccination campaigns; health insurance; mobile clinics; clean water schemes.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which improving literacy helps a country such as Pakistan to develop. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Literate workers can learn new skills and use technology, so productivity in farming, industry and IT rises and incomes increase; educated mothers understand nutrition, hygiene and vaccination, so child deaths fall; literate women usually have fewer children, slowing population growth; literate citizens can understand their rights and take part in decisions.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: skills and productivity; health awareness; lower birth rates; better jobs and incomes; participation / awareness of rights.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Spending on health care is more important than spending on education for Pakistan's development.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Health: a healthy workforce misses fewer days and is more productive; reducing child and maternal deaths and diseases such as hepatitis, TB and polio saves lives now; disease outbreaks after floods show the need for health services. Education: literacy is still only about 60%, and education raises skills, incomes and awareness; educated mothers improve family health, so education also improves health; schooling for girls reduces birth rates. Judgement: e.g. education has wider long-term effects, including on health, but basic health care is needed for children to attend and learn.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the range of hills in northern Punjab where the Khewra mine is located.
parts.answer: The Salt Range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the mineral mined at Khewra.
parts.answer: Rock salt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three uses of rock salt.
parts.answer: Any three: table salt and food preservation; raw material for the chemical industry (soda ash, caustic soda); tanning leather; decorative items such as salt lamps and tiles; export; livestock licks.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two areas of Pakistan where limestone is found.
parts.answer: Any two: Salt Range; Kohat; Margalla Hills / around Islamabad; Rohri (Sindh); Daudkhel / Mianwali; Dera Ghazi Khan; Thatta.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main industrial use of limestone in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Making cement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why cement factories are usually built close to limestone deposits. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Limestone is heavy and bulky and large amounts are needed for each tonne of cement, so carrying it long distances would be very costly; the raw material loses weight in processing, so it is cheaper to make cement at the quarry and transport the finished product; other raw materials such as clay and gypsum are often found nearby in the same areas.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: bulky / heavy raw material; weight lost in processing; transport cost; other raw materials (clay, gypsum, coal) nearby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two areas where gypsum is found in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two: Salt Range (e.g. Khewra, Dandot); Kohat; Dera Ghazi Khan; parts of Balochistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two uses of gypsum in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It is added to cement in small amounts to control how fast it sets, so the cement industry is the main user; it is used to make plaster of Paris for building, ceilings and moulds; it is spread on saline or sodic (alkaline) soils to improve them, so it helps farmers reclaim land affected by salinity; it is used in making some fertilisers.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: cement (setting time); plaster of Paris; soil improvement (salinity); fertiliser; chalk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the area of Balochistan best known for chromite mining.
parts.answer: Muslim Bagh (Killa Saifullah district).
parts.working: B1; accept Zhob area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two uses of chromite.
parts.answer: Making stainless steel and other alloys; refractory bricks for furnaces; chemicals for leather tanning and dyes.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why most of Pakistan's chromite is exported as ore rather than processed in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Pakistan has few stainless steel or ferro-chrome plants, so there is little demand at home; processing needs a lot of cheap electricity, which is expensive and in short supply; mining is done by small operators who lack the capital and technology to build processing plants; buyers such as China pay for raw ore, so it is a quick source of income.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: lack of processing industry; energy cost; lack of capital / technology; small-scale mining; foreign demand for ore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the district of Balochistan where the Saindak and Reko Diq deposits are found.
parts.answer: Chagai.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two minerals obtained from these deposits.
parts.answer: Copper and gold (also silver).
parts.working: B1 for two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two difficulties of developing large mines at Reko Diq. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The area is a remote desert near the borders with Iran and Afghanistan, so roads, railways and power lines must be built at great cost; water is very scarce but is needed for processing ore; the project needs billions of dollars of investment and technology from foreign companies, and legal disputes over contracts delayed it for years; security concerns in the region increase costs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: remoteness and lack of infrastructure; water shortage; extreme climate; capital and foreign investment; legal disputes; security.

stem:
Production of four minerals in Pakistan in two years (hypothetical figures, million tonnes):
Rock salt: Year 1 2.1, Year 2 3.4
Limestone: Year 1 40.0, Year 2 52.0
Gypsum: Year 1 1.6, Year 2 2.2
Coal: Year 1 3.9, Year 2 9.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in production of each mineral between Year 1 and Year 2. Give your answers to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Rock salt: 61.9%; Limestone: 30.0%; Gypsum: 37.5%; Coal: 133.3%
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which mineral had the largest percentage increase and suggest a reason for it.
parts.answer: Coal: new open-cast mining of lignite at Thar to supply coal-fired power stations.
parts.working: B1 coal; B1 reason (Thar coal for power).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why limestone production is so much larger than that of the other minerals.
parts.answer: Huge demand from the cement industry for construction (housing, dams, roads).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one coalfield in Sindh and one in Balochistan.
parts.answer: Sindh: Thar, Lakhra or Sonda. Balochistan: Degari, Sor Range, Mach or Khost–Sharig.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two uses of coal in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Generating electricity in thermal power stations; fuel in brick kilns; fuel in cement factories; steel making (mostly imported coking coal).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the coal found in the Thar coalfield.
parts.answer: It is lignite, a low-grade brown coal with high moisture and ash content and low heat value; the reserves are very large (about 175 billion tonnes, among the largest in the world).
parts.working: B1 lignite / low grade; B1 very large reserves (approximate figure accepted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Thar coal is important for Pakistan's future energy supply. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Pakistan imports large amounts of oil, gas and coal for power, which costs scarce foreign exchange; using local Thar coal reduces this import bill; the reserves are big enough to supply power stations for many decades, improving energy security; power from local coal can be cheaper than from imported fuel, helping reduce load-shedding; developing it creates jobs and infrastructure in a poor desert region.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: reduces imports / saves foreign exchange; large reserves / energy security; cheaper electricity; reduce load-shedding; jobs and development in Thar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why low-grade lignite from Thar is burnt in power stations built at the coalfield rather than transported to cities. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Lignite has a high moisture content and low energy per tonne, so moving it long distances would mean paying to transport much water and ash; it can catch fire easily when dried, making transport risky; it is cheaper to send the electricity through transmission lines to the national grid than to move the bulky coal.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: low energy per tonne / high moisture; transport cost; self-ignition risk; electricity easier to transmit; pithead plants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Pakistan should make much greater use of its coal resources.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: large local reserves such as Thar can reduce imports of oil and LNG, saving foreign exchange; coal power provides reliable power day and night, unlike solar and wind; mining and power stations create jobs in poor areas. Against: burning coal releases carbon dioxide, which adds to climate change that already harms Pakistan through floods and heatwaves; air pollution and ash cause health problems; open-cast mining displaces villages and uses scarce water; renewables such as solar and wind are becoming cheaper and are plentiful in Sindh and Balochistan. Judgement: e.g. Thar coal is useful in the short term for energy security, but renewables should be expanded faster.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one area of Pakistan where marble is quarried.
parts.answer: Any one: Mardan / Buner; Mohmand; Khyber; Swat; Chagai (onyx).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two uses of marble.
parts.answer: Floors, walls and building facing; decorative items and handicrafts; monuments and tombstones; crushed for chips, lime and paint.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why Pakistan earns relatively little from its marble exports.
parts.answer: Much marble is wasted or damaged by blasting, so few large blocks are produced; little is cut and polished to export standard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two places in Pakistan where iron ore is found.
parts.answer: Any two: Kalabagh; Chiniot; Dilband (Mastung); Nokkundi (Chagai); Hazara.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan Steel Mills in Karachi has relied on imported iron ore. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Much of Pakistan's iron ore, such as at Kalabagh, is low-grade with a low iron content and impurities, so it needs costly processing; richer deposits are in remote areas such as Chagai or were found only recently (Chiniot), with no rail link to Karachi; the mill was built at Port Qasim so that ore and coking coal could be imported cheaply by sea.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: low-grade ore; remoteness / transport costs; deposits not developed; coastal location designed for imports; high-quality ore available abroad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gemstones found in (i) the Swat valley and (ii) the Hunza valley.
parts.answer: (i) emeralds; (ii) rubies.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which Pakistan could earn more from its gemstones. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Training local workers in cutting and polishing would allow finished stones to be sold for much higher prices than rough stones; using modern mining methods instead of blasting would reduce damage to stones; setting up gem testing and certification centres would give buyers confidence and attract foreign traders; promoting jewellery making and exhibitions would add value and create jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: cutting and polishing / value addition; modern extraction; certification; marketing / exhibitions; jewellery industry; reduce smuggling.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Classify each of these minerals as metallic or non-metallic:
(i) chromite  (ii) gypsum  (iii) copper  (iv) rock salt
parts.answer: (i) metallic; (ii) non-metallic; (iii) metallic; (iv) non-metallic
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is meant by a mineral resource?
parts.answer: A naturally occurring substance in the Earth's crust that can be extracted and used by people.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why minerals are described as non-renewable resources.
parts.answer: They take millions of years to form, so once they have been extracted and used up they cannot be replaced within a human lifetime.
parts.working: B1 formed over very long periods; B1 cannot be replaced once used.

stem:
Share of the value of Pakistan's exports of some minerals in one year (hypothetical, %):
Marble and onyx: 31
Rock salt: 25
Chromite: 18
Gemstones: 11
Other: 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle needed for each sector if this information is drawn as a pie chart.
parts.answer: Marble and onyx 111.6°, Rock salt 90°, Chromite 64.8°, Gemstones 39.6°, Other 54°
parts.working: M1 % × 3.6; A1 all correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the value of Pakistan's mineral exports is small compared with its mineral reserves. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Many deposits are in remote, mountainous or desert areas of Balochistan and Gilgit-Baltistan with poor roads and railways, so transport is costly; most mining uses outdated methods and small operators lack capital, so output is low and quality poor; minerals are often exported raw rather than processed, so they earn low prices; surveys of reserves are incomplete and security problems discourage investors.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: remoteness / infrastructure; outdated methods / lack of capital; raw exports; lack of surveys and skilled workers; security / policy uncertainty.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Barytes is mined near Khuzdar in Balochistan. State its main use in Pakistan.
parts.answer: In drilling mud for oil and gas wells (also in paint and chemicals).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the mineral obtained from the Koh-e-Sultan area of Chagai and give one use.
parts.answer: Sulphur; used for making sulphuric acid, fertilisers or matches.
parts.working: B1 sulphur; B1 use.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why mineral production in Balochistan is important for the people of the province.
parts.answer: It provides jobs and incomes in areas with few other activities; royalties and investment can pay for roads, schools and clinics; it supports local businesses such as transport.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Balochistan produces only a small share of Pakistan's mineral output even though it has many mineral deposits. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The province is large, mountainous and thinly populated, with long distances to ports and markets and few roads and railways, so moving ore is costly; water and electricity for mining and processing are scarce; there is a shortage of skilled workers and capital, and much mining is small-scale and traditional; security problems and disputes over royalties have discouraged investors.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: remoteness / infrastructure; lack of water and power; lack of skills and capital; traditional methods; security / disputes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Developing mineral resources is the best way to improve living standards in Balochistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: projects such as Saindak, Reko Diq and coal mines can bring jobs, royalties and investment; roads, power lines and water schemes built for mines also serve local people; Gwadar port can export minerals. Against: modern mines employ relatively few local workers and profits may go to companies and the federal government; mining can damage water supplies and grazing land; other sectors such as fishing along the Makran coast, fruit farming (apples, dates), livestock, solar energy and tourism can benefit more people; education and health spending are also needed. Judgement: e.g. minerals can help if local people share the benefits and are trained, but a wider development plan is needed.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two places in the Salt Range or Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, other than Khewra, where rock salt is mined.
parts.answer: Any two: Warcha; Kalabagh; Bahadur Khel (Karak); Jatta.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the Khewra salt mine is used for purposes other than producing salt.
parts.answer: It is a major tourist attraction with tours, a salt mosque and lit-up salt features; a clinic uses the salt-rich air for treating asthma and breathing problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two uses (tourism; health/asthma clinic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: China clay (kaolin) is found near Shah Dheri in Swat. State two uses of china clay.
parts.answer: Pottery, ceramics and sanitary ware; paper making; paint; rubber; tiles.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the mineral industry supports other industries in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Limestone and gypsum are raw materials for the cement industry, which in turn supplies construction; rock salt supplies the chemical industry, which makes soda ash for glass, soap and textiles; coal fuels brick kilns, cement plants and power stations; china clay and silica sand supply ceramics and glass factories; barytes supplies oil and gas drilling.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: cement; chemicals; energy; ceramics / glass; oil and gas drilling; steel (iron ore).

stem:
Some minerals produced in four provinces:
Balochistan: chromite, copper, barytes, sulphur, coal, marble (onyx)
Punjab: rock salt, gypsum, coal, limestone
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: marble, rock salt, china clay, emerald
Sindh: coal, limestone

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the table only, state the number of minerals listed for each province.
parts.answer: Balochistan 6, Punjab 4, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 4, Sindh 2
parts.working: B1 all correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the table only, name the minerals that are listed for more than one province.
parts.answer: Coal (Balochistan, Punjab, Sindh); rock salt (Punjab, KP); limestone (Punjab, Sindh); marble (Balochistan, KP).
parts.working: B2 all four; B1 two or three.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why mineral deposits are often found in mountainous and plateau areas of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Folding and faulting during mountain building brought old rocks with minerals close to the surface; erosion of mountains exposes rock layers and mineral veins; igneous activity in these areas formed metallic ores such as copper and chromite.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons.

check: len(['chromite','copper','barytes','sulphur','coal','marble']) == 6 and len(['rock salt','gypsum','coal','limestone']) == 4 and len(['marble','rock salt','china clay','emerald']) == 4 and len(['coal','limestone']) == 2
author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by open-cast (open-pit) mining?
parts.answer: Removing the soil and rock above a mineral deposit near the surface and digging the mineral out from a large open pit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why coal in Balochistan is mined by underground (shaft or drift) methods, while Thar coal is mined open-cast. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In Balochistan the coal seams are thin and lie at steep angles deep within folded mountain rocks, so it would be too costly to remove all the rock above them; tunnels follow the seams instead. At Thar the lignite lies in thick, almost flat seams under sand at a depth of about 150–200 m, so it is cheaper to remove the overburden and dig out large amounts in a pit.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: Balochistan – thin, steep, folded seams; deep; tunnels follow the seams. Thar – thick flat seams; under loose sand; overburden removal economic; large output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Khewra uses the room-and-pillar method, in which about half of the salt is left as pillars to hold up the roof. If a section of the mine contains 2 million tonnes of salt, estimate how much can be extracted.
parts.answer: 2 × 0.5 = 1 million tonnes
parts.working: B1 1 million tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the room-and-pillar method of mining.
parts.answer: Tunnels (rooms) are cut into the mineral layer in a regular grid; blocks of the mineral are left standing between them as pillars to support the roof.
parts.working: B1 rooms/tunnels cut; B1 pillars left to support roof.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of the room-and-pillar method. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Advantage: the pillars support the roof, so it is relatively safe and the land above does not collapse, protecting buildings and farmland. Disadvantage: a large share of the mineral is left in the pillars and never used, so the resource is wasted and the mine's output is lower.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 for its development, one advantage and one disadvantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by using explosives (blasting) to quarry marble in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Blasting cracks and shatters the stone, so a large share of the marble is wasted and only small blocks can be sold, lowering the value of exports; waste rock is dumped on slopes and in streams, blocking water channels and destroying farmland; dust and noise harm the health of workers and nearby villagers; flying rock can injure workers.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: wastage / cracked blocks; lower value; waste dumping and river pollution; dust and noise; accidents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to marble quarrying methods.
parts.answer: Using diamond wire saws or chain saws to cut whole blocks; training workers in modern techniques and safety; giving loans for machinery; setting up marble cities / processing zones with modern cutting and polishing plants.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two dangers faced by workers in underground coal mines in Balochistan.
parts.answer: Explosions of methane gas; roof collapses; flooding; breathing coal dust, causing lung disease; poor ventilation / lack of oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the safety of coal miners could be improved. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Gas detectors and better ventilation shafts would warn miners of methane build-up and remove the gas before it can explode; strong roof supports (steel props) and regular inspections would reduce collapses; providing helmets, masks and breathing equipment would protect miners from dust and gas; training and enforcing mining laws would make owners follow safety rules.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: gas detection and ventilation; roof supports and inspections; protective equipment; training; enforcement of laws; rescue teams.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two environmental problems caused by open-cast coal mining in Thar. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Huge amounts of overburden (sand and rock) must be removed and dumped, destroying grazing land and changing the landscape; groundwater must be pumped out of the pit, and this saline water has been stored in reservoirs, affecting nearby land and wells; dust from blasting and moving coal affects people's health and crops; coal-fired power plants nearby release smoke, ash and carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: overburden dumping / loss of land; dewatering and saline effluent; lowering of water table; dust; emissions from power plants; loss of habitat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Open-cast mining in Thar has brought more benefits than problems to local people.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Benefits: local people have been given jobs, including as truck drivers (including women drivers), and some have received training; new roads, an airport, schools, a hospital and clean water plants have been built; compensation has been paid for land and new housing provided for some displaced families. Problems: some villages and grazing land have been lost and people have been relocated; saline water from mine dewatering has affected land; dust and pollution threaten health; many skilled jobs went to outsiders; traditional herding livelihoods are harder. Judgement: e.g. benefits are growing, but only if displaced families and herders share fairly in them.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

stem:
Deaths recorded in coal mine accidents in one province over five years (hypothetical figures):
Year 1: 48, Year 2: 61, Year 3: 39, Year 4: 72, Year 5: 55

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of deaths per year over the five years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate by what percentage the worst year was above the mean. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.working: M1 difference ÷ mean × 100; A1 30.9%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why deaths in small private coal mines remain high.
parts.answer: Mine owners use outdated methods and do not invest in safety equipment; mining laws are weakly enforced and inspections are rare; workers are poorly trained and paid by output, so they take risks; mines are remote, so rescue is slow.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two effects of limestone quarrying on the hills near large cities.
parts.answer: Hillsides are cut away, scarring the landscape; trees and vegetation are removed, causing soil erosion; dust covers crops and homes; blasting noise and vibration disturb people and wildlife.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the damage caused by quarrying can be reduced. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Banning quarrying in protected areas such as national parks keeps important landscapes and forests safe; requiring companies to restore quarries by filling, terracing and replanting trees after use reduces erosion and scars; spraying water on roads and using covered trucks reduces dust; setting time limits on blasting reduces disturbance.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: bans / protected areas; reclamation and replanting; dust control; regulations on blasting; locating quarries away from settlements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At one block of the Thar coalfield the coal seam is about 12 m thick and lies under about 150 m of overburden. Calculate the ratio of overburden thickness to coal thickness in the form n : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the ratio you calculated affects the cost of mining. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The higher the ratio, the more sand and rock must be removed for each tonne of coal, so fuel, machinery and labour costs per tonne rise; a high ratio makes low-value lignite less profitable.
parts.working: B1 more material to remove per tonne; B1 higher cost / lower profit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the land can be restored after open-cast mining ends. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The pit can be refilled with stored overburden and topsoil, then levelled so it can be used for grazing or farming; trees and grasses can be planted to stabilise the soil and prevent wind erosion; old pits can be turned into water reservoirs or fish ponds; monitoring and drainage reduce salinity in restored land.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: backfilling and replacing topsoil; replanting; reservoirs / ponds; recreation use; salinity control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why much mining in Pakistan is still carried out by small operators using traditional methods. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Many deposits such as chromite and marble occur in small, scattered pockets that large companies do not find profitable; small operators lack capital to buy machinery, so they rely on picks, shovels and blasting; mining leases are often short or insecure, so owners do not invest in long-term equipment; cheap labour is available in poor areas.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: small scattered deposits; lack of capital / credit; insecure leases; cheap labour; lack of technical knowledge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two social problems linked to small-scale mining.
parts.answer: Child labour; low wages and debt bondage; poor health from dust; lack of compensation after accidents.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which mining can affect water supplies in nearby areas. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Pumping water out of mines lowers the water table, so nearby wells may dry up; waste water containing salts, chemicals or metals can flow into streams and soak into groundwater, making it unsafe for drinking and irrigation; processing ore (e.g. copper at Saindak) uses large amounts of scarce water in desert areas; sediment from mine waste clogs channels.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: dewatering lowers water table; contamination by saline/chemical effluent; heavy water use in processing; sediment / siltation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Mining companies should be made to spend part of their profits on the local communities where they work.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: local people bear the costs of dust, water loss, land loss and accidents, so they deserve schools, clinics, clean water and training; this reduces conflict and protests, making mining more secure; projects in Thar and Chagai show how community spending can improve living standards. Against: high charges may discourage investors and reduce national revenue from royalties and taxes; the government, not companies, should be responsible for services; money may be wasted or captured by local elites without proper monitoring. Judgement: e.g. a fixed share for community development, managed transparently with local people, is fair and helps mining succeed.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): simple points. L2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view, or simple points for both. L3 (5–6): developed points for both views, a named Pakistani example and a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the transport of minerals can damage the environment.
parts.answer: Heavy trucks damage roads and raise dust; spills of coal or ore pollute land and water; exhaust fumes cause air pollution; new roads through forests or grazing land destroy habitats.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits that a new mine can bring to a remote area of Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It creates jobs for local people, raising incomes and reducing the need to migrate; roads, electricity and water supplies built for the mine can also be used by villages; new shops, transport services and workshops grow to serve the mine and its workers; royalties may be spent on schools and health centres.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for its development, for two points. Points: jobs; infrastructure; local business; royalties / services; skills training.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the airport that handles the largest number of passengers in Pakistan and the city in which it is located.
parts.answer: Jinnah International Airport, Karachi.
parts.working: 1 mark airport name; 1 mark Karachi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of air transport over road transport for travel between Karachi and Islamabad.
parts.answer: Much faster over the long distance (under 2 hours compared with a day or more by road); avoids traffic congestion and road accidents / more comfortable for business travellers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: faster over long distance; saves time for business people; safer/fewer accidents; comfortable; not affected by road congestion or blockages.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why air transport is not used to carry most of Pakistan's freight.
parts.answer: It is very expensive per tonne carried; aircraft can carry only small loads compared with trucks, trains or ships.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: high cost/fuel cost; small carrying capacity; bulky goods (coal, cement, grain) unsuitable; needs airports at both ends, so goods still need road transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why air transport is important for reaching places such as Gilgit and Skardu.
parts.answer: These towns are in high mountains where roads such as the Karakoram Highway are long, winding and often blocked by landslides or snow, so a road journey from Islamabad can take a day or more. A flight takes about an hour, so air links bring in tourists, officials and urgent supplies, and help in emergencies such as medical evacuation.
parts.working: 1 mark per point + 1 mark per development, two points max 4: mountainous terrain/long winding roads → road journeys slow; landslides/snow block roads → air may be only link; tourism → quick access brings visitors and income; emergencies/medical evacuation/relief supplies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why flights to these northern airports are often cancelled.
parts.answer: Bad weather such as low cloud, rain or snow reduces visibility; narrow valleys surrounded by high mountains make landing dangerous unless the weather is clear.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: cloud/fog/poor visibility; snow/storms in winter; mountains/narrow valleys require visual approach; short runways limit aircraft size.

stem:
The table shows passenger numbers at five airports in Pakistan in one year (illustrative figures, million passengers):
Karachi 7.2
Lahore 5.4
Islamabad 4.8
Peshawar 1.5
Multan 0.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of passengers handled by the five airports.
parts.answer: 19.8 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total handled by Karachi. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many times more passengers did Lahore handle than Multan?
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why Karachi airport handles more passengers than the other airports.
parts.answer: Karachi is Pakistan's largest city and main commercial and industrial centre, so many business travellers fly in and out; it is also a major gateway for international flights, including to the Gulf where many Pakistanis work.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: largest population; main business/financial/industrial centre; port city with trade links; many international routes, e.g. to the Gulf; long-established airport with large terminal capacity.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of a site that is suitable for building a large international airport.
parts.answer: Large area of flat, open land; away from the city centre but with good road links to it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: flat land; large area/room to expand; cheap land; away from tall buildings and dense housing (noise, safety); good road/rail access to city; good weather/visibility; well-drained ground.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the new Islamabad International Airport was built some distance outside the city instead of expanding the old airport in Rawalpindi.
parts.answer: The old airport was surrounded by dense housing and the city, so there was no room to lengthen runways or build larger terminals. A site outside the city has more space for long runways for large wide-bodied aircraft and future expansion, and aircraft noise and safety risks affect fewer people.
parts.working: Two developed points, 2 marks each: lack of space at old site → could not expand runways/terminals; new site has large flat area → longer runways/bigger aircraft/room to grow; noise and safety → fewer people affected; congestion around old airport → new site linked by motorway/Srinagar Highway access.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the national airline and private airlines in providing air services in Pakistan.
parts.answer: The national carrier, PIA, operates domestic routes including less profitable ones to remote areas, plus international routes. Private airlines such as Airblue and AirSial mainly fly busy routes between large cities and to the Gulf, which increases competition and choice.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3: PIA national carrier; serves domestic and international routes; flies to remote northern areas; private airlines (named example) on busy trunk routes; competition lowers fares/improves service; private airlines fly to Gulf/Middle East.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems that have affected the national airline in recent years.
parts.answer: Heavy financial losses and debt, partly from an ageing fleet with high fuel and maintenance costs, meant the government repeatedly had to support it. Safety concerns led to some foreign countries banning its flights for a period, so it lost profitable international routes and passengers.
parts.working: 1 + 1 development for each of two problems: financial losses/debt; too many employees/high costs; old aircraft → high maintenance/fuel cost; safety concerns/foreign flight bans → lost routes; competition from Gulf airlines; poor punctuality → loss of customers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'cargo terminal' at an airport.
parts.answer: A part of the airport with warehouses and handling equipment where freight is loaded, unloaded, stored and cleared through customs.
parts.working: 1 mark for idea of facilities for handling/storing freight (not passengers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three types of Pakistani export that are suitable for sending by air, and explain why.
parts.answer: Fresh mangoes or kinnow, fresh fish/seafood, and high-value goods such as surgical instruments or cut flowers. They are perishable or of high value and low weight, so the higher cost of air freight is worth the speed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two suitable examples (perishable fruit, fresh fish, surgical instruments, garments for urgent orders, flowers); 1 mark for reason: perishable/high value-to-weight/urgent delivery.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: Pakistan should spend more on expanding its airports.
View B: Pakistan should spend more on railways and roads instead of airports.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: Balanced answer, e.g. A: airports support tourism, business and exports of perishable goods and connect remote areas; B: most people cannot afford flights, while roads and railways carry most passengers and freight cheaply, so spending there benefits more people and industry. Judgement supported by reasons.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1) simple point for one view; L2 (2–3) developed points for one view or simple for both; L3 (4) developed points for both views with a supported conclusion. Credit: airport expansion → tourism, foreign investment, exports of perishables, remote access; roads/rail → affordable to majority, bulk freight, links farms to markets, wider employment.

stem:
The table shows passengers (million) using Pakistan's airports in three years (illustrative figures).
Year 1: international 7.4, domestic 5.0
Year 2: international 7.9, domestic 5.6
Year 3: international 8.6, domestic 6.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in the number of international passengers between Year 1 and Year 3.
parts.answer: An increase of 1.2 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in domestic passengers from Year 1 to Year 3. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of all passengers in Year 3 who were international. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why many international flights from Pakistan go to cities in the Gulf.
parts.answer: Large numbers of Pakistani workers live and work in Gulf countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia; many people travel to Saudi Arabia for Hajj and Umrah.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: migrant workers in Gulf; pilgrimage (Hajj/Umrah); Gulf hubs (Dubai, Doha) for connecting flights to Europe/America; trade/business links; short flying distance.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the motorway that links Islamabad and Lahore.
parts.working: 1 mark M-2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the national highway that runs from Karachi to Torkham on the border with Afghanistan.
parts.answer: N-5 (the Grand Trunk Road along its northern section)
parts.working: 1 mark N-5 / GT Road.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between a motorway and an ordinary national highway.
parts.answer: A motorway has controlled access (entry and exit only at interchanges) and dual carriageways with several lanes each way, so traffic moves faster; a highway may pass through towns and has many junctions, slow vehicles and animal carts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two contrasts: limited/controlled access vs open access; dual carriageway/multi-lane; higher speed limits; bypasses towns; no slow traffic (carts, tractors) allowed; service areas; toll charged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three advantages of road transport for farmers in Punjab.
parts.answer: Trucks can collect crops directly from farms and deliver them door to door to markets or factories; roads reach villages that have no railway; road transport is quick and flexible for small loads and perishable crops such as vegetables.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: door-to-door; reaches villages/flexible routes; suitable for small loads; fast for short distances; perishable crops reach markets fresh; tractor trolleys can use roads.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of the increasing use of trucks to carry goods long distances.
parts.answer: Heavy, overloaded trucks damage road surfaces, so the government must spend large sums on repairs; they also burn diesel, causing air pollution and increasing oil imports.
parts.working: 1 mark disadvantage + 1 development: road damage → repair costs; air pollution/smog → health problems; fuel use → oil imports; congestion/accidents.

stem:
A bus company compares two routes between Islamabad and Lahore (illustrative figures).
Motorway route: 367 km at an average speed of 110 km/h.
GT Road route: 380 km at an average speed of 60 km/h.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the motorway journey. Give your answer in hours and minutes to the nearest minute.
parts.answer: 3 hours 20 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the GT Road journey, in hours and minutes.
parts.answer: 6 hours 20 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how much time the motorway saves, to the nearest minute.
parts.answer: 3 hours (2 h 59.8 min ≈ 3 h 0 min)
parts.working: 6.333 h − 3.336 h = 2.997 h ≈ 3 h (accept 3 h 0 min using the rounded times).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the faster journey brings benefits to businesses.
parts.answer: Goods and staff reach markets and factories sooner, so delivery is more reliable and costs such as wages and vehicle hire per trip fall; perishable goods arrive fresh.
parts.working: 1 mark point + 1 development: time saved → lower transport costs; reliable delivery → better for industry/exporters; perishables fresher; more trips per vehicle per day.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route and importance of the Karakoram Highway.
parts.answer: It runs north from Hasan Abdal through Abbottabad and Mansehra, along the Indus and Hunza valleys past Gilgit, to the Khunjerab Pass on the border with China. It is Pakistan's only road link with China, carries trade goods, supports tourism in Gilgit-Baltistan and is part of the CPEC route.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4: starts near Hasan Abdal/Islamabad region; follows Indus/Hunza valleys; through Gilgit/Hunza; reaches Khunjerab Pass/China border; one of highest paved roads; trade with China; CPEC link; tourism; access for remote communities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems of building and maintaining roads in the northern mountains.
parts.answer: Steep slopes and weak rock cause frequent landslides, which block roads and need expensive clearing. Heavy winter snow and glacial floods damage road surfaces and bridges, so roads are closed for months and repair costs are high.
parts.working: Two developed points, 2 marks each: steep relief/landslides; snow and ice/winter closure; floods and glacial lake outbursts damaging bridges; earthquakes; high cost/blasting rock; few workers/remote supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) road projects.
parts.answer: To build and upgrade roads and motorways that link Gwadar and other southern ports with northern Pakistan and western China, improving trade routes and economic development.
parts.working: 1 mark for linking Gwadar/ports with China/Khunjerab; 1 mark for trade/economic development aim.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which better roads in Balochistan could benefit people living there.
parts.answer: Better roads would cut travel time to markets, so farmers and fishermen could sell produce in larger towns at better prices. They would also improve access to schools and hospitals and attract investment such as mining and small industries, creating jobs.
parts.working: Two developed points: access to markets → better prices; access to services (health, education); investment/industry/mining → jobs; tourism; reduced isolation/security; cheaper goods brought in.

stem:
A road network in an imaginary province has the following lengths (km):
Motorways 2,000
National highways 12,000
Provincial roads 100,000
Rural (district) roads 186,000
Total 300,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total road length that is made up of motorways and national highways together. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of rural roads to motorways in its simplest form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why, in a country such as Pakistan, national highways and motorways carry most long-distance freight even though they are a small share of the road length.
parts.answer: They connect the main cities, ports and industrial areas along the busiest routes (e.g. Karachi–Lahore–Peshawar), so long-distance trucks use them; they are wider and better surfaced, allowing faster heavy vehicles, while rural roads are narrow and mostly carry local traffic.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: link major cities/ports/industry; long-distance routes; better quality/wider lanes for heavy trucks; faster/cheaper per tonne; rural roads local/poor quality/unpaved.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: Building motorways is the best way to develop Pakistan's transport system.
View B: Improving existing roads and rural roads is more useful than building new motorways.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: A: motorways give fast, safe links between cities and ports, attract industry and investment along their routes and reduce journey times for exporters. B: motorways are very expensive and charge tolls, many villagers cannot use them, while upgrading rural roads links farms to markets, reduces crop losses and improves access to schools and clinics for the majority. Supported judgement.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple statements; L2 (3–4) developed points for one view or simple for both; L3 (5–6) developed points for both views and a reasoned judgement. Credit: speed, safety, trade, industrial zones, CPEC (A); cost, tolls, limited access, rural majority, farm-to-market, maintenance backlog, potholes, overloading (B).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the government body that regulates telecommunications in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA)
parts.working: 1 mark PTA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three ways in which mobile phones are used by people in rural areas of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Checking market prices for crops before selling; sending and receiving money through mobile banking such as Easypaisa or JazzCash; contacting relatives working in cities or abroad.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: market prices; weather forecasts; mobile banking/money transfer; contact with family/migrants; emergency calls; agricultural advice; online learning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the growth of the internet has helped young people in Pakistan to earn a living.
parts.answer: Freelancing: young people sell skills such as programming, graphic design and writing to clients abroad through online platforms, earning foreign currency without leaving home. Online businesses: they sell goods through social media and e-commerce sites, reaching customers across the country with little start-up cost.
parts.working: Two developed points: freelancing/IT services → foreign earnings; e-commerce/online selling → low start-up cost, wide market; online learning of skills → better jobs; ride-hailing/delivery apps → flexible work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why internet access is lower in rural areas than in cities.
parts.answer: Fewer mobile towers and fibre-optic cables reach remote villages because it is less profitable for companies; people have lower incomes and literacy, so fewer can afford or use smartphones.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: weak coverage/fewer towers; cost of laying cables in mountains/deserts; low incomes; low literacy/digital skills; unreliable electricity supply.

stem:
The table shows broadband (mainly mobile internet) subscribers in a country (illustrative figures).
Year 1: 24 million
Year 2: 70 million
Year 3: 124 million
Population in Year 3: 240 million

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in broadband subscribers from Year 1 to Year 3. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of broadband subscribers per 100 people in Year 3. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons for the rapid growth in broadband subscribers.
parts.answer: Introduction of 3G and 4G mobile networks allowed internet on mobile phones; cheaper smartphones and data packages made access affordable.
