parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: 3G/4G auction and rollout; cheap smartphones; low-cost data bundles; more towers/fibre; demand for social media, banking, online education (e.g. during pandemic closures).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'submarine fibre-optic cable'.
parts.answer: A cable laid on the sea bed that carries internet and telephone data as light signals between countries.
parts.working: 1 mark: cable on sea floor carrying data/internet between countries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Karachi is the main landing point for Pakistan's international submarine cables.
parts.answer: Karachi is Pakistan's main coastal city, so cables from the Arabian Sea can come ashore there; it is also the largest city and business centre with the greatest demand for data, and already has telecom exchanges and links to the national fibre network.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: coastal location; largest demand/commercial centre; existing infrastructure/exchanges; links inland to national fibre backbone; port/industrial base.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a land fibre-optic cable to China through the Khunjerab Pass is important for Pakistan.
parts.answer: It provides an alternative route for internet traffic, so connectivity is not lost if undersea cables near Karachi are damaged; it also supports CPEC trade and communication with China.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: backup/alternative route; reduced dependence on sea cables; supports CPEC; connects northern areas; faster links with China.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which improvements in telecommunications are helping Pakistan's economic development. Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Benefits: mobile banking brings unbanked people into the financial system; IT exports and freelancing earn foreign exchange; e-commerce and online services create jobs; farmers get price and weather information; e-government cuts delays. Limits: gender and rural–urban digital divide; low literacy; power cuts and slow speeds; internet shutdowns and cyber-security concerns; high taxes on phones and data. Judgement: important and growing, but benefits are uneven.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) developed points on one side or simple on both; L3 (5–6) developed points on both sides with a judgement on 'extent'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two cities at the ends of Pakistan's main railway line, ML-1.
parts.answer: Karachi and Peshawar
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of rail transport for carrying freight over long distances.
parts.answer: It can carry heavy, bulky goods such as coal, cement and wheat in large quantities; it is cheaper per tonne-km over long distances and uses less fuel than many trucks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: bulk/heavy loads; cheaper over long distance; less fuel/pollution per tonne; reduces road congestion and damage; safer for hazardous goods such as oil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two reasons why many passengers now prefer road transport to rail.
parts.answer: Buses and cars offer door-to-door travel and frequent departures; trains are often slow and late, with old coaches.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: flexibility/door-to-door; frequent services; faster on motorways; trains delayed/slow; poor facilities on trains; stations far from homes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan Railways has made financial losses.
parts.answer: Many locomotives and coaches are old and break down, so services are delayed and passengers and freight move to road transport, reducing income. The railway also has high costs from a large workforce and pensions, while fares are kept low.
parts.working: Two developed points: old/poorly maintained rolling stock → delays; loss of freight to trucks → falling revenue; mainly single track → slow, limited capacity; high staff/pension costs; fuel costs; encroachment and theft; mismanagement/corruption; accidents reduce confidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the planned upgrade of ML-1 is expected to improve rail transport.
parts.answer: Track will be doubled and rebuilt so trains can run faster (up to about 160 km/h for passenger trains) and more often; signalling will be modernised, improving safety; capacity for freight will increase, reducing truck traffic.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3: dual track; higher speeds/shorter journeys; modern signalling/safety; more freight capacity; level crossings/bridges improved; part of CPEC.

stem:
A cement company in the Potwar region compares transport costs (illustrative figures).
Rail: Rs 4 per tonne per km
Road: Rs 6 per tonne per km

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of moving 500 tonnes of cement 1,200 km by rail.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of moving the same load the same distance by road.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the saving by rail as a percentage of the road cost. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the cement company might still choose road transport.
parts.answer: Trucks can deliver directly to building sites without loading and unloading at stations; road transport is faster and more reliable, as freight trains may be delayed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: door-to-door; avoids double handling/transfer costs; quicker/more reliable; railway may not reach destination; flexible timing; small orders.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: The government should invest heavily in railways.
View B: Money is better spent on roads and motorways than on railways.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: A: railways move bulk freight cheaply and with less fuel and pollution per tonne, reduce road congestion and damage, and the ML-1 upgrade could link ports with industry and China. B: roads give door-to-door flexibility, reach villages the railway does not, and the railway has a record of losses and slow, unreliable services. Reasoned judgement.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple statements; L2 (3–4) developed points for one view; L3 (5–6) developed points on both views with supported conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'dry port'.
parts.answer: An inland terminal, away from the coast, where imported and exported goods are cleared by customs and transferred between road/rail and containers.
parts.working: 1 mark inland location; 1 mark customs clearance/handling of goods for seaports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two cities in Pakistan that have a dry port.
parts.answer: Any two of: Lahore, Faisalabad, Sialkot, Peshawar, Quetta, Multan, Hyderabad, Rawalpindi.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of dry ports for exporters in Sialkot.
parts.answer: Goods such as sports goods and surgical instruments can be cleared by customs and sealed in containers in Sialkot, so they go straight onto ships at Karachi without delay, saving time and cost.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage + 1 development: customs clearance close to factory; reduces delay/congestion at seaport; lower cost; containers sealed so less damage/theft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name Pakistan's three main seaports.
parts.answer: Karachi Port, Port Qasim (Port Muhammad Bin Qasim), Gwadar Port
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Port Qasim was built when Karachi Port already existed.
parts.answer: Karachi Port was congested, causing ships to wait and trade to be delayed, so a second port was needed to share the cargo. Port Qasim had space nearby for bulk cargo and industries such as the steel mill and power plants, and now handles imports like coal, oil and LNG.
parts.working: Two developed points: congestion at Karachi; growing trade volumes; space for expansion/industry nearby (Pakistan Steel, power plants); handling bulk cargo (coal, LNG, oil, grain); reduced strategic dependence on one port.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the advantages of the location of Gwadar Port.
parts.answer: It is a deep-sea port on the Arabian Sea in Balochistan, close to the entrance of the Gulf and major shipping routes from the Gulf; it is the southern end of the CPEC route, giving western China and Central Asian countries a shorter route to the sea.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3: deep water for large ships; near Strait of Hormuz/Gulf oil routes; CPEC link to China; access for landlocked Afghanistan/Central Asia; reduces pressure on Karachi; space for free zone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Gwadar Port has so far handled much less cargo than Karachi.
parts.answer: Gwadar is far from Pakistan's main industrial and population centres, and road and rail links to the rest of the country are still limited, so it is cheaper for most traders to use Karachi. There is also a shortage of fresh water and electricity in Gwadar, and security concerns discourage investment and shipping lines.
parts.working: Two developed points: distance from markets/industry; incomplete road/rail links; water and power shortages; security problems; few shipping lines call there; Karachi's established facilities and services.

stem:
The table shows cargo handled at three seaports in one year (illustrative figures, million tonnes):
Karachi Port 52
Port Qasim 46
Gwadar Port 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total cargo handled by the three ports.
parts.answer: 100 million tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more cargo Karachi handled than Gwadar.
parts.answer: 26 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: If imports were 75% of the cargo at Port Qasim, calculate the tonnage of exports at Port Qasim.
parts.answer: 11.5 million tonnes
parts.working: M1 25% of 46 = 0.25 × 46; A1 11.5 million tonnes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why imports are a much larger share than exports at Pakistan's ports.
parts.answer: Imports include very heavy bulk cargoes such as crude oil, petroleum products, LNG and coal, while many exports such as textiles are of high value but low weight.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: bulky fuel imports; trade deficit/imports greater than exports in value; exports are light manufactured goods; imports of machinery, steel, edible oil.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which a good transport network helps industry to develop.
parts.answer: Raw materials can be brought to factories cheaply and on time; finished goods reach markets and ports quickly; workers can travel to factories more easily.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: raw materials supply; access to markets/ports for export; lower transport costs; workers' commuting; attracts investment; industrial estates along motorways.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a new road to a remote village could improve farmers' incomes.
parts.answer: Farmers can take crops to larger markets quickly, so less produce rots and they get higher prices instead of selling cheaply to middlemen.
parts.working: 1 mark point + 1 development: market access → better prices/fewer middlemen; less spoilage of perishables; cheaper fertiliser/seed delivered; can grow cash crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which poor transport limits economic development in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Delays at congested ports and on poor roads increase the cost and time of exporting, making Pakistani goods less competitive abroad. Remote areas such as parts of Balochistan stay isolated, so minerals, fish and farm products cannot easily reach markets and few industries locate there.
parts.working: Two developed points: high transport costs → uncompetitive exports; delays/unreliable deliveries; isolation of regions → regional inequality; perishables wasted; investors discouraged; road accidents and congestion costs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which transport infrastructure projects themselves create employment.
parts.answer: Construction jobs building roads, bridges and railways; later jobs in maintenance, toll plazas, service areas, transport companies and logistics.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: construction; materials industries (cement, steel); maintenance; toll/service stations; trucking/logistics; businesses along new routes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which improving transport links is the most important factor in developing the less developed regions of Pakistan, such as Balochistan. Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Transport is important: it opens access to markets, ports (Gwadar) and services, attracts mining and industry and reduces isolation. Other factors may matter as much or more: reliable water and electricity, education and skills, security and law and order, investment and government policy, local ownership of resources. Judgement weighs transport against these.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) developed points on transport or other factors; L3 (5–6) developed points on both, with an evaluation of 'extent'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'renewable energy resource'.
parts.answer: A source of energy that is naturally replaced and will not run out when used, such as sunlight, wind or flowing water.
parts.working: 1 mark: replenished naturally / will not be used up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two renewable sources of energy, other than hydel, that are used to generate electricity in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Solar and wind (also accept bagasse/biomass).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: solar; wind; bagasse/biomass; biogas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the area in Sindh where most of Pakistan's wind farms are located.
parts.answer: The Gharo–Keti Bandar wind corridor (around Jhimpir/Thatta)
parts.working: 1 mark Gharo–Keti Bandar corridor / Jhimpir / Thatta district.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a solar panel system can provide electricity for a house in a village not connected to the national grid.
parts.answer: Photovoltaic panels on the roof turn sunlight directly into electricity (direct current); it charges batteries so power can be used at night; an inverter changes it to alternating current for lights, fans and appliances.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3: PV panels/cells; convert sunlight to electricity; battery storage for night; inverter; panels facing south/in sun; no grid connection needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why much of Pakistan is suitable for solar power.
parts.answer: Most of the country has many hours of strong sunshine for most of the year; large areas of flat, unused desert land (e.g. Cholistan, Balochistan) are available for solar parks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: high sunshine hours/clear skies; high intensity in low latitudes; deserts with little cloud; cheap flat land; dry climate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of using biogas in rural areas of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Biogas from animal dung provides free fuel for cooking and lighting, so families save money and need not cut trees for firewood, reducing deforestation. The slurry left after gas production is a good fertiliser, improving crop yields.
parts.working: Two developed points: cheap/free fuel → savings; reduces firewood use → less deforestation; cleaner than burning dung/wood → less indoor smoke, better health; slurry as fertiliser; uses waste/hygiene; saves women's time collecting fuel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why biogas plants are not more widely used.
parts.answer: Initial cost of building the digester is too high for poor farmers; a family needs several animals to supply enough dung every day.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: initial cost; need enough cattle/dung; lack of awareness/technical skill; maintenance; gas output falls in cold weather; water needed.

stem: A house in Multan has a rooftop solar system rated at 3 kW. On average it produces its full rated power for the equivalent of 4 hours a day (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electricity generated by the system in one 30-day month.
parts.answer: 360 kWh

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the money saved in one month if grid electricity costs Rs 50 per kWh.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The system cost Rs 540,000. Calculate how many months it would take for the savings to repay this cost.
parts.answer: 30 months

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why many households and businesses in Pakistani cities have installed rooftop solar panels in recent years.
parts.answer: Grid electricity prices have risen sharply, so solar quickly pays for itself; load-shedding makes grid supply unreliable; panel prices have fallen greatly, and net metering lets owners sell extra power to the grid.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: rising tariffs; load-shedding/unreliable supply; cheaper (imported) panels; net metering; abundant sunshine; reduces bills for businesses.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the coastal area of southern Sindh is suitable for wind farms.
parts.answer: Strong and steady winds blow from the sea, especially during the summer monsoon months, so turbines turn for many hours. The land is flat and thinly populated, so large turbines can be spaced out cheaply, and it is close to Karachi, a large market for electricity.
parts.working: Two developed points: strong/consistent sea winds (esp. April–September); flat open land; low population/cheap land; near Karachi/national grid; few obstacles to wind.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two disadvantages of wind power.
parts.answer: Output varies because wind speed changes, so it cannot provide a steady supply; turbines are expensive to build and the best sites may be far from the grid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: unreliable/variable; high initial cost; noise; visual impact; harm to birds; needs large area; transmission lines needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'bagasse' and explain how it is used to produce electricity.
parts.answer: Bagasse is the dry fibrous waste left after juice is crushed out of sugar cane. Sugar mills burn it in boilers to make steam, which turns turbines to generate electricity for the mill, with surplus sold to the grid.
parts.working: 1 mark definition (sugar-cane waste after crushing); 1 mark burnt to heat water/steam; 1 mark steam turns turbine/generator, surplus to grid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why bagasse power can only be produced for part of the year.
parts.answer: Sugar cane is crushed only during the harvest/crushing season (roughly November to March), so bagasse is not available all year unless it is stored.
parts.working: 1 mark seasonal harvest/crushing season; 1 mark storage difficult/bulky so supply stops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by tidal power.
parts.answer: Electricity generated using the rise and fall of the sea's tides to drive turbines.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the creeks of the Indus delta have been considered for tidal power.
parts.answer: The delta coast has many narrow creeks where tidal water flows in and out strongly; it is close to Karachi and the coastal industries that need electricity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: many creeks/inlets channel tides; reasonable tidal range; near Karachi demand; unused coastal land.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan has not yet developed tidal power.
parts.answer: The technology is very expensive and unproven at large scale, so investors prefer cheaper solar, wind and fossil fuels. Barriers and turbines could harm mangrove forests, fish breeding grounds and the livelihoods of fishing communities in the delta.
parts.working: Two developed points: high cost/lack of technology; low tidal range in places; environmental damage to mangroves/fishing; silt from the Indus; cyclones/storms; other options cheaper.

stem:
A planning document lists new generating capacity planned for one region (illustrative figures, MW):
Hydel 300
Wind 100
Solar 150
Bagasse 50
Nuclear 400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle needed to draw each source on a pie chart.
parts.answer: Hydel 108°, wind 36°, solar 54°, bagasse 18°, nuclear 144°
parts.working: Total 1,000 MW share: hydel 300 → 108°; wind 100 → 36°; solar 150 → 54°; bagasse 50 → 18°; nuclear 400 → 144°. Award 3 for all five correct, 2 for three or four, 1 for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of this new capacity that comes from solar and wind together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Which of the sources in the table is not renewable?
parts.answer: Nuclear
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by geothermal energy.
parts.answer: Heat from inside the Earth, carried by hot water or steam, used to generate electricity or heat buildings.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why parts of northern Pakistan and western Balochistan have potential for geothermal energy.
parts.answer: These areas lie in active tectonic zones where plates meet, with hot springs (e.g. in Gilgit-Baltistan) and old volcanic areas (e.g. Chagai), showing heat close to the surface.
parts.working: 1 mark tectonic/plate boundary/earthquake zone; 1 mark evidence: hot springs/volcanic features.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two difficulties of developing geothermal power in these areas.
parts.answer: The areas are remote and mountainous, so building plants and long transmission lines to the cities is very costly. Detailed surveys and deep drilling are needed and are expensive and risky, and Pakistan lacks experience and funding for this technology.
parts.working: Two developed points: remoteness/rugged terrain; distance from demand/transmission cost; high exploration/drilling cost; lack of technology/expertise; earthquake risk; security in Balochistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: Pakistan should rely mainly on solar and wind power for its future electricity.
View B: Pakistan should continue to rely mainly on hydel and thermal power.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: A: abundant sunshine and coastal wind, no fuel import bill, falling costs, quick to install, clean, rooftop solar reduces load on grid. B: solar and wind are intermittent and need storage or back-up; hydel and thermal give steady base-load; existing plants and Thar coal reserves; grid not designed for many variable sources. Supported judgement.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple statements; L2 (3–4) developed points for one view or simple for both; L3 (5–6) developed points for both views and a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which renewable energy can solve the energy problems of remote rural areas of Pakistan. Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Yes: off-grid solar home systems, micro-hydel on mountain streams in the north, biogas from dung and small wind turbines on the coast can give power without costly grid extension. Limits: high upfront cost for poor families, batteries expensive, small systems cannot run heavy machinery or tube wells easily, need for maintenance skills, seasonal limits (frozen streams, cloudy monsoon days). Judgement on extent.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) developed points one side; L3 (5–6) developed points on both sides with judgement. Credit named types matched to areas (micro-hydel in Gilgit-Baltistan/Chitral, solar in Balochistan/Thar).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the area in Sindh that has Pakistan's largest coal reserves.
parts.answer: Thar (Thar coalfield, Tharparkar)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the plateau in northern Punjab where oil has been produced for many years.
parts.answer: Potwar Plateau
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas field in Balochistan, discovered in 1952, that gave its name to Pakistan's piped gas.
parts.answer: Sui
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two uses of natural gas in Pakistan other than generating electricity.
parts.answer: Cooking and heating in homes; making fertiliser (urea) in industry.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: domestic cooking/heating; fertiliser manufacture; industrial fuel (cement, textiles); CNG for vehicles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the quality of most coal found in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Mostly low-grade lignite or sub-bituminous coal with a high content of moisture, ash and sulphur, so it gives less heat per tonne.
parts.working: 1 mark low grade/lignite; 1 mark high ash/sulphur/moisture or low heating value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems of using Thar coal to generate electricity.
parts.answer: The coal lies deep under thick sand, so huge amounts of overburden must be removed and water pumped out, making mining expensive. Burning lignite releases a lot of carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and ash, causing air pollution and health problems, and power plants need water in a desert area.
parts.working: Two developed points: deep/under sand → costly mining; low quality → much coal per unit electricity; air pollution/greenhouse gases; water shortage in desert; remote → transmission lines needed; displacement of local people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan imports most of the oil it uses.
parts.answer: Pakistan's own oil fields in the Potwar Plateau and Sindh are small and produce only a small fraction of national demand. Demand keeps rising with the growing number of vehicles, industries and thermal power stations, so the gap must be filled with imports from countries such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
parts.working: Two developed points: small reserves/low production; difficult exploration (cost, security); rising demand from transport, industry, power; refining capacity limited → also import petroleum products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two effects on Pakistan's economy of a large rise in world oil prices.
parts.answer: The import bill rises, increasing the trade deficit and putting pressure on foreign exchange reserves; transport and electricity costs rise, causing inflation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: higher import bill/trade deficit; currency falls/reserves drop; inflation; higher electricity tariffs; higher costs for industry and farmers.

stem:
Illustrative data for a country's natural gas:
Remaining reserves: 15 trillion cubic feet
Production per year: 1.2 trillion cubic feet
Demand per year: 1.8 trillion cubic feet

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years the reserves would last at the current rate of production, if no new gas is found.
parts.answer: 12.5 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the shortfall between demand and production each year.
parts.answer: 0.6 trillion cubic feet

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of demand met by domestic production. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how Pakistan has tried to meet the shortfall in gas supply.
parts.answer: Importing liquefied natural gas (LNG), mainly from Qatar, through terminals at Port Qasim; exploring for new gas fields; reducing gas supply to some users such as CNG stations and industry in winter; planning pipelines from Iran and Turkmenistan (TAPI).
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3: LNG imports; LNG terminals at Port Qasim; supplier Qatar; new exploration; rationing/load management; proposed pipelines (Iran–Pakistan, TAPI).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two oil refineries in Pakistan and state where each is located.
parts.answer: Attock Refinery, near Rawalpindi; Pak-Arab Refinery (PARCO), at Mahmood Kot near Multan (also accept National Refinery or Pakistan Refinery in Karachi).
parts.working: 1 mark each correct refinery with location.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some refineries are located at the coast and one is located inland in the Potwar region.
parts.answer: Coastal refineries in Karachi are where imported crude oil arrives by tanker, so it can be refined without costly transport inland. The Attock refinery was built close to the Potwar oil fields to process local crude oil and serve northern markets.
parts.working: 2 marks coastal: imported crude arrives by sea/port facilities/market in Karachi; 2 marks inland: near local oilfields/raw material/northern markets; PARCO linked by pipeline (credit).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the gas pipeline network is densest in Punjab and Sindh.
parts.answer: Most of Pakistan's population, cities and industries are in Punjab and Sindh, creating the greatest demand; the land is mostly flat plains, which makes laying pipelines easier and cheaper; major gas fields (Sui, Qadirpur, Mari) lie in or near Sindh.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: population density; industry/fertiliser plants; flat land; nearness to gas fields; power stations; cities like Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Balochistan, where Sui is located, has had relatively little benefit from its own gas.
parts.answer: The population is small and scattered over a huge area, so supplying gas to villages through pipelines is costly and uneconomic. Most gas was piped to industrial and urban centres elsewhere, and disputes over royalties and security problems have limited investment in local distribution.
parts.working: Two developed points: scattered population/large area; high cost of distribution; gas sent to Punjab/Sindh industry; limited royalties/development spending; security problems; mountainous terrain.

stem:
Coal-fired generating capacity in a country (illustrative figures, MW):
Plants using local coal 1,500
Plants using imported coal 2,500
Plants using a blend of local and imported coal 2,000
Total 6,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total from imported coal. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many more megawatts of plants using only local coal are needed for local-coal and imported-coal plants to have equal capacity, assuming imported-coal capacity stays the same.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: Pakistan should build more power stations that use Thar coal.
View B: Pakistan should stop building coal-fired power stations.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: A: huge local reserves, reduces import bill and dependence on foreign fuel, energy security, development and jobs in Tharparkar, steady base-load supply. B: lignite is polluting (CO₂, SO₂, ash), adds to climate change to which Pakistan is very vulnerable, needs scarce water, displaces communities, and solar/wind are now cheaper. Reasoned judgement.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple; L2 (3–4) developed for one view; L3 (5–6) developed for both views with conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why CNG became a popular fuel for cars and rickshaws in Pakistan.
parts.answer: It was cheaper than petrol; it produces less air pollution, and Pakistan had its own gas so it reduced oil imports.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: cheaper than petrol/diesel; local supply; cleaner; government encouraged it to cut oil imports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many CNG stations have since closed or face supply cuts, especially in winter.
parts.answer: Domestic gas production has fallen while demand has grown, so there is not enough gas. In winter households need more gas for heating, and the government gives priority to homes and power stations, so CNG stations are cut off first; imported LNG is more expensive, so CNG is no longer much cheaper than petrol.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: falling reserves/production; rising demand; winter heating demand; priority to domestic users/power; expensive LNG raises price; government policy restricting new connections.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'load-shedding'.
parts.answer: Planned cutting of electricity supply to different areas in turn because demand is greater than supply.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of load-shedding on industry.
parts.answer: Factories have to stop machines during power cuts, so production falls and export orders may be delivered late or lost. Many firms buy generators and diesel, which raises costs and makes their goods less competitive.
parts.working: Two developed points: lost production/output; late delivery/lost orders; extra cost of generators/fuel; workers idle/laid off; damage to machinery; investors discouraged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why the demand for electricity in Pakistan has increased.
parts.answer: Rapid population growth; urbanisation, with more homes using fans, air conditioners and refrigerators; growth of industry and the extension of electricity to more villages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: population growth; urbanisation; rising living standards/more appliances; industrial growth; rural electrification; tube wells for irrigation; hotter summers increasing air-conditioner use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which households can reduce their use of electricity.
parts.answer: Use energy-saving LED bulbs; switch off lights and appliances when not in use (also: efficient inverter air conditioners, solar water heaters).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible measures.

stem:
Illustrative electricity figures for a country:
Summer peak demand: 28,000 MW
Summer available supply: 24,500 MW
Winter peak demand: 16,000 MW

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the shortfall in electricity at the summer peak.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the shortfall as a percentage of peak demand. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the difference between summer and winter peak demand.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why demand is much higher in summer than in winter.
parts.answer: Very high temperatures mean heavy use of fans, air conditioners and coolers; tube wells pump water for irrigating summer (kharif) crops.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: heat/air conditioning/fans; refrigeration; irrigation tube wells for kharif crops; longer working hours in factories (credit), winter heating mostly uses gas.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In one year a country's power stations generated 140 TWh (terawatt-hours) of electricity, but only 115 TWh was billed to customers (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electricity lost in transmission and distribution.
parts.answer: 25 TWh

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the losses as a percentage of electricity generated. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons for high transmission and distribution losses in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Old, overloaded transmission lines and transformers waste electricity as heat, especially over long distances from hydel stations in the north to cities in the south. Electricity theft through illegal connections (kundas) and meter tampering means power is used but never billed.
parts.working: Two developed points: old/overloaded infrastructure; long distances; theft/illegal connections; meter tampering; poor maintenance; low-voltage lines in rural areas.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one place in Pakistan where a nuclear power station is located.
parts.answer: Karachi (K-2 and K-3 at the KANUPP site) or Chashma (Punjab, C-1 to C-4)
parts.working: 1 mark: Karachi/KANUPP site or Chashma.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages and one disadvantage of nuclear power for Pakistan.
parts.answer: Advantages: a small amount of fuel produces a large, steady amount of electricity (base load) regardless of weather; it produces almost no carbon dioxide or smoke. Disadvantage: very high construction cost and the risk of accidents and radioactive waste that must be stored safely for a very long time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages (reliable base load; little fuel needed/less import bill; low emissions) and 1 mark for a disadvantage (cost; radioactive waste; accident risk; need for foreign technology/fuel; needs cooling water).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'circular debt' in Pakistan's power sector and why it is a problem.
parts.answer: Circular debt is the build-up of unpaid bills along the chain: consumers and distribution companies do not pay in full (because of theft, losses and subsidies), so the power purchaser cannot pay generating companies, which in turn cannot pay fuel suppliers. Generators then cannot buy fuel, so plants stand idle and load-shedding increases, while the government must use public money to clear the debt.
parts.working: 2 marks meaning: unpaid dues passed along the chain (consumers/DISCOs → purchaser → generators/IPPs → fuel suppliers); 2 marks problem: fuel shortages/idle plants → load-shedding; drain on government budget; discourages investment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the government could reduce circular debt.
parts.answer: Reduce theft and line losses by better metering and enforcement; improve bill collection and set tariffs that cover costs (with targeted subsidies for the poor only).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: reduce theft/losses; better recovery of bills; cost-reflective tariffs; renegotiate contracts with IPPs; privatise/improve DISCO management; shift to cheaper local fuels/renewables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which Pakistan's energy shortage is caused by a lack of generating capacity rather than by other factors. Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Capacity: demand grew faster than new plants for many years; seasonal fall in hydel output in winter. Other factors: installed capacity now often exceeds demand, but plants stand idle because of circular debt and fuel shortages; expensive imported fuels make electricity costly; transmission bottlenecks prevent power reaching consumers; high losses and theft; inefficient old plants. Judgement on extent.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) developed points on one side; L3 (5–6) developed points on capacity and other factors with a judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how electricity is generated in a thermal power station.
parts.answer: A fuel such as oil, gas or coal is burned to heat water in a boiler; the steam produced turns a turbine; the turbine drives a generator that produces electricity.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fuel burned to heat water/make steam; steam turns turbine; turbine drives generator.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why thermal power stations are often built near large cities such as Karachi or Lahore.
parts.answer: They are close to the market, so less electricity is lost in transmission; coastal or city sites have access to imported fuel by port, pipeline or rail.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: near demand/market; less transmission loss; access to fuel (port, gas pipeline); cooling water from sea/river; workers available.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one environmental problem caused by thermal power stations.
parts.answer: Air pollution from burning fossil fuels (smoke, CO₂, SO₂) causing smog, acid rain and climate change.
parts.working: 1 mark: air pollution/greenhouse gases/acid rain/hot water discharge/ash disposal.

stem:
A country generated electricity from the following sources in one year (illustrative figures, TWh):
Thermal (oil, gas, LNG, coal) 85
Hydel 38
Nuclear 12
Wind and solar 5
Total 140

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the share of thermal power in the total generation. Give your answer as a percentage to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle for thermal power if the data were shown on a pie chart. Give your answer to the nearest degree.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages for Pakistan of depending so heavily on thermal power.
parts.answer: Much of the fuel (oil, LNG and some coal) is imported, so a large thermal share raises the import bill and the trade deficit and makes electricity prices rise when world fuel prices rise. Burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases and pollutants, adding to smog in cities and climate change.
parts.working: Two developed points: imported fuel → import bill/foreign exchange; price volatility → high tariffs/circular debt; pollution/climate change; non-renewable reserves running out; old inefficient plants waste fuel.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the river on which each of these dams is built: (i) Tarbela (ii) Mangla.
parts.answer: (i) Indus (ii) Jhelum
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why hydel power stations in Pakistan produce less electricity in winter than in summer.
parts.answer: In winter there is little rain and the snow and glaciers in the mountains are frozen, so river flow is low. Water stored in the reservoirs is also released mainly for irrigation needs and levels fall towards the end of winter, so less water flows through the turbines.
parts.working: Two developed points: low river flow in winter → less water through turbines; snow/ice melt only in summer; monsoon rain in summer; reservoir levels low/drawn down; irrigation release priorities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of hydel power compared with thermal power.
parts.answer: It uses a renewable resource with no fuel cost, so electricity is cheap once the dam is built; it causes no air pollution.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: renewable; no fuel imports; cheap running costs; no air pollution; dams also store water for irrigation and flood control.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: Pakistan should build more large dams such as Diamer-Bhasha.
View B: Pakistan should build small hydel schemes and other renewables instead of large dams.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: A: large dams give big amounts of cheap electricity and store water for irrigation and flood control, compensate for silting of Tarbela and Mangla. B: large dams are very expensive and take many years, displace people, flood land and heritage sites, silt up, are in earthquake zones and far from demand; small schemes and solar/wind are quicker, cheaper and serve remote communities. Supported judgement.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple; L2 (3–4) developed points one view; L3 (5–6) developed points both views with a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three factors that make it difficult for Pakistan to increase its exports.
parts.answer: High costs of electricity and gas for factories; a narrow range of export goods, mainly textiles; competition from countries such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and China.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: high energy costs/load-shedding; narrow export base; low value addition; competition; quality/standards problems; political instability; poor infrastructure/port delays; tariffs and barriers abroad; low productivity/skills.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how load-shedding affects Pakistan's ability to export.
parts.answer: Power cuts stop factory production, so exporters miss delivery deadlines and foreign buyers may move their orders to more reliable suppliers.
parts.working: 1 mark effect on production + 1 mark consequence for exports (late orders/lost buyers/higher costs → less competitive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'value addition' in trade.
parts.answer: Processing a raw material into a more finished product so it can be sold for a higher price, e.g. turning raw cotton into garments.
parts.working: 1 mark for processing/manufacturing to increase value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan earns more from exporting garments than from exporting the same weight of raw cotton.
parts.answer: Garments have gone through spinning, weaving, dyeing and stitching, so the labour, skill and processing are included in the price. Raw cotton is a primary product sold cheaply and its price changes a lot on world markets, while finished goods sell at higher and more stable prices.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: processing adds value; more labour/skills/jobs included; primary product prices low/volatile; brand/design increases price; idea illustrated with cotton → yarn → cloth → garments.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one Pakistani city famous for exporting sports goods and surgical instruments.
parts.answer: Sialkot
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a fall in the value of the Pakistani rupee against the US dollar affects trade.
parts.answer: Pakistani exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, which may increase demand for goods such as textiles and rice. Imports such as oil and machinery become more expensive in rupees, which raises costs for industry and consumers and can cause inflation.
parts.working: Two developed points: exports cheaper → more competitive; imports dearer → higher import bill/inflation; imported raw materials dearer → exporters' costs rise; debt repayment cost rises.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by GSP+ status.
parts.answer: A European Union scheme that allows a developing country to export many goods to the EU with zero or reduced import duties, in return for following international conventions on human rights, labour rights, the environment and good governance.
parts.working: 1 mark reduced/zero tariffs into EU; 1 mark conditional on implementing international conventions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which GSP+ status has benefited Pakistan's textile industry.
parts.answer: Without import duties, Pakistani textiles and garments are cheaper in EU shops than goods from competitors who pay duties, so EU exports grew. Higher orders led factories to invest in new machinery and employ more workers.
parts.working: Two developed points: tariff-free access → price competitiveness; increased exports to EU (e.g. Germany, Spain, Netherlands); investment and jobs; foreign exchange earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan's exports depend heavily on the cotton crop.
parts.answer: Textiles are Pakistan's largest export, and most of them are made from locally grown cotton, so a good crop supplies mills cheaply. A poor cotton harvest, caused for example by floods, pests or heat, forces mills to import cotton at higher cost or cut production, reducing exports.
parts.working: Two developed points: textiles largest share of exports; local raw material; crop failure → imports/higher costs; cotton yarn and cloth also exported; whole chain (ginning, spinning, weaving) depends on it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other natural events that can reduce Pakistan's exports.
parts.answer: Floods (e.g. the 2022 floods destroying crops such as cotton and rice); droughts or heatwaves reducing crop yields.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: floods; drought; heatwaves; pest attacks (e.g. locusts, pink bollworm); earthquakes damaging infrastructure.

stem: Two countries make the same shirt. Country X sells it for US$10.00 and must pay an import duty of 12% in the buying country. Country Y sells it for US$10.50 but pays no import duty because of a trade agreement (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of import duty paid on one shirt from Country X.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final price in the importing country of a shirt from Country X and from Country Y.
parts.answer: Country X: US$11.20; Country Y: US$10.50

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why trade agreements that remove import duties are important for a country such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Without duty its goods are cheaper than those of competitors who still pay duty, as Country Y shows, so buyers place more orders. This increases export earnings and jobs, and the small profit margins in textiles mean even a few per cent of duty can decide where orders go.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: price competitiveness; more orders/exports; jobs and foreign exchange; small margins in textiles; illustrated with the figures.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which improvements in transport and ports help Pakistan's trade.
parts.answer: Faster clearance and less congestion at Karachi and Port Qasim reduce the time and cost of shipping goods, making exports more competitive. Motorways and dry ports allow goods from inland cities such as Faisalabad and Sialkot to reach ships quickly and reliably.
parts.working: Two developed points: lower transport costs; faster/reliable delivery; dry ports and customs clearance inland; Gwadar/CPEC new routes; transit trade with Afghanistan/Central Asia.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why trade with neighbouring Afghanistan is often lower than expected.
parts.answer: Border closures at crossings such as Torkham and Chaman because of security and political tensions stop trucks from crossing, so trade is interrupted.
parts.working: 1 mark reason + 1 development: border closures; security; political disputes; informal/smuggling trade; Afghan transit trade misuse; payment/banking problems.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a narrow export base is a weakness for Pakistan's economy.
parts.answer: When a country relies on a few products, mainly textiles, rice and leather, a fall in world demand or prices for those goods, or a poor cotton crop, sharply reduces total export earnings. It also means Pakistan competes head-on with many low-wage producers in the same goods, and earnings grow slowly because the goods are mostly low value.
parts.working: 2 developed points: vulnerability to price/demand changes; dependence on one crop (cotton); strong competition in same products; low-value goods → slow growth in earnings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which Pakistan could diversify its exports.
parts.answer: Develop IT and software exports; develop high-value manufactured goods such as engineering goods, pharmaceuticals or processed foods (also: minerals from Reko Diq, fruit and halal meat).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two realistic suggestions.

stem:
A Faisalabad textile exporter's cost of producing 1,000 metres of cloth (illustrative figures):
Year 1: raw materials and labour Rs 250 per metre, energy Rs 150 per metre
Year 2: raw materials and labour Rs 250 per metre, energy Rs 270 per metre

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the exporter's total cost of producing 1,000 metres in each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in total cost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how rising energy costs affect Pakistan's ability to compete in world markets.
parts.answer: Higher production costs force exporters to raise prices or accept lower profits. Competitors such as Bangladesh and Vietnam with cheaper energy can offer lower prices, so foreign buyers switch orders, and some Pakistani mills close or cut workers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: higher cost → higher price or lower profit; competitors cheaper; lost orders; mill closures/unemployment; less investment.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: The most important factor limiting Pakistan's exports is the high cost of energy.
View B: The most important factor limiting Pakistan's exports is the narrow range and low value of the goods exported.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: A: electricity and gas tariffs are high and supply unreliable, so costs rise and orders are lost to competitors; mills close. B: exports concentrated in textiles and rice, mostly low value, vulnerable to price changes and competition; little high-tech or branded output. Reasoned judgement, possibly linking both (energy costs discourage investment in higher-value goods).
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple; L2 (3–4) developed points for one view; L3 (5–6) developed points for both views with conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which political stability is important for increasing Pakistan's foreign trade. Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Important: instability and frequent policy changes discourage foreign investors and buyers, cause strikes and shutdowns that delay shipments, and affect the exchange rate and trade agreements. Other factors also matter: energy costs and supply, quality and standards, skills and technology, infrastructure and ports, world demand, natural disasters such as floods. Judgement on extent.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) developed points on one side; L3 (5–6) developed points on political stability and other factors with judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two quality or standards requirements that exporters of food products, such as mangoes or rice, must meet to sell to Europe.
parts.answer: Produce must be free of pests such as fruit flies (e.g. hot-water treatment of mangoes); pesticide residues must be below set limits (also: proper packaging, labelling, traceability, certified hygiene).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: pest-free/plant health certificate; pesticide residue limits; aflatoxin limits for rice/spices; hygiene/certification; labelling and traceability; cold-chain packaging.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how failing to meet these standards can harm Pakistan's trade.
parts.answer: Shipments may be rejected or the country can be banned from exporting that product, so exporters lose income and buyers turn to other suppliers.
parts.working: 1 mark rejection/ban; 1 mark consequence (lost earnings/reputation/buyers switch).

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'balance of trade'.
parts.answer: The difference between the value of a country's exports of goods and the value of its imports of goods over a period, usually a year.
parts.working: 1 mark difference between exports and imports; 1 mark value of goods/over a period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'trade deficit'.
parts.answer: When the value of imports is greater than the value of exports.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the country that is Pakistan's largest single source of imports.
parts.answer: China
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade
stem:
Illustrative trade figures for a country (US$ billion):
Year 1: exports 28, imports 53
Year 2: exports 31, imports 55

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the balance of trade in each year.
parts.answer: Year 1: −US$25 billion; Year 2: −US$24 billion
parts.working: Year 1: 28 − 53 = −25 (1); Year 2: 31 − 55 = −24 (1). Must show deficit/negative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the balance of trade improved or worsened between Year 1 and Year 2, and give a reason from the data.
parts.answer: Improved slightly: the deficit fell by US$1 billion because exports rose by US$3 billion while imports rose by only US$2 billion.
parts.working: 1 mark improved; 1 mark reason using figures.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two countries that are major buyers of Pakistan's exports.
parts.answer: Any two of: USA, China, UK, Germany, UAE, Netherlands, Afghanistan, Spain, Italy, Belgium.
parts.working: 1 mark each; USA, China and UK most common.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the USA is one of Pakistan's largest export markets.
parts.answer: It is a very large, rich consumer market that buys large quantities of textiles such as bed linen, towels, denim and garments; American retailers buy from Pakistan because its cotton textiles are good value.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: large wealthy market; high demand for textiles/garments; competitive Pakistani prices; long-standing trade links; quotas abolished so more access.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade
stem:
Illustrative values of exports from Pakistan to its top five markets in one year (US$ billion):
USA 5.4
China 2.8
United Kingdom 2.6
Germany 2.2
UAE 2.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total value of exports to the five countries.
parts.answer: US$15.0 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the five-country total that went to the USA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: If total exports were US$30 billion, calculate the percentage that went to countries not in the table.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using the table, describe the pattern of Pakistan's main export markets.
parts.answer: The USA is by far the largest single market (US$5.4 billion, about twice China's US$2.8 billion); two of the five (the UK and Germany) are in Europe, showing the importance of Western markets; China is the main Asian market and the UAE the main market in the Middle East.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2: USA largest/about double the next; two European markets (UK, Germany)/Western markets important; China second; Gulf market (UAE); figures quoted.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Pakistan has had a trade deficit for most years since independence.
parts.answer: Pakistan must import large amounts of oil, LNG and machinery that it cannot produce, and these are expensive. Its exports are mostly low-value goods such as textiles and rice, so earnings do not cover the import bill.
parts.working: Two developed points: fuel imports; machinery/capital goods; edible oil, food and chemicals; narrow/low-value exports; growing population raises consumer demand; weak industrial base.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how money sent home by Pakistanis working abroad helps the country when it has a trade deficit.
parts.answer: Remittances bring in foreign currency (mainly US dollars), which helps pay for imports and reduces pressure on foreign exchange reserves and the current account.
parts.working: 1 mark foreign exchange earnings; 1 mark helps pay for imports/supports reserves/current account.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade
stem:
Illustrative figures for Pakistan's trade with China in one year (US$ billion):
Exports to China: 2.8
Imports from China: 15.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Pakistan's balance of trade with China in this year.
parts.answer: −US$13.0 billion (a deficit)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of imports from China as a multiple of exports to China. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 5.6 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two types of goods that Pakistan imports from China and explain why.
parts.answer: Machinery and electrical equipment (including power and CPEC project equipment); mobile phones, electronics and chemicals. China produces them cheaply and in large quantities, and CPEC projects use Chinese equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark for two goods (machinery, electronics/phones, chemicals, iron and steel, synthetic yarn); 1 mark reason (cheap/large-scale producer; CPEC equipment; FTA lowers duties).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one export that Pakistan sells to China.
parts.answer: Cotton yarn (also accept copper, rice, sesame seeds, seafood, chromite).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan imports large amounts of goods from Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar.
parts.answer: These countries are major producers of crude oil, petroleum products and LNG, which Pakistan needs for transport, industry and electricity but produces too little of. They are close by, so shipping costs are low, and Saudi Arabia has sometimes supplied oil on deferred payment, which helps Pakistan's reserves.
parts.working: Two developed points: oil/LNG producers; Pakistan's energy shortage; short sea distance; deferred payment/friendly relations; re-exports through Dubai.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one product that Pakistan exports to Gulf countries.
parts.answer: Rice (also accept fruit and vegetables, meat, textiles, cement).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade
stem:
Illustrative trade figures for a country (US$ billion):
Year 1: exports 30, imports 55
Year 2: exports 31, imports 50
Year 3: exports 32, imports 46

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in exports from Year 1 to Year 3. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 6.7% increase

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in imports from Year 1 to Year 3. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 16.4% decrease

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the export/import ratio (exports ÷ imports × 100) for Year 3 to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why a government might deliberately reduce imports, and one disadvantage of doing so.
parts.answer: Reasons: to reduce the trade deficit; to protect foreign exchange reserves and the value of the rupee (e.g. by raising import duties or restricting luxury imports). Disadvantage: industries that need imported raw materials and machinery may slow down, reducing output, exports and jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two reasons (reduce deficit; protect reserves/currency; protect local industry; meet IMF conditions); 1 mark for disadvantage (shortage of inputs; slower growth; inflation; retaliation).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the balance of trade and the balance of payments.
parts.answer: The balance of trade compares only the value of exports and imports of goods. The balance of payments records all money flows between a country and the rest of the world, including services, remittances, interest, loans and investment, so a country with a trade deficit may have a smaller current account deficit if remittances are large.
parts.working: 1 mark trade = goods only; 1 mark payments = all transactions (services, remittances, capital/investment, loans); 1 mark example/link to remittances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two problems for Pakistan of a large and persistent trade deficit.
parts.answer: Foreign exchange reserves fall, so the country must borrow from abroad (e.g. the IMF) and debt rises; the rupee loses value, raising the price of imports and causing inflation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: falling reserves; borrowing/debt; currency depreciation; inflation; IMF conditions/austerity; slower growth.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Read the two views:
View A: Pakistan should focus on trade with neighbouring countries such as China, Afghanistan, Iran and the Central Asian republics.
View B: Pakistan should focus on trade with distant markets such as the USA and the European Union.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer, referring to both views.
parts.answer: A: shorter distances and lower transport costs; CPEC road links to China; Afghanistan and Central Asia are landlocked and can use Pakistani ports and buy Pakistani food and goods; regional agreements. B: USA and EU are rich, large markets that pay higher prices for textiles; GSP+ gives duty-free access to the EU; neighbours' trade often disrupted by border closures, insecurity and political tensions. Reasoned judgement.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple statements; L2 (3–4) developed points for one view; L3 (5–6) developed points for both with a supported conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade
stem:
Illustrative trade figures for a country (US$ billion):
Year 1: exports 24, imports 40
Year 2: exports 26, imports 47
Year 3: exports 28, imports 55
Year 4: exports 31, imports 62

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: Imports rose every year, from US$40 billion to US$62 billion (an increase of US$22 billion); exports rose more slowly, from US$24 billion to US$31 billion; so the trade deficit widened from US$16 billion to US$31 billion.
parts.working: 1 mark imports rising with figures; 1 mark exports rising more slowly with figures; 1 mark deficit widening with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the trade deficit in Year 4 as a percentage of imports in Year 4. Give your answer to one decimal place.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which Pakistan can reduce its trade deficit by increasing exports rather than by reducing imports. Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Increasing exports: value addition in textiles, IT exports, new markets, use of GSP+ and FTAs, minerals and food exports; but limited by energy costs, competition, narrow base and slow change. Reducing imports: develop local energy (Thar coal, hydel, solar) to cut fuel imports, grow more edible oil seeds, import substitution, duties on luxuries; but many imports (machinery, raw materials) are needed for growth and exports. Judgement on extent, recognising both are needed.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) developed points on one approach; L3 (5–6) developed points on both approaches with judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two of Pakistan's main exports.
parts.answer: Any two of: cotton textiles (yarn, cloth, bed linen, towels, garments/knitwear), rice, leather goods, sports goods, surgical instruments, fruit, fish, cement.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two of Pakistan's main imports.
parts.answer: Any two of: petroleum and petroleum products, LNG, machinery, edible (palm) oil, chemicals, iron and steel, vehicles, tea, mobile phones.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why Pakistan imports large amounts of palm oil and from which region most of it comes.
parts.answer: Pakistan does not grow enough oilseeds to meet demand for cooking oil and ghee; most palm oil comes from Indonesia and Malaysia in South-East Asia.
parts.working: 1 mark reason (domestic oilseed production too low/high demand for cooking oil); 1 mark Indonesia/Malaysia/South-East Asia.

stem:
Illustrative values of a country's exports in one year (US$ billion):
Textiles 18.0
Rice 3.6
Leather and sports goods 1.8
Other goods 6.6
Total 30.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle that textiles would take on a pie chart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of exports made up of rice.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angles for the other three categories.
parts.answer: Rice 43.2°, leather and sports goods 21.6°, other goods 79.2°
parts.working: Rice 3.6 → 43.2°; leather/sports 1.8 → 21.6°; other 6.6 → 79.2° (2 marks all three; 1 mark for two).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rice is an important export for Pakistan.
parts.answer: Pakistan grows large amounts of rice, especially high-quality basmati in the Punjab (e.g. around Gujranwala and Sialkot), which sells at high prices in the Gulf, Europe and elsewhere. Rice exports earn foreign exchange and support the incomes of farmers, mill workers and traders.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: large production/surplus; basmati quality and premium price; markets (Gulf, EU, China, Africa); foreign exchange; employment in farming and milling; second-largest export group after textiles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the value of rice exports may fall in some years.
parts.answer: Floods or water shortages reduce the harvest; competition from India and other producers lowers prices or takes markets.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: floods/drought/water shortage; competition (India, Vietnam, Thailand); quality/pesticide rejections; fall in world prices; export bans to control local prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why petroleum products and LNG form the largest group of Pakistan's imports.
parts.answer: Pakistan's own oil and gas production is small and gas reserves are declining, so it must buy fuel abroad. Demand is very high because transport, industry and thermal power stations all depend on oil and gas, so the import bill is large, especially when world prices are high.
parts.working: Two developed points: limited domestic reserves/declining gas; demand from transport, industry, power; thermal-dominated electricity; rising vehicle numbers; high world prices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which Pakistan could reduce its fuel imports.
parts.answer: Generate more electricity from local and renewable sources such as hydel, solar, wind and Thar coal; improve public transport and energy efficiency to reduce fuel use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: renewables/hydel; Thar coal; more exploration; public transport (metro buses, ML-1 railway); electric vehicles; energy efficiency; reduce losses.

stem:
Illustrative export figures for a country:
Year 1: total exports US$26 billion, of which 70% were manufactured goods
Year 2: total exports US$32 billion, of which 75% were manufactured goods

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of manufactured goods exported in Year 1 and in Year 2.
parts.answer: Year 1: US$18.2 billion; Year 2: US$24.0 billion

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the value of manufactured exports. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an increase in the share of manufactured goods in exports is good for a country's economy.
parts.answer: Manufactured goods have value added, so they earn more per unit than raw materials; their prices are more stable than primary products; making them creates industrial jobs and develops skills and technology.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: value addition/higher earnings; price stability; employment; industrial growth/skills; less dependence on weather/crops.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which Pakistan's exports are still dominated by agricultural products and goods made from them. Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: Dominated: textiles are based on locally grown cotton; rice, fruit (mangoes, kinnow), vegetables, fish and meat; leather from livestock; so weather and crops strongly affect exports. Less dominated: growing exports of IT and software services, surgical instruments and sports goods (Sialkot), cement, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, engineering goods; textiles now often use imported cotton and synthetic fibres, and garments are manufactured products with value added. Judgement on extent.
parts.working: Levels: L1 (1–2) simple points; L2 (3–4) developed points on one side; L3 (5–6) developed points on both sides with a judgement.
